parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The reaction

A + 2B + 2C → D + 2E

was studied. The following initial rates data were collected at 298 K in Table 4.1.

**Table 4.1**

| experiment | [A] / mol dm^-3^ | [B] / mol dm^-3^ | [C] /  mol dm^-3^ | initial rate / mol dm^-3 ^s^-1^ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 1 | 0.040 | 0.120 | 0.050 | 1.20 x 10^-5^ |
| 2 | 0.060 | 0.120 | 0.050 | 1.80 x 10^-5^ |
| 3 | 0.040 | 0.060 | 0.050 | 3.00 x 10^-6^ |
| 4 | 0.080 | 0.060 | 0.150 | 6.00 x 10^-6^ |

(i) Construct the rate equation for the reaction.

rate = k[A][B]^2

Suggest a two-step mechanism for this reaction where the first step is the rate-determining step.
parts.solutionMd:
To suggest a two-step mechanism:

- The rate equation is:

Rate = *k*[A][B]<sup>2 </sup>

- This means the rate-determining (slow) step must involve 1 A and 2 B, and it must not involve C (because C is zero order)
- So, the slow (rate-determining) step is:

A + 2B → Intermediate **[1 mark]**

- Then, use a fast step to react the intermediate with C and form the products, so that the two steps add up to the overall reaction
- So, the fast step is:

Intermediate + 2C → D + 2E **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a slow step that matches the rate equation stoichiometry (contains A once and B twice, and no C)
> 
> 1 mark for a fast step thatproduces products and the two steps add to the overall equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Build the **slow step from the rate equation**, not from the overall equation.
> 
> Any reactant with **zero order** (here, C) should not appear in the slow step, but it can appear in a fast step.
> 
> Finally, check that adding the two steps together gives the overall reaction and that the intermediate cancels.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction between I<sup>−</sup> and S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup> is slow due to high activation energy.

S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>−</sup> ⇌ 2SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> (aq)   *E*<sup>θ</sup>=+2.01 V

Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>−</sup>⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)  *E*<sup>θ</sup>=+0.77 V

I<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2e<sup>−</sup> ⇌ 2I<sup>−</sup> (aq)  *E*<sup>θ</sup>=+0.54 V

Explain, using the *E*<sup>θ </sup>values provided, why Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions are an effective catalyst for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions are an effective catalyst because the direct reaction between two negative ions (I<sup>-</sup> and S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2-</sup>) is split into two feasible redox steps involving Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe<sup>3+</sup>:

- Fe<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised by S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>:

*E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ </sup>=* E*<sup>θ </sup>(S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>/SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>) − *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>)

*E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ </sup>= +2.01 − 0.77 = +1.24 V

So this step is feasible because *E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ</sup> is positive **[1 mark]**

- Fe<sup>3+</sup> oxidises I<sup>−</sup>:

*E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ </sup>= *E*<sup>θ</sup>(Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup>) - *E*<sup>θ</sup>(I<sub>2</sub>/I<sup>-</sup>)

*E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ </sup>= +0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V

So this step is feasible because *E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ</sup> is positive **[1 mark]**

- Therefore, Fe<sup>2+</sup> provides an alternative pathway made of two energetically feasible steps, which lowers the activation energy by avoiding repulsion between two negative ions (I− and S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2−</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating *E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ</sup> for Fe<sup>2+ </sup>reducing S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2− </sup>as +2.01 - 0.77 V = +1.24 V and stating this is feasible
> 
> 1 mark for calculating *E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ</sup> for Fe<sup>3+ </sup>reducing I- as 0.77 - 0.54 = +0.23 V and stating this is feasible
> 
> 1 mark for stating that Fe<sup>2+</sup>/Fe<sup>3+</sup> provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy by avoiding repulsion between two negative ions

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not stop after calculating *E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ</sup>.
> 
> You must state what the sign means: a **positive ***E*<sub>cell</sub><sup>θ</sup> shows each step is **feasible**.
> 
> Then link this to catalysis by explaining that Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> split one difficult redox change into two easier steps, lowering activation energy rather than changing the overall cell potential.

parts.problemMd:
Iron acts as a catalyst in the Haber process.

Complete the diagram to show the electron configuration of an atom of  ${}_{56}^{26}\mathrm{Fe}$.

![Blank electron box diagram for completing the electron configuration of an iron atom](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/26-reaction-kinetics/26-2-homogeneous-and-heterogeneous-catalysts/assets/001-blank-electron-box-diagram-for-completing-the-el.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed electron configuration of  ${}_{56}^{26}\mathrm{Fe}$ is:

![Electron box diagram showing the complete electron configuration of iron with argon core, 4s2 and 3d6 subshells filled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/26-reaction-kinetics/26-2-homogeneous-and-heterogeneous-catalysts/assets/002-electron-box-diagram-showing-the-complete-electr.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct electron box notation for Fe

> **[exam-tip]**
> Iron has an argon core ([Ar]) with 8 additional electrons arranged as 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>6</sup>. Note that the 3d subshell is not completely filled (it can hold up to 10 electrons), so the correct configuration is [Ar] 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>6</sup>, not [Ar] 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>8</sup>.

parts.problemMd: State and explain whether the iron used in the Haber process acts as a homogeneous or heterogeneous catalyst.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iron acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Haber process:
> 
> - Heterogeneous **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) the iron catalyst is in a different state / phase to the reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the Haber process, the reactants nitrogen and hydrogen are gases, while the iron catalyst is a solid. Since the catalyst and reactants are in different states, iron acts as a heterogeneous catalyst.
> 
> You need to include both the identification (heterogeneous) and the explanation (different state or phase to the reactants) to score both marks.

parts.problemMd: Describe the mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst in a chemical reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst in a chemical reaction is:
> 
> - Reactants adsorb onto the surface of the catalyst **[1 mark]**
> - The bonds in the reactants weaken **[1 mark]**
> - Products are desorbed from the surface of the catalyst **[1 mark]**
> 
> For the first marking point, the keyword that must be seen is adsorb (not absorb)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three key steps for heterogeneous catalysis are adsorption, bond weakening (allowing the reaction to occur), and desorption. Examiners are looking for these three specific terms.
> 
> Note that the catalyst itself is not consumed. It is regenerated when the products desorb, which is why it is classified as a catalyst.

parts.problemMd: Define the term *homogeneous catalysis*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Homogeneous catalysis is:
> 
> - Where the catalyst is in the same phase / state as the reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You need to know the definitions for both homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysis. The key distinction is whether the catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants (homogeneous) or a different phase (heterogeneous).

parts.problemMd: Describe the mode of action of a homogeneous catalyst.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mode of action of a homogeneous catalyst is:
> 
> - The catalyst reacts with a reactant to form an intermediate (complex) **[1 mark]**
> - The intermediate provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy **[1 mark]**
> - The intermediate reacts to form the products
> **AND**
> the catalyst is regenerated **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three key points for homogeneous catalysis are:
> 
> 1. Formation of an intermediate (between the catalyst and a reactant)
> 2. An alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
> 3. Products form and the catalyst is regenerated
> 
> The mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst (adsorption, bond weakening, desorption) is more commonly tested, but you should know both.

parts.problemMd: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using a homogeneous catalyst rather than a heterogeneous catalyst in an industrial process.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One advantage and one disadvantage of using a homogeneous catalyst rather than a heterogeneous catalyst are:
> 
> Advantage:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - High selectivity / fewer unwanted side reactions
> - Can operate at lower temperatures / pressures, reducing energy consumption
> - Easier to control
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Disadvantage:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Separation / purification of the products is challenging / expensive / time-consuming
> - The catalyst can become poisoned
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although this type of question is less common in exam papers, you should know at least one advantage and one disadvantage of both homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts.

parts.problemMd:
Larger hydrocarbon molecules are cracked into smaller alkanes and alkenes by passing their vapours over a heated catalyst.

Identify a suitable catalyst for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A suitable catalyst for catalytic cracking is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Aluminium oxide / alumina / Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
> - Aluminosilicates
> - Zeolite
> - (Hot) pumice stone
> - Porous / ceramic pot
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common answers are aluminium oxide (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) and zeolite. Although cracking is covered in an earlier section of the specification, questions on the catalysts used can appear in the context of this topic on catalysis.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Larger hydrocarbon molecules are cracked into smaller alkanes and alkenes by passing their vapours over a heated catalyst.

State and explain whether this process is an example of homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysis.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Catalytic cracking is an example of heterogeneous catalysis:
> 
> - Heterogeneous **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) the catalyst is in a different state / phase to the reactants **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The catalyst (aluminium oxide, zeolite, etc.) is a solid, while the hydrocarbon reactants are passed over it as vapours in the gaseous phase. Since the catalyst and reactants are in different states, this is an example of heterogeneous catalysis.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Larger hydrocarbon molecules are cracked into smaller alkanes and alkenes by passing their vapours over a heated catalyst.

Explain why using a powdered solid catalyst increases the rate of this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using a powdered solid catalyst increases the rate of the reaction because:
> 
> - It has a greater surface area **[1 mark]**
> - There are more active sites available (for adsorption of reactant molecules) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question combines collision theory with the mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst. A powdered solid has a much greater surface area than a solid block or pellet of the same material. The greater surface area means more active sites are available for reactant molecules to adsorb onto, increasing the rate of the reaction.

name: Similarities & Trends in the Properties of the Group 2 Metals, Magnesium to Barium, & Their Compounds

parts.problemMd:
i) State the formula of magnesium carbonate.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction of magnesium carbonate with dilute nitric acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of magnesium carbonate is:
> 
> - MgCO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An equation for the reaction of magnesium carbonate with dilute nitric acid:
> 
> - MgCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> → Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The general pattern for a metal carbonate reacting with an acid is:
> 
> metal carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide + water
> 
> You need to be able to deduce the formulae for each substance. The salt formed from magnesium and nitric acid is magnesium nitrate, Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Carbon dioxide and water are always produced in acid-carbonate reactions.

parts.problemMd:
i) Identify the compound that will decompose at the lowest temperature.

- calcium carbonate
- strontium carbonate
- barium carbonate

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the thermal decomposition of the carbonate identified in (b)(i). Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The compound that decomposes at the lowest temperature is:
> 
> - Calcium carbonate **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate:
> 
> - CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow error carried forward from (i): if a different carbonate is identified in (i), award the mark for the corresponding correctly balanced decomposition equation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Calcium carbonate decomposes at the lowest temperature because Ca<sup>2+</sup> has the smallest ionic radius of the Group 2 ions listed, giving it the greatest charge density and polarising power.
> 
> The trend in thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group: CaCO<sub>3</sub> decomposes at the lowest temperature, BaCO<sub>3</sub> at the highest.

parts.problemMd: Explain why calcium nitrate decomposes at a lower temperature than barium nitrate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Calcium nitrate decomposes at a lower temperature than barium nitrate because:
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius than Ba<sup>2+</sup> / Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a greater charge density **[1 mark]**
> - (therefore) Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a greater polarising power / greater ability to distort the electron cloud of the nitrate ion **[1 mark]**
> - (therefore) the N-O bonds in the nitrate ion are weakened to a greater extent, so a lower temperature is required for decomposition **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a 3-mark explain question that follows a three-step reasoning chain:
> 
> - ionic radius (or charge density)
> - → polarising power
> - → bond weakening.
> 
> The first mark is for stating that Ca<sup>2+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius or greater charge density than Ba<sup>2+</sup>. The second mark is for the consequence: greater polarising power. The third mark is for linking this to the weakening of the N-O bonds in the nitrate ion, which lowers the decomposition temperature.
> 
> A common mistake is to write only "Ca<sup>2+</sup> is smaller" without explaining the consequences for polarisation and bond strength.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Group 2 compounds.

Strontium reacts with water.

i) Construct a balanced equation for the reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Describe a test to identify the gas produced.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction is:

Sr (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct balanced equation: Sr + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (s), (l), (aq), (g)
> 
> '(s)' for Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> is not accepted

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) A test to identify the gas produced:
> 
> - Apply a lighted splint to the gas
> **AND**
> A squeaky pop is heard / the gas ignites with a squeaky pop **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both the test and the observation must be stated to score the mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to give (s) for Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>, but strontium hydroxide dissolves in water, so the correct state symbol is (aq).
> 
> For part ii), both the test (applying a lighted splint) and the observation (squeaky pop) must be given to score the mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about Group 2 compounds.

Calcium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid to produce calcium sulfate and water.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) State the trend in the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction is:

Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct balanced equation: Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → CaSO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (aq), (aq), (s), (l)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The trend in the solubility of the Group 2 sulfates going down Group 2:
> 
> - The solubility of the Group 2 sulfates decreases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The general equation for this type of reaction is:
> 
> metal hydroxide + acid → salt + water.
> 
> The solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases going down the group, but the solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases. These trends are opposite and a common source of confusion.

parts.problemMd:
The trend in solubility of the Group 2 sulfates is due to the lattice energy, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub>, and enthalpy change of hydration, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub>, of the Group 2 sulfates changing.

State the trend in Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub> and Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> of Group 2 sulfates going down Group 2.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub> and Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> of Group 2 sulfates going down Group 2:
> 
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub> decreases (becomes less negative) **[1 mark]**
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> decreases (becomes less negative) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub> and Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> decrease going down Group 2, but by different amounts:
> 
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub> decreases by a relatively small amount
> - Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*hyd*</sub> decreases by a relatively large amount, because ionic radius increases down the group
> 
> As a result, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> becomes more endothermic going down the group, and solubility decreases.

parts.problemMd:
The elements in Group 2 from Mg to Ba can be used to show the trends in properties down a group in the Periodic Table.

The Group 2 elements react with water.

i) State the trend in reactivity with water of the elements down Group 2 from Mg to Ba.

[1]

ii) Predict a possible pH for the solutions formed when Group 2 elements are added to water.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The trend in reactivity with water of the elements down Group 2 from Mg to Ba:
> 
> - Reactivity increases (going down Group 2) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) A possible pH for the solutions formed when Group 2 elements are added to water:
> 
> - Any value from 10 to 12 inclusive **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 2 elements react more vigorously with water further down the group. Note that beryllium does not react with water, and magnesium only reacts with steam, not liquid water.
> 
> A metal hydroxide is formed, which releases OH<sup>-</sup> ions into solution, making it alkaline. Group 2 hydroxide solutions typically have a pH in the range of 10–12.

parts.problemMd: State the **formula** of the hydroxide of the element in Group 2 from Mg to Ba that is most soluble in water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The formula of the most soluble Group 2 hydroxide:
> 
> - Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases going down the group. Barium hydroxide is the most soluble, while magnesium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble.

parts.problemMd:
A trend in the thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates can also be observed.

i) State the oxidation number of nitrogen in Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for the thermal decomposition of Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. Include state symbols.

[2]

iii) State the trend in thermal stability of Group 2 nitrates.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The oxidation number of nitrogen in Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - +5 **[1 mark]**

ii) The equation for the thermal decomposition of Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is:

2Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2CaO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly balanced equation: 2Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2CaO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (s), (s), (g), (g)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The trend in thermal stability of Group 2 nitrates going down Group 2:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases / become more thermally stable **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation state of nitrogen in Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>: calcium is +2 and each oxygen is -2. With two NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> groups giving -12, and calcium giving +2, the two nitrogen atoms must contribute +10, so each nitrogen is +5.
> 
> Group 2 nitrates thermally decompose to give a metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide (toxic brown gas) and oxygen.
> 
> The thermal stability of Group 2 nitrates increases down the group because the cation size increases, reducing its polarising power over the nitrate ion. The less the nitrate ion is polarised, the more energy is required to decompose the compound.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Group 2 nitrates.

Strontium nitrate is a Group 2 nitrate used to produce a colour in fireworks.

i) State the formula of strontium nitrate.

[1]

ii) State the colour that strontium nitrate produces in fireworks.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of strontium nitrate:
> 
> - Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The colour that strontium nitrate produces in fireworks:
> 
> - Red / scarlet / crimson **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Brick red' is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 2 flame colours to know:
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> gives brick red
> - Sr<sup>2+</sup> gives crimson/red
> - Ba<sup>2+</sup> gives pale green
> 
> Note that lilac flames are associated with potassium (Group 1), not Group 2.
> 
> For strontium nitrate, two nitrate ions (NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) are needed per Sr<sup>2+</sup> ion to give overall neutrality, so the formula is Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about Group 2 nitrates.

Strontium nitrate is a Group 2 nitrate used to produce a colour in fireworks.

The formula of strontium nitrate: Sr(NO~3~)~2~

i) Construct an equation for the reaction that occurs when strontium nitrate is heated. Include state symbols.

[2]

ii) Give **one** observation of this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the reaction when strontium nitrate is heated:

2Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2SrO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly balanced equation: 2Sr(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2SrO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (s), (s), (g), (g)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) One observation of this reaction:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Brown fumes / brown gas (NO<sub>2</sub>)
> - White solid / white residue forms (SrO)
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates follows the general pattern:
> 
> metal nitrate → metal oxide + nitrogen dioxide + oxygen.
> 
> The nitrogen dioxide appears as brown fumes, and the metal oxide forms as a white solid.

parts.problemMd:
The nitrate ion, NO<sub>3</sub> , contains a dative covalent bond.

Complete the following ‘dot-and-cross’ diagram of the bonding in the nitrate ion.

Use the following code for your electrons:

•  electrons from oxygen

x electrons from nitrogen

□ added electron(s) responsible for the overall negative charge

![Incomplete dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrate ion, showing the central nitrogen atom bonded to three oxygen atoms with electron shells partially filled](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/27-group-2/27-1-similarities-and-trends-in-the-properties-of-the-group-2-metals-magnesium-to-barium-and-their-compounds/assets/001-incomplete-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrate-.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The completed dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrate ion is:

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrate ion, showing a dative covalent bond to one oxygen with both electrons marked ×, all three atoms with a full octet, and one □ electron representing the overall 1− charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/27-group-2/27-1-similarities-and-trends-in-the-properties-of-the-group-2-metals-magnesium-to-barium-and-their-compounds/assets/002-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrate-i.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a dative covalent bond shown to one oxygen atom, with both electrons from nitrogen (marked ×)
> 
> 1 mark for 8 electrons around the nitrogen atom, arranged as 1 double bond and 2 single bonds
> 
> 1 mark for a total of 24 electrons shown, including exactly one □ electron representing the negative charge

> **[exam-tip]**
> The negative charge on the nitrate ion means one extra electron has been added, which must be shown using the □ symbol (not a dot or cross) to score the third mark.
> 
> A dative covalent bond is formed when both electrons come from the same atom. Both electrons in the dative bond must be shown as × (nitrogen electrons) to score the first mark.
> 
> Each atom in the completed diagram should have 8 electrons around it (a full octet).

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain the trend in thermal stabilities of the nitrates of the Group 2 elements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in thermal stabilities of Group 2 nitrates:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - The ionic radius / size of the Group 2 cation increases
> **OR**
> The charge density of the Group 2 cation decreases **[1 mark]**
> - (So) polarisation / distortion of the nitrate ion decreases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This trend and explanation apply equally to Group 2 carbonates and nitrates.
> 
> As the Group 2 cation increases in size going down the group, its polarising power over the nitrate ion decreases. A less polarised nitrate ion requires more energy to decompose, so thermal stability increases.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium is a Group 2 metal.

Construct an equation, including state symbols, for the reaction between:

i) magnesium and steam

[1]

ii) magnesium and sulfuric acid

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction between magnesium and steam:
> 
> - Mg (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → MgO (s) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between magnesium and sulfuric acid:
> 
> - Mg (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → MgSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be correct in both equations to score the marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> Magnesium reacts with steam (H<sub>2</sub>O (g)) to form magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas. With dilute acids, the general equation is:
> 
> metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
> 
> Group 2 elements are expected to react with oxygen, water/steam, dilute HCl, and dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium sulfate is soluble in water.

Describe and explain how the solubilities of the sulfates of the Group 2 elements vary down the group.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in solubility of Group 2 sulfates going down the group:
> 
> - Solubility decreases / the sulfates become less soluble **[1 mark]**
> - Both lattice energy and enthalpy of hydration decrease / become less negative **[1 mark]**
> - The enthalpy of hydration decreases by more than the lattice energy / the decrease in hydration enthalpy is greater than the decrease in lattice energy **[1 mark]**
> - So Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> becomes more endothermic / more positive going down the group **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> can be positive (endothermic) or negative (exothermic), a compound is more likely to be soluble when Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> is negative or has a small positive value. As Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> becomes more positive going down the group, solubility decreases.
> 
> Note that the trend for Group 2 hydroxides is the opposite: hydroxide solubility increases going down the group because the lattice energy decreases by more than the hydration enthalpy.

parts.problemMd:
The following table lists some enthalpy changes for magnesium and strontium compounds | **Enthalpy change ** | **Value for magnesium **

**/ kJ mol****-1** | **Value for strontium**

**/ kJ mol****-1** | |---|---|---| | lattice enthalpy of **M**(OH)2 | -2993 | -2467 | | enthalpy change of hydration of **M**2+(g) | -1890 | -1414 | | enthalpy change of hydration of OH–(g) | -550 | -550 | Use the above data to calculate values of Δ*H*θsol for Mg(OH)2 and for Sr(OH)2. Mg(OH)2 ..................................... kJ mol-1 Sr(OH)2. .................................... kJ mol-1
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> for each compound:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>(total) − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>

- For Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = [(−1890) + 2(−550)] − (−2993)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = −2990 − (−2993)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = **+3 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- For Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = [(−1414) + 2(−550)] − (−2467)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = −2514 − (−2467)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = **-47 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>(Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>) = +3 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>; allow ±1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>(Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>) = −47 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>; allow ±1 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> In both cases, the hydration enthalpy of OH<sup>-</sup> must be multiplied by 2 as there are two hydroxide ions in M(OH)<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula for enthalpy change of solution:
> 
> Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = sum of all Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> values − Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>
> 
> Remember to multiply the hydration enthalpy of OH<sup>-</sup> by 2 as there are two OH<sup>-</sup> ions in each formula unit of M(OH)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Group 2 carbonates.

Group 2 carbonates can react with acids.

i) State the difference between the reactions of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid and with sulfuric acid, and explain this difference.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction between calcium carbonate and sulfuric acid. Include state symbols.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The difference between the reactions of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid and with sulfuric acid:
> 
> - Calcium carbonate forms a soluble salt (CaCl<sub>2</sub>) with hydrochloric acid but forms an insoluble salt (CaSO<sub>4</sub>) with sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> - CaSO<sub>4</sub> is insoluble / Group 2 sulfates are insoluble, so the insoluble layer coats the surface of the carbonate and prevents further reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the reaction between calcium carbonate and sulfuric acid:
> 
> - CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> All state symbols must be correct to score the mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> All Group 2 metal carbonates react with acids to give:
> 
> metal carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide
> 
> The key difference is the solubility of the salt formed. Group 2 chlorides are all soluble, but calcium sulfate is insoluble, forming a protective coating that halts the reaction.
> 
> A common error is to write 2H<sub>2</sub>O in the equation for this reaction, when the equation contains 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain the trend observed in the thermal stability of the carbonates of the Group 2 elements.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - The ionic radius / size of the Group 2 cation increases
> **OR**
> The charge density of the Group 2 cation decreases **[1 mark]**
> - (So) polarisation / distortion of the carbonate ion (CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>) decreases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This explanation applies equally to Group 2 nitrates. As the cation increases in size going down the group, its polarising power over the carbonate ion decreases. Less polarisation means the C-O bond is harder to weaken, so more energy is required to decompose the compound and thermal stability increases.

parts.problemMd:
Zinc is found in d block of the Periodic table but is not a transition element.

i) Explain why zinc is not classed as a transition element.

[1]

ii) Describe three characteristic chemical properties of transition elements that are not shown by Group 2 elements.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Why zinc is not classed as a transition element:
> 
> - It forms an ion (Zn<sup>2+</sup>) with a complete 3d subshell
> **OR**
> Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a full / complete 3d<sup>10</sup> configuration **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Characteristic chemical properties of transition elements not shown by Group 2 elements:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Form coloured ions / coloured compounds
> - Show variable oxidation states
> - Form complex ions / complexes
> - Act as catalysts / show catalytic behaviour
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A transition element is defined as an element that can form at least one stable ion with an incomplete d-subshell. Zinc forms only Zn<sup>2+</sup>, which has the configuration [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup>, where the 3d subshell is complete in the ion, so zinc does not meet the definition.
> 
> The characteristic properties of transition elements arise from their partially filled d-subshells:
> 
> - Coloured ions (d-d electron transitions absorb visible light)
> - Variable oxidation states (d electrons at similar energies)
> - Complex ion formation
> - Catalytic activity

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Group 2 hydroxides.

Samples of magnesium, calcium, strontium and barium are reacted with water to form their hydroxides. The resulting solutions are then filtered to collect the precipitates.

Explain the trend in the expected mass for the precipitates.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in expected mass for the precipitates:
> 
> - Magnesium hydroxide produces the greatest mass of precipitate, with mass decreasing going down the group
> **OR**
> Barium hydroxide produces the least mass of precipitate, with mass increasing going up the group **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) the solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases going down the group **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key insight is that more soluble hydroxides will produce less precipitate after filtering. Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble so a large amount precipitates; barium hydroxide is very soluble so little or no precipitate forms. The trend in the precipitate mass directly reflects the inverse of the solubility trend.

A student determined that a 50 cm<sup>3</sup> solution of an unknown Group 2 metal hydroxide contained 802 mg of the metal hydroxide.

Identify the metal hydroxide in the unknown sample.
parts.solutionMd:
To identify the metal hydroxide, convert the given data to g dm<sup>-3</sup>:

- Convert mass from mg to g:

$\frac{802}{1000}$ = 0.802 g in 50 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Scale from 50 cm<sup>3</sup> to 1 dm<sup>3</sup>:

0.802 x 20 = 16.04 g dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Compare the value with the data in Table 4.1:

closest value is strontium hydroxide (17.70 g dm<sup>-3</sup>)

- The unknown metal hydroxide is **strontium hydroxide** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the solubility of the unknown Group 2 metal hydroxide: 16.04 g dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark identifying the unknown Group 2 metal hydroxide as strontium hydroxide
> 
> Allow error carried forward from the calculation to the identification, e.g. accept the identification that corresponds to the closest table value if the conversion step is incorrect

> **[exam-tip]**
> The table is in g dm<sup>-3</sup> but the data given is in mg and cm<sup>3</sup>. Two conversions are needed:
>

> - Then multiply by (1000 ÷ 50) = 20 to scale from 50 cm<sup>3</sup> to 1 dm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> The result will not exactly match a table value, so you should choose the closest.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction between magnesium hydroxide and sulfuric acid. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced equation for the reaction between magnesium hydroxide and sulfuric acid is:

Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → MgSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly balanced equation: Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for all four correct state symbols: (s), (aq), (aq), (l)
> 
> '(aq)' for Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble in water, so it is treated as a solid (s) in equations, not aqueous.
> 
> Magnesium sulfate (MgSO<sub>4</sub>) is soluble. Group 2 sulfate solubility decreases going down the group but MgSO<sub>4</sub> at the top of the group is soluble, so (aq) is correct.

parts.problemMd:
The solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases going down the group because the enthalpy of solution, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>, gets more exothermic.

i) Define the term enthalpy of solution, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>.

[2]

ii) Explain why going down Group 2 the enthalpy of solution, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>, gets more exothermic.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The definition of enthalpy of solution, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub>:
> 
> - The enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic solid **[1 mark]**
> - dissolves to form a dilute solution under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Why Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> becomes more exothermic going down Group 2:
> 
> - The enthalpy change of hydration (of M<sup>2+</sup>) decreases / becomes less negative going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - The lattice energy decreases / becomes less negative going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - The decrease in lattice energy is greater than / outweighs the decrease in enthalpy of hydration **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For Group 2 hydroxides, the lattice energy decreases faster than the hydration enthalpy going down the group. This is because OH<sup>-</sup> is a small, compact anion, so the lattice is particularly sensitive to cation size. The net effect is that less energy is needed to break the lattice than is lost in hydration, so Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> becomes more negative (more exothermic) and solubility increases.
> 
> This is the opposite trend to Group 2 sulfates and carbonates: for larger anions, the hydration enthalpy decreases faster than the lattice energy, making Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> less exothermic going down the group.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about magnesium.

Magnesium forms a nitrate, Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, which decomposes on heating as shown below:

2Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2MgO (s) + 4NO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g)

Using oxidation states, explain why the reaction involves both oxidation and reduction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using oxidation states to explain both oxidation and reduction:
> 
> - The oxidation state of nitrogen (N) changes from +5 (in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) to +4 (in NO<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - The oxidation state of oxygen (O) changes from -2 (in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) to 0 (in O<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Nitrogen is reduced
> **AND**
> Oxygen is oxidised **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When using oxidation states to explain redox, you must quote the actual values. Stating that an element has 'lost' or 'gained' electrons without citing oxidation state changes will not score marks.
> 
> Key rules:
> 
> - Oxygen is -2 (except in peroxides)
> - Nitrogen in NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> is +5
> - Nitrogen in NO<sub>2</sub> is +4
> - Oxygen in O<sub>2</sub> is 0
> 
> Magnesium goes from +2 in Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> to +2 in MgO. There is no change, so it is neither oxidised nor reduced.

parts.problemMd:
The values for the first, second and third ionisation energies of magnesium are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **Ionisation energy / kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| **First ionisation energy** | 738 |
| **Second ionisation energy** | 1451 |
| **Third ionisation energy** | 7732 |

i) Construct an equation for the second ionisation energy of magnesium.

[2]

ii) Explain the trend in the first three ionisation energies of magnesium.

[3]

iii) Explain why magnesium has a greater second ionisation energy than barium.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for the second ionisation energy of magnesium is:

Mg<sup>+</sup> (g) → Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct equation: Mg<sup>+</sup> → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for all species shown with state symbol (g)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The trend in the first three ionisation energies of magnesium:
> 
> - Successive ionisation energies increase **[1 mark]**
> - The 2nd IE is greater than the 1st because the same nuclear charge acts on fewer electrons / less electron-electron repulsion, giving greater effective nuclear attraction **[1 mark]**
> - There is a large increase between the 2nd and 3rd IE because the 3rd electron is removed from the 2p subshell (n=2), which is closer to the nucleus and experiences less shielding than the 3s subshell (n=3) from which the 1st and 2nd electrons are removed **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) Why the second ionisation energy of magnesium is greater than that of barium:
> 
> - Mg<sup>+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius / fewer electron shells than Ba<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Less shielding (of the outer electron from the nucleus in Mg<sup>+</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - Greater nuclear attraction / the outer electron is more strongly attracted to the nucleus **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For successive ionisation energies, write out the electronic configuration to identify large jumps: Mg is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup>. The 1st and 2nd electrons are removed from 3s (n=3); the 3rd from 2p (n=2), which is an inner shell, closer to nucleus, much less shielded. This produces the large jump.
> 
> A common error for part iii) is to cite 'nuclear charge' as the reason Mg has a higher IE than Ba. This is wrong as Ba has a higher nuclear charge (more protons). The correct reasoning is smaller ionic radius, less shielding, and therefore greater effective nuclear attraction per remaining electron.

parts.problemMd:
Metal peroxides contain the <sup>-</sup>O–O<sup>-</sup> ion.

The peroxides of the Group 2 elements, MO<sub>2</sub>, decompose in a similar way to Group 2 metal carbonates.

i) Construct an equation for the thermal decomposition of strontium peroxide, SrO<sub>2</sub>.

[1]

ii) Suggest how the temperature at which thermal decomposition of MO<sub>2</sub> occurs varies down Group 2. Explain your answer.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the thermal decomposition of strontium peroxide:
> 
> - 2SrO<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2SrO (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow without state symbols; allow 1:1 ratio (SrO<sub>2</sub> → SrO + ½O<sub>2</sub>) if balanced

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) How the temperature for thermal decomposition of MO<sub>2</sub> varies going down Group 2:
> 
> - Temperature required for decomposition increases going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) the charge density of the cation decreases going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - (So) there is less polarisation of the O<sub>2</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion / the O-O bond is polarised less / weakened less **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The clue in the question is that MO<sub>2</sub> decomposition is similar to Group 2 carbonates. In both cases, a larger cation with lower charge density polarises the anion less, making the relevant bond harder to break (O-O in peroxides, C-O in carbonates). More energy (higher temperature) is therefore needed.
> 
> The general equation is: 2MO<sub>2</sub> (s) → 2MO (s) + O<sub>2</sub> (g), where the solid metal oxide and gaseous oxygen are analogous to MO and CO<sub>2</sub> in carbonate decomposition.

[1]

ii) Use the data from Table 2.1 in part **(a)** to calculate the value of *K*<sub>sp</sub> at 293 K. Include units in your answer and show your working.

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = ................................................ units = ..............................

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The expression for *K*<sub>sp</sub> of Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Sr<sup>2+</sup>][OH<sup>-</sup>]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate *K*<sub>sp</sub> for Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> at 293 K:

- Convert solubility to mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (M<sub>r</sub> of Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> = 87.6 + 34 = 121.6 g mol<sup>-1</sup>):

[Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>] = $\frac{17.70}{121.6}$

[Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub>] = 0.146 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Note that [OH<sup>-</sup>] = 2 x [Sr<sup>2+</sup>] = 2 x 0.146 = 0.292 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

- Calculate *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 0.146 x (0.292)<sup>2</sup>

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = **0.0124** **[1 mark]**

- Units:

**mol**<sup>**3**</sup>** dm**<sup>**-9**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow *K*<sub>sp</sub> in the range 0.012–0.013
> 
> The units must be consistent with the expression: [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>3</sup> = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common mistake is to forget that [OH<sup>-</sup>] = 2[Sr<sup>2+</sup>] as each formula unit of Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> releases two OH<sup>-</sup> ions. The [OH<sup>-</sup>] must be doubled before squaring in the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression.
> 
> The units for *K*<sub>sp</sub> come from the concentration terms in the expression: [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>] x [mol dm<sup>-3</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Table 2.1 shows the solubility data for the Group 2 metal hydroxides.

**Table 2.1**

| **Group 2 metal hydroxide** | **Solubility / g dm**^-3^** at 20 °C** |
| --- | :---: |
| Magnesium hydroxide | 0.140 |
| Calcium hydroxide | 1.730 |
| Strontium hydroxide | 17.70 |
| Barium hydroxide | 38.90 |

Use the data from Table 2.1 in part **(a)** to calculate the pH of a saturated solution of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> at 293 K. Show your working.

*K*<sub>w</sub> at 293 K = 0.681 x 10<sup>-14</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

pH = ....................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pH of a saturated solution of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> at 293 K:

- Convert solubility to mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (M<sub>r</sub> of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> = 24.3 + 34 = 58.3 g mol<sup>-1</sup>):

[Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>] = $\frac{0.140}{58.3}$

[Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0024 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Find [OH<sup>-</sup>] using the dissociation equation:

Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> → Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2OH<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

[OH<sup>-</sup>] = 2 x 0.0024

[OH<sup>-</sup>] = 0.0048 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] using *K*<sub>w</sub>:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = `\frac{K_w}{[OH^-]}`

[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\frac{0.681\times10^{-14}}{0.0048}$

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 1.42 x 10<sup>-12</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate pH:

pH = −log(1.42 x 10<sup>-12</sup>) = **11.8** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow [Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>] in the range 0.0024–0.0025 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Also accept pH = 11.85
> 
> Do not allow using pH + pOH = 14

> **[exam-tip]**
> Many students miss the step of multiplying [Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>] by 2 to get [OH<sup>-</sup>], even though the dissociation equation shows each formula unit releases two OH<sup>-</sup> ions.
> 
> Since the temperature is 293 K (not 298 K), you cannot assume pH + pOH = 14.
> 
> Use the *K*<sub>w</sub> value given in the question to calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] via: [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>w</sub> ÷ [OH<sup>-</sup>].

parts.problemMd:
Calcium carbonate can be thermally decomposed to make calcium oxide.

CaCO<sub>3 </sub>(s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)   Δ*H *= + 178 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

Table 3.1 below shows the standard entropies of each substance.

**Table 3.1**

| **Substance** | CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) | CaO (s) | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S / J K**<sup>**–1**</sup>** mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> | 89 | 40 | 214 |

i) Use the information in Table 3.1 to show that calcium carbonate is stable at room temperature (25 <sup>o</sup>C).

[4]

ii) Calculate the minimum temperature needed to decompose calcium carbonate

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To show that CaCO<sub>3</sub> is stable at 25°C, calculate Δ*G* at 298 K:

- Calculate Δ*S*:

Δ*S* = (40 + 214) − 89

Δ*S* = +165 J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert units:

165 ÷ 1000 = 0.165 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Substitute into Δ*G* = Δ*H* − *T*Δ*S*:

Δ*G* = +178 − (298 x 0.165) **[1 mark]**

Δ*G* = **+129 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Since Δ*G* > 0, the reaction is not feasible / spontaneous at 298 K; CaCO<sub>3</sub> does not decompose and is therefore stable at room temperature **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow Δ*G* in the range +127 to +131 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> The substitution mark requires consistent units — using 0.165 kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>, not 165

ii) To calculate the minimum temperature for decomposition, set Δ*G* = 0:

- Rearrange to find *T*:

*T* = $\frac{ΔH}{ΔS}$ **[1 mark]**

*T* = $\frac{178}{0.165}$ = **1079 K** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Also accept *T* = 806°C
> 
> Allow error carried forward from incorrect Δ*S* provided the method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Δ*S* values are in J K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> but Δ*H* is in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, so you should always convert Δ*S* to kJ K<sup>-1</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> before substituting into the Δ*G* equation.
> 
> If Δ*G* > 0 the reaction is not feasible (not spontaneous). At the minimum temperature for decomposition, Δ*G* = 0, giving *T* = Δ*H*/Δ*S*.

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain the trend that is observed in the thermal decomposition of the Group 2 carbonates.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates:
> 
> - Carbonates become more thermally stable / more difficult to decompose / require a higher temperature going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - The ionic radius of the Group 2 cation increases
> **OR**
> The charge density of the Group 2 cation decreases going down Group 2 **[1 mark]**
> - (So) there is less polarisation of the carbonate ion (CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>) / the C-O bond is polarised / weakened less **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This explanation applies equally to Group 2 nitrates — replace 'C-O bond' with 'N-O bond'. The key principle:
> 
> - Smaller, denser cation
> - → greater polarising power
> - → more distortion of the anion
> - → easier to break the bond
> - → lower thermal stability

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct an equation to show the equilibrium for the solubility product of CaCO<sub>3</sub>. Include state symbols.

[1]

ii) With reference to your equation in part **(c)(i)**, suggest what is observed when a few cm<sup>3</sup> of concentrated K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) are added to a saturated solution of CaCO<sub>3</sub>. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equilibrium expression for the solubility product of CaCO<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) ⇌ Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) What is observed when K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to a saturated solution of CaCO<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - A white solid / precipitate (of CaCO<sub>3</sub>) forms / appears **[1 mark]**
> - [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>] increases, shifting the equilibrium to the left; CaCO<sub>3</sub> precipitates out of solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is the common ion effect.
> 
> Adding CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> (already present in the equilibrium) increases its concentration, causing the system to shift left (Le Chatelier’s principle) to reduce [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>].
> 
> Ca<sup>2+</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> recombine to form solid CaCO<sub>3</sub>, reducing the solubility of calcium carbonate.

parts.problemMd:
CaCO<sub>3</sub> has a solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, in water at 298 K of 5 x 10<sup>-9</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

Calculate the solubility of CaCO<sub>3</sub> in water at 298 K, in g dm<sup>-3</sup>.

solubility of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = ............................. g dm<sup>-3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the solubility of CaCO<sub>3</sub>:

- Recognise that [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] = [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = *s*, so *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup>:

*s*<sup>2</sup> = 5 x 10<sup>-9</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the molar solubility:

*s* = $\sqrt{5\times10^{-9}}$ 
*s* = 7.07 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert to g dm<sup>-3</sup> (M<sub>r</sub> of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = 100.1 g mol<sup>-1</sup>):

solubility = 7.07 x 10<sup>-5</sup> x 100.1 
solubility = **7.08 x 10**<sup>**-3**</sup>** g dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow solubility in the range 7.0–7.2 x 10<sup>-3</sup> g dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>][CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = *s* x *s* = *s*<sup>2</sup>. Since both ions are produced in a 1:1 ratio, the molar solubility is simply √*K*<sub>sp</sub>. Remember to multiply by the molar mass to convert mol dm<sup>-3</sup> to g dm<sup>-3</sup>.

name: General Physical & Chemical Properties of the First Row of Transition Elements, Titanium to Copper

parts.problemMd: Define the term *transition element*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of a transition element:
> 
> - A d-block element **[1 mark]**
> - That forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete / partially filled 3d subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both marks are needed for the complete definition. The first mark is for identifying it as a d-block element, and the second mark is for the key criterion: it must form at least one stable ion with a partially filled 3d subshell.
> 
> Two d-block elements do not qualify as transition elements: scandium (Sc<sup>3+</sup> has an empty 3d subshell) and zinc (Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a full 3d subshell, [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>). Neither ion has a partially filled d subshell.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Define the term *transition element*.

A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete / partially filled 3d subshell.

i) State the full electronic configuration of Ti<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]

ii) Explain, using the electronic configuration, why zinc is found in the d-block of the periodic table but is not classified as a transition element.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration of Ti<sup>2+</sup>:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>2</sup>
> **OR**
> [Ar]3d<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Zinc is not classified as a transition element because:
> 
> - The Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion has a complete / full 3d subshell **[1 mark]**
> - The electronic configuration of Zn<sup>2+</sup> is 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>10</sup> / [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>, showing no partially filled 3d subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), both the full notation (1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>2</sup>) and the noble gas shorthand ([Ar]3d<sup>2</sup>) are accepted.
> 
> For part ii), the critical point is the electronic configuration of the Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion, not the Zn atom. The Zn atom has configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, but when it forms Zn<sup>2+</sup> it loses both 4s electrons, leaving [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>. Since the 3d subshell is completely full, Zn<sup>2+</sup> does not have a partially filled d subshell, so zinc does not qualify as a transition element.

parts.problemMd: State **two** characteristic properties of transition elements, other than the formation of coloured ions.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two characteristic properties of transition elements, other than the formation of coloured ions:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Form complexes / complex ions
> - Have variable oxidation states
> - Behave as / act as catalysts
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Transition elements have four characteristic properties: formation of coloured ions, formation of complex ions, variable oxidation states, and catalytic activity.
> 
> Exam questions often follow up by asking you to explain one of these in more detail. For example, variable oxidation states arise because the 3d and 4s subshells are similar in energy, so electrons can be removed from either subshell with gradually increasing ionisation energies.

parts.problemMd:
Copper, vanadium and iron are all transition elements.

i) State the full electronic configuration of a Cu atom and a Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion.

[2]

ii) State three characteristic properties of copper and its compounds.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration of a Cu atom and a Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion:
> 
> - Cu atom: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Three characteristic properties of copper and its compounds:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Variable oxidation states
> - Form coloured ions / compounds
> - Form complexes / complex ions
> - Act as catalysts
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), copper has an anomalous electronic configuration. The expected configuration would be [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>, but the actual configuration is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup>, because a fully filled 3d subshell is particularly stable. When Cu loses two electrons to form Cu<sup>2+</sup>, it loses the 4s<sup>1</sup> electron first, then one 3d electron, giving [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>.
> 
> For part ii), the four characteristic properties of transition elements are: variable oxidation states, formation of coloured ions, formation of complex ions, and catalytic activity. These apply to all first-row transition elements, not just copper.

parts.problemMd:
The chloride ion is a monodentate ligand. When concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) ions the water ligands are replaced.

i) Define the term *monodentate ligand*.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction that occurs when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq).

[1]

iii) Draw the 3D structure of the complex ion formed in this reaction.

[1]

iv) State the shape of the complex ion.

[1]

v) State the change in coordination number.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The definition of monodentate ligand:
> 
> - A molecule / ion that has a lone pair of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - That donates one lone pair to form one coordinate (dative covalent) bond to a central metal atom / ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction:
> 
> - [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>-</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

iii) The 3D structure of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>:

![Tetrahedral CuCl4 2- complex ion with copper at the centre and four chloride ligands at the vertices of a tetrahedron](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-1-general-physical-and-chemical-properties-of-the-first-row-of-transition-elements-titanium-to-copper/assets/001-tetrahedral-cucl4-2-complex-ion-with-copper-at-t.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct tetrahedral structure with the 2− charge on the complex
> 
> iv) The shape of the complex ion:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> v) The change in coordination number:
> 
> - 6 to 4 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), a monodentate ligand forms exactly one coordinate bond. The prefix 'mono' means one. Contrast this with bidentate ligands (e.g. ethane-1,2-diamine), which form two coordinate bonds per ligand molecule.
> 
> For part ii), when concentrated HCl is added, four chloride ions replace all six water ligands. Cl<sup>-</sup> is a larger ligand than H<sub>2</sub>O, so only four can fit around the Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion.
> 
> The shape changes from octahedral ([Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, six ligands) to tetrahedral ([CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>, four ligands). These two complexes also have different colours:
> 
> - [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is blue
> - [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> is yellow-green

parts.problemMd:
Vanadium(V) oxide is the catalyst used in the Contact process as shown by the reactions:

SO<sub>2</sub> + V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub> + V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>

V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub> → V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub>

i) Construct the overall equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Use the equations to explain how V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> acts as a catalyst in this reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The overall equation for this reaction:
> 
> - SO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub>
> **OR**
> 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> acts as a catalyst in this reaction because:
> 
> - It is regenerated at the end of the reaction / not consumed overall **[1 mark]**
> - Vanadium has variable oxidation states (changes from +5 to +4 and back to +5) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), to find the overall equation, add the two steps and cancel species that appear on both sides. V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>5</sub> cancels (reactant in step 1, product in step 2) and V<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> cancels (product in step 1, reactant in step 2), leaving SO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> For part ii), the first mark is for identifying that the catalyst is regenerated (not consumed). The second mark is for the mechanism: vanadium cycles between oxidation states +5 and +4 across the two steps, providing an alternative reaction pathway. This ability to cycle between oxidation states is a general property of transition metal catalysts.

parts.problemMd:
When iron(II) compounds dissolve in water they form [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, the hexaaquairon(II) complex.

i) State the full electronic configuration of an iron(II) ion.

[1]

ii) Predict the shape and bond angle of the hexaaquairon(II) complex.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration of an iron(II) ion:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>6</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The shape and bond angle of the hexaaquairon(II) complex:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**
> - 90° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the iron(II) ion has lost two electrons from the 4s subshell of the iron atom ([Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>), leaving [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup>.
> 
> For part ii), the hexaaqua complex has six water ligands arranged symmetrically around the central Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion. Six bonding pairs repel equally, giving an octahedral geometry with 90° bond angles.

parts.problemMd: Explain why transition metals exhibit variable oxidation states compared to the elements in Group 1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Transition metals exhibit variable oxidation states but Group 1 elements do not because:
> 
> Transition metals:
> 
> - The 3d and 4s subshells are similar in energy
> **OR**
> Successive ionisation energies increase gradually **[1 mark]**
> 
> Group 1 elements:
> 
> - The second electron occupies a much lower energy level / inner shell
> **OR**
> There is a very large increase in ionisation energy between the first and second ionisation energies **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Transition metals can exist in multiple oxidation states because the 3d and 4s subshells have similar energies. Electrons from either subshell can be removed with gradually increasing ionisation energies, so transition metals can form ions with different charges (e.g. Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup>; Ti<sup>2+</sup>, Ti<sup>3+</sup>, and Ti<sup>4+</sup>).
> 
> For Group 1 elements, the first electron removed comes from the outer shell, but the second would come from a much lower energy inner shell. The very large jump in ionisation energy makes a second ionisation effectively impossible under normal conditions, so Group 1 elements exist only in the +1 oxidation state.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Oxidation state** | **Final answer:** **+3** | **Final answer:** **+2** | **Final answer:** **+3** | **Final answer:** **+3** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for +3 in [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for +2 in [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for +3 in [Cr(OH)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for +3 in Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>
> 
> The sign must be written before the number: +3 not 3+.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation state of the transition element, use the overall charge and the known oxidation states of the other atoms:
> 
> - Neutral ligands (H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>): oxidation state = 0
> - OH<sup>-</sup> ligand: oxidation state = −1
> - O in Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>: oxidation state = −2
> 
> For [Cr(OH)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3-</sup>: Cr + (6 x −1) = −3, so Cr = +3.
> 
> For Mn<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>: (2 x Mn) + (3 x −2) = 0, so Mn = +3.
> 
> A common error is to write the oxidation state as 3+ rather than +3. CIE mark schemes will not award the mark for the wrong notation.

parts.problemMd:
Water acts as a ligand when it reacts with zinc and cobalt ions, forming the complexes [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

i) State the full electronic configuration for the metal ion in each of the following complexes.

[Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>:

[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>:

[2]

ii) Explain why zinc is not classified as a transition element.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration for the metal ions:
> 
> - [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>10</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>7</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Zinc is not classified as a transition element because:
> 
> - The Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion has a complete / full 3d subshell **[1 mark]**
> - The electronic configuration of Zn<sup>2+</sup> is [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>, showing no partially filled 3d subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), when writing the electronic configuration of an ion, the 4s electrons are removed first. Both Zn<sup>2+</sup> and Co<sup>2+</sup> lose their two 4s electrons:
> 
> - Zn: [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> → Zn<sup>2+</sup>: [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup> (3d subshell is full)
> - Co: [Ar]3d<sup>7</sup>4s<sup>2</sup> → Co<sup>2+</sup>: [Ar]3d<sup>7</sup> (3d subshell is incomplete)
> 
> For part ii), the definition of a transition element requires at least one stable ion with a partially filled 3d subshell. The Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion has a complete 3d subshell ([Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>), so zinc does not qualify.

parts.problemMd:
EUK-134 is a complex ion of manganese(III) that acts as an antioxidant.

![EUK-134 complex ion structure showing manganese centre with surrounding ligands](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-1-general-physical-and-chemical-properties-of-the-first-row-of-transition-elements-titanium-to-copper/assets/002-euk-134-complex-ion-structure-showing-manganese-.png)

i) State the full electronic configuration of the manganese(III) ion in the complex shown above.

[1]

ii) Define the term *ligand*.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configuration of the manganese(III) ion:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>4</sup>
> **OR**
> [Ar]3d<sup>4</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The definition of a ligand:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

EUK-134 is a complex ion of manganese(III) that acts as an antioxidant.

EUK-134 acts as a catalyst to decrease the concentration of oxidising agents.

State **two** characteristic properties of transition elements that allow EUK-134 to act in this way.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two characteristic properties of transition elements that allow EUK-134 to act in this way:
> 
> - Variable oxidation states
> **OR**
> Acts as a reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> - Catalytic properties / acts as a catalyst **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> EUK-134 decreases the concentration of oxidising agents by two related mechanisms:
> 
> 1. Variable oxidation states: manganese can cycle between oxidation states (e.g. Mn<sup>3+</sup> and Mn<sup>2+</sup>), allowing it to accept electrons from oxidising agents and act as a reducing agent.
> 2. Catalytic activity: the variable oxidation states allow EUK-134 to provide an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy, speeding up the removal of oxidising agents.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about transition metal complexes.

Define the terms ligand and complex ion.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definitions of the terms are:
> 
> - Ligand: a molecule or ion that has one or more lone pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Complex ion: a molecule or ion formed by a central metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should know the definitions of these key terms as they are commonly tested at the start of transition metal questions.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Transition metals can form complexes with different ligands.

Identify **one** species from the following list that does not act as a ligand. Explain your answer.

CO          H<sub>2</sub>O          SCN<sup>–</sup>          H<sub>2</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The species that does not act as a ligand is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub> / hydrogen **[1 mark]**
> - H<sub>2</sub> has no lone pairs of electrons, so it cannot form a coordinate bond with the metal ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ligands must have at least one lone pair of electrons to donate to the central metal ion. Water (H<sub>2</sub>O), thiocyanate (SCN<sup>–</sup>) and carbon monoxide (CO) all have lone pairs and can act as ligands. Hydrogen (H<sub>2</sub>) has no lone pairs, so it cannot.

parts.problemMd:
A complex ion contains one Co<sup>2+</sup> ion, four ammonia molecules and two chloride ions.

i) State the formula of this complex ion.

[1]

ii) State the geometry of this complex ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The formula of this complex ion is:
> 
> - [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>] **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The geometry of this complex ion is:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each Cl<sup>–</sup> ligand has a charge of –1 and each NH<sub>3</sub> ligand is neutral. The Co<sup>2+</sup> ion has a charge of +2, so the overall charge on the complex is: +2 + (2 × –1) = 0. A neutral complex does not need square brackets with a charge.
> 
> With 6 ligands bonded to the central metal ion, the geometry is octahedral.

parts.problemMd:
The H<sub>2</sub>O ligands in [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> can be exchanged for other ligands.

Deduce the geometry of the complex ions formed after the following substitutions.

i) All the H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are exchanged for OH<sup>–</sup> ligands.

[1]

ii) The six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are exchanged for four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Exchanging all H<sub>2</sub>O ligands for OH<sup>–</sup> ligands:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Exchanging six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands for four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Shape' is accepted in place of 'geometry'.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When all six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are replaced by six OH<sup>–</sup> ligands, the coordination number stays at 6, so the geometry remains octahedral.
> 
> When six H<sub>2</sub>O ligands are replaced by four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands, the coordination number changes from 6 to 4. Four large ligands such as Cl<sup>–</sup> adopt a tetrahedral arrangement to minimise repulsion.

![Two octahedral copper complexes: left, Cu with two water and four ammonia ligands; right, Cu with one water and five ammonia ligands in similar arrangement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-2-general-characteristic-chemical-properties-of-the-first-set-of-transition-elements-titanium-to-copper/assets/004-two-octahedral-copper-complexes-left-cu-with-two.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct cis-isomer structure with the two water molecules adjacent to each other

> **[exam-tip]**
> You are expected to know the ligand exchange reactions of copper(II) complexes with ammonia, including the colours and physical states at each stage.
