parts.problemMd:
The feasibility of redox reactions can be determined using standard electrode potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup>, values.

The following electrochemical cell is set up.

Pb<sup>4+</sup> (aq) + 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → 2Mn<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + Pb<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**θ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mn | –1.18 |
| Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mn<sup>2+</sup> | +1.49 |
| Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Pb | –0.13 |
| Pb<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Pb<sup>2+</sup> | +1.69 |

Construct the reduction half-equation and the oxidation half-equation for the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The half-equations for the reaction are:
> 
> - Reduction: Pb<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> → Pb<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation: Mn<sup>2+</sup> → Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow ⇌ instead of → in the reduction half-equation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The overall reaction shows Pb going from +4 to +2 (gaining electrons / reduction) and Mn going from +2 to +3 (losing electrons / oxidation). Select the matching half-equations from the table.
> 
> For the oxidation half-equation, reverse the direction from the table: Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Mn<sup>2+</sup> in the table becomes Mn<sup>2+</sup> → Mn<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> when written as an oxidation.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The feasibility of redox reactions can be determined using standard electrode potential, *E*^θ^, values.

The following electrochemical cell is set up.

Pb^4+^ (aq) + 2Mn^2+^ (aq) → 2Mn^3+^ (aq) + Pb^2+^ (aq)

| **Electrode reaction** | ***E***^**θ**^** / V** |
| :---: | :---: |
| Mn^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Mn | –1.18 |
| Mn^3+^ + e^–^ ⇌ Mn^2+^ | +1.49 |
| Pb^2+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Pb | –0.13 |
| Pb^4+^ + 2e^–^ ⇌ Pb^2+^ | +1.69 |

Use Table 3.1 and your answer to part (a) to calculate the standard cell potential, *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>, for the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the standard cell potential *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub>:

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduction</sub> – *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidation</sub>

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = (+1.69) – (+1.49)

*E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = **+0.20 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 0.20 V without the + sign.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the formula *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>reduction</sub> – *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>oxidation</sub>. The reduction half-equation has *E*<sup>θ</sup> = +1.69 V (Pb<sup>4+</sup>/Pb<sup>2+</sup>) and the value for the oxidation half-equation as written in the table is +1.49 V (Mn<sup>3+</sup>/Mn<sup>2+</sup>). Subtracting: +1.69 – 1.49 = +0.20 V.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

To calculate the standard cell potential *E*^θ^~cell~:

*E*^θ^~cell~ = *E*^θ^~reduction~ – *E*^θ^~oxidation~

*E*^θ^~cell~ = (+1.69) – (+1.49)

*E*^θ^~cell~ = +0.20 V

Use your answer to part (b) to deduce whether the reaction is feasible. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reaction is:
> 
> - Feasible **[1 mark]**
> - The standard cell potential / *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> is positive **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A positive *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> value indicates the reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions. A negative *E*<sup>θ</sup><sub>cell</sub> value would indicate the reaction is not feasible in the forward direction.

parts.problemMd:
Potassium manganate(VII) can be used to titrate a sample containing an unknown percentage of iron(II).

i) Complete the half-equation for the reduction of manganate(VII) ions, MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>, to manganese(II) ions, Mn<sup>2+</sup>.

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + ........H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + ........e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + ........H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

[1]

ii) State, in terms of electron transfer, whether this half-equation represents oxidation or reduction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The completed half-equation is:
> 
> - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation represents:
> 
> - Reduction; electrons are gained **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance the manganate(VII) half-equation, work in steps.
> 
> - First, balance the oxygens using H<sub>2</sub>O: four oxygens in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> give 4H<sub>2</sub>O.
> - Then balance the hydrogens using H<sup>+</sup>: four H<sub>2</sub>O require 8H<sup>+</sup>.
> - Finally, balance the charge: the left side has a total charge of +7 before adding electrons, and the right side has +2, so 5e<sup>–</sup> are needed.
> 
> Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

parts.problemMd:
i) Construct the half-equation for the oxidation of Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup>. Include state symbols.

[1]

ii) State, in terms of electron transfer, whether this half-equation represents oxidation or reduction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation for the oxidation of Fe<sup>2+</sup> to Fe<sup>3+</sup> is:
> 
> - Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation represents:
> 
> - Oxidation; electrons are lost **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The iron half-equation is straightforward: Fe<sup>2+</sup> loses one electron to become Fe<sup>3+</sup>. Always include state symbols, even though, in this context both iron species are in aqueous solution.
> 
> Contrast this with the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> half-equation in part (a): there, electrons are gained (reduction), whereas here electrons are lost (oxidation).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

i) Complete the half-equation for the reduction of manganate(VII) ions, MnO4–, to manganese(II) ions, Mn2+.

MnO4– (aq) + ........H+ (aq) + ........e– → Mn2+ (aq) + ........H2O (l)

The completed half-equation is:
MnO4– (aq) + 8H+ (aq) + 5e– → Mn2+ (aq) + 4H2O (l)

i) Construct the half-equation for the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+. Include state symbols.

The half-equation for the oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ is:
Fe2+ (aq) → Fe3+ (aq) + e–

Using your answers to parts (a) and (b), construct the overall ionic equation for the reaction between Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions and MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> ions.
parts.solutionMd:
The overall ionic equation is:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing throughout

> **[exam-tip]**
> To combine the two half-equations, first balance the electrons. The MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> equation uses 5e<sup>–</sup> and the Fe<sup>2+</sup> equation produces 1e<sup>–</sup>, so multiply the Fe<sup>2+</sup> equation by 5. Then add the two equations and cancel the electrons:
> 
> - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> - 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq) + 5e<sup>–</sup>
> 
> The 5e<sup>–</sup> cancel to give the overall equation.

parts.problemMd:
A solution is made by dissolving CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O in an excess of aqueous ammonia. This solution contains the copper complex [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

i) State the expression for the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]

ii) State the colour of the solution of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The expression for the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = $\frac{[ \text{Cu} ( NH_{3} )_{4} ]^{2} +}{[ \text{Cu} ( \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} )_{6} ]^{2} + [ NH_{3} ]^{4} }$ **[1 mark]**
> 
> Water / H<sub>2</sub>O must not be included in the *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression.
> 
> ii) The colour of the solution of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - Deep / dark / royal blue **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Kstab expression is constructed like a Kc expression: the concentration of the complex in the numerator, and the concentrations of the separated metal ion and ligands in the denominator. Water ligands are not included (they are the solvent).
> 
> CuSO<sub>4</sub>•5H<sub>2</sub>O dissolves in water to give [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (pale blue). Adding excess ammonia displaces the water ligands to give [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, which is a characteristic deep/dark blue.

parts.problemMd:
The solution of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is heated gently so that NH<sub>3</sub> is released. A precipitate of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> forms and is collected.

A sample of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

A sample of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> is added to dilute sulfuric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Z**.

Construct an equation for the reaction of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> to form Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> when the solution is heated.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction of [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> to form Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> on heating is:
> 
> - [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2NH<sub>3</sub>
> **OR**
> [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> On heating, the NH<sub>3</sub> ligands are driven off and the remaining water hydrolyses the copper ion to give Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub>. When NH<sub>3</sub> leaves as a gas, some may remain in solution as NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (giving the first equation) or all may leave as NH<sub>3</sub> gas (giving the second equation). Both are acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

Construct an equation for the reaction of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> with concentrated hydrochloric acid, forming **Y**.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation for the reaction of Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> with concentrated hydrochloric acid to form **Y** is:

Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2H<sup>+</sup>

**OR**

Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> complex including charge
> 
> 1 mark for the rest of the equation fully correct and balanced

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> contains Cu<sup>2+</sup> with two OH<sup>–</sup> ions. In concentrated HCl, four Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands (which are larger than water) displace all ligands to give tetrahedral [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup>. The two OH<sup>–</sup> ions react with two of the H<sup>+</sup> ions from HCl to give 2H<sub>2</sub>O, leaving 2H<sup>+</sup> unreacted on the right-hand side.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to dilute sulfuric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Z**.

Complete Table 1.1 with the colour and geometry of complex **Y** and the colour, geometry and formula of complex **Z**.

**Table 1.1**

|   | ** Y** | **Z** |
|---|---|---|
| colour of complex |   |   |
| geometry of complex |   |   |
| formula of complex | [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|   | **Y** | **Z** |
|---|---|---|
| colour of complex | **Final answer:** **Yellow** | **Final answer:** **(Pale) blue** |
| geometry of complex | **Final answer:** **Tetrahedral** | **Final answer:** **Octahedral** |
| formula of complex | [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup> | **Final answer:** **[Cu(H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O)**<sub>**6**</sub>**]**<sup>**2+**</sup> |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for any three answer cells correct
> 
> 2 marks for all five answer cells correct
> 
> Allow 'blue' for the colour of Z.

> **[exam-tip]**
> [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> is yellow and tetrahedral. This is one of the rare copper(II) complexes that is not blue. The large size of Cl<sup>–</sup> means only four ligands can coordinate to the central Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion, giving a tetrahedral geometry.
> 
> When Cu(OH)<sub>2</sub> is added to dilute sulfuric acid, it dissolves to give Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) which then forms [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> with the classic pale blue octahedral hexaaqua complex.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Y**.

A sample of Cu(OH)~2~ is added to dilute sulfuric acid to form a coloured copper complex, **Z**.

|   | **Y** | **Z** |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| colour of complex |   |   |
| geometry of complex |   |   |
| formula of complex | [CuCl~4~]^2-^ |   |

Explain why complexes **Y** and **Z** are coloured and why their colours are different.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Complexes **Y** and **Z** are coloured and have different colours because:
> 
> - The d orbitals split into two sets of energy levels of different energy **[1 mark]**
> - Electrons absorb a specific frequency / wavelength of light / photons **[1 mark]**
> - The absorbed energy promotes / excites electron(s) to the higher energy level **[1 mark]**
> - The colour observed is complementary to the wavelength / colour absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The d–d energy gap / Δ*E* is different for **Y** and **Z**, so a different frequency / wavelength of light is absorbed for each complex **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The origin of colour in transition metal complexes is frequently identified by examiners as an area students find difficult. The key chain of reasoning is: d orbital splitting causes a specific energy gap; an electron absorbs a photon of that exact energy and is promoted; the colour you see is the complementary colour (what is not absorbed).
> 
> The reason Y and Z have different colours is that they have different ligands (Cl<sup>–</sup> vs H<sub>2</sub>O), which cause different amounts of d orbital splitting, and therefore different frequencies of light are absorbed.

parts.problemMd:

An aqueous solution of copper(II) contains the [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex ion.

Define the term complex ion.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A complete definition of a complex ion requires two components: the central metal atom or ion, and the ligands surrounding it. A one-sentence answer that includes both components will gain full marks.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **A**, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>, is a tridentate ligand.

![Structural formula of compound A: a central secondary amine linked to two ethylamine groups, representing diethylenetriamine.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-2-general-characteristic-chemical-properties-of-the-first-set-of-transition-elements-titanium-to-copper/assets/009-structural-formula-of-compound-a-a-central-secon.png)

i) Explain why one molecule of **A** can form three coordinate bonds.

[1]

ii) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub> reacts with aqueous chromium(III) ions, [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, in a 2:1 ratio to form a new complex ion.

Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One molecule of **A** can form three coordinate bonds because:
> 
> - Each nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that can be donated to the central metal ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + 2C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub> → [Cr(C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand must have at least one lone pair of electrons to donate to the central metal ion. Compound A has three nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair, so it can form three coordinate bonds (it is tridentate).
> 
> Since each molecule of A is tridentate (forms 3 coordinate bonds) and [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> has 6 water ligands, two molecules of A are needed to replace all six water ligands.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the transition metal copper.

i) State the full electronic configuration of a Cu atom and a Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion.

[2]

ii) State **four** characteristic features of the chemistry of copper and its compounds.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The full electronic configurations are:
> 
> - Cu atom: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion: 1s<sup>2</sup>2s<sup>2</sup>2p<sup>6</sup>3s<sup>2</sup>3p<sup>6</sup>3d<sup>9</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> For the Cu atom, allow 3d and 4s in either order.
> 
> ii) Four characteristic features of copper and its compounds:
> 
> Any **four** from (1 mark each):
> 
> - Variable oxidation states
> - Forms coloured ions / compounds
> - Forms complex ions
> - Acts as a catalyst
> - Has an incomplete d subshell (in at least one of its common oxidation states)
> 
> **[4 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Copper has the unusual electronic configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>4s<sup>1</sup> (not [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>4s<sup>2</sup>), because a fully filled d subshell is particularly stable. When it forms Cu<sup>2+</sup>, it loses the 4s electron and one 3d electron to give a 3d<sup>9</sup> configuration.
> 
> The characteristic features listed above apply to all transition metals. You can remember them as: variable oxidation states, colour, complex formation, and catalytic behaviour.

parts.problemMd:
The chloride ion is a monodentate ligand. When concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> ions the water ligands are replaced.

i) Explain what is meant by the term monodentate ligand.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation to represent the ligand substitution reaction.

[1]

iii) Draw a diagram to show the structure of the complex ion formed.

[1]

iv) State the geometry of the complex ion formed.

[1]

v) State the change in coordination number.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A monodentate ligand is:
> 
> - A ligand that forms one coordinate bond / donates one lone pair of electrons to a central metal atom or ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the ligand substitution reaction is:
> 
> - [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

iii) The structure of the complex ion formed is:

![Hand-drawn tetrahedral complex showing a central Cu atom bonded to four Cl ligands with wedge and dashed bonds, in square brackets with a 2− charge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-2-general-characteristic-chemical-properties-of-the-first-set-of-transition-elements-titanium-to-copper/assets/006-hand-drawn-tetrahedral-complex-showing-a-central.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct tetrahedral structure of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup>
> 
> iv) The geometry of the complex ion formed is:
> 
> - Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> v) The change in coordination number is:
> 
> - 6 to 4 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A monodentate ligand donates one lone pair of electrons (forms one coordinate bond). The Cl<sup>–</sup> ion has lone pairs available for donation.
> 
> In the ligand substitution, six water ligands (smaller) are replaced by four chloride ions (larger). Fewer ligands can fit around the copper ion when they are larger, so the coordination number drops from 6 to 4 and the geometry changes from octahedral to tetrahedral.

parts.problemMd:
[Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is an example of a complex ion containing cobalt.

i) Deduce the oxidation state of cobalt in this complex ion. Explain your answer.

[2]

ii) State the geometry of this complex ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is:
> 
> - +3 **[1 mark]**
> - The 4 NH<sub>3</sub> ligands are neutral and the 2 Cl<sup>–</sup> ligands each contribute –1 (total –2). The overall charge is +1, so: x + 0 + (–2) = +1, giving x = +3 **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The geometry of this complex ion is:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> The complex has six monodentate ligands (4 NH<sub>3</sub> + 2 Cl<sup>–</sup>) around the central Co<sup>3+</sup> ion, which gives an octahedral geometry.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the oxidation state: set the unknown as x, substitute the charges of all other species (NH<sub>3</sub> = 0, Cl<sup>–</sup> = –1, overall charge = +1), and solve for x.
> 
> The overall charge on the complex tells you about the central metal ion. Here: x + 4(0) + 2(–1) = +1, so x = +3.

parts.problemMd:
Complex ions have a central transition metal ion surrounded by ligands.

Explain why the ammonium ion cannot act as a ligand.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ammonium ion cannot act as a ligand because:
> 
> - Ammonium ions do not have a lone pair (of electrons for bonding) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand must have a lone pair of electrons to form a dative covalent (coordinate) bond with the transition metal ion. In this type of bond, both electrons are donated by the ligand.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the complex ions [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> both form coloured solutions but exhibit different colours to each other.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> form coloured solutions with different colours because:
> 
> - The d orbitals / sub-shells split (into two different energy levels)
> **OR**
> The d orbitals / sub-shells change from degenerate to non-degenerate **[1 mark]**
> - Different ligands lead to different energy level splits **[1 mark]**
> - The difference in energy / Δ*E* leads to different frequencies / wavelengths / photons of light being absorbed
> **OR**
> The difference in energy / Δ*E* is absorbed by an electron (being promoted) **[1 mark]**
> - The different unabsorbed frequencies / wavelengths / photons are reflected / transmitted **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Factors affecting the colour of a complex ion include the type and size of ligands, the identity and nuclear charge of the metal ion, its oxidation state, and the shape of the complex. In this case, both complexes have the same metal ion, oxidation state, and shape. The ligand is the only structural difference.
> 
> When a ligand coordinates to the cobalt ion, it causes the 3d energy level to split into two sub-levels. Different ligands cause different degrees of splitting, so different frequencies of light are absorbed. The colour observed is the complementary colour to the light that is absorbed.

|---|---|
| **ethane-1,2-diamine** | **EDTA**<sup>4-</sup> |

**Fig. 1.1**

Compare the complex ions formed by cobalt(III) ions with each ligand. In your answer, state **one** similarity and **three** differences. Ignore any difference in colour.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A comparison of the complex ions formed by Co<sup>3+</sup> with ethane-1,2-diamine (en) and with EDTA<sup>4–</sup>:
> 
> One similarity between the complex ions:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Both ligands form dative covalent bonds with the cobalt(III) ion / both ligands donate lone pairs of electrons to cobalt(III)
> - Both complex ions have a coordination number of 6 / have six coordinate bonds
> - Both complex ions are octahedral in shape
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Three differences between the complex ions:
> 
> - EDTA<sup>4–</sup> is hexadentate
> **AND**
> en is bidentate
> **OR**
> The ratio of cobalt(III) to EDTA<sup>4–</sup> is 1:1
> **AND**
> The ratio of cobalt(III) to en is 1:3 **[1 mark]**
> - The EDTA complex is anionic / negatively charged / has a charge of 1–
> **AND**
> The en complex is cationic / positively charged / has a charge of 3+ **[1 mark]**
> - The EDTA complex has a greater stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub> / is more thermodynamically stable than the en complex **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethane-1,2-diamine (en) and EDTA<sup>4–</sup> are common ligands that frequently appear in CIE exam questions. Know the denticity of each (en = bidentate; EDTA<sup>4–</sup> = hexadentate) and the charge each confers on the resulting complex ion.
> 
> When comparing complex ions, structure your answer as direct comparisons rather than writing separate descriptions of each complex.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrated chromium(III) chloride, CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O, dissolves in water to form a number of different complex ions containing both chloride and water ligands.

The general formula of these complex ions is [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>x</sub>(Cl)<sub>y</sub>]<sup>(3–y)+</sup>

In an experiment, 0.10 mol of a complex reacted with excess silver nitrate solution to produce 0.20 mol of silver chloride.

Chloride ions which are ligands within the complex do not react with silver nitrate.

Deduce the formula of this chromium(III) complex ion. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Deducing the formula of the chromium(III) complex ion:
> 
> - The formula is [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(Cl)]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - 0.10 mol of complex produces 0.20 mol AgCl, so 0.20 mol of chloride ions are free in solution
> **OR**
> 0.10 mol of chloride ions remain coordinated as ligands
> **OR**
> One chloride ion acts as a ligand **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ionic equation for the reaction of chloride ions with silver nitrate is Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s), showing a 1:1 molar ratio.
> 
> Since 0.10 mol of complex produces 0.20 mol of AgCl, 0.20 mol of chloride ions are free in solution. Each formula unit releases 2 free Cl<sup>–</sup> ions. From CrCl<sub>3</sub>.6H<sub>2</sub>O, there are 3 Cl<sup>–</sup> in total, so 1 must remain as a ligand within the complex.
> 
> With one Cl<sup>–</sup> ligand and using the general formula [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>x</sub>(Cl)]<sup>2+</sup>, the complex is octahedral with six coordinate bonds, giving x = 5.

parts.problemMd:
Cobalt(II) and copper(II) undergo similar reactions to each other.

Cobalt(II) nitrate and copper(II) nitrate both decompose in a similar manner to that of Group 2 nitrates.

Construct an equation for the thermal decomposition of Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the thermal decomposition of Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → CoO + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> 2Co(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2CoO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 2 metal nitrates thermally decompose to form the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and oxygen:
> 
> M(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → MO + 2NO<sub>2</sub> + ½O<sub>2</sub>.
> 
> Cobalt(II) nitrate follows the same pattern. Make sure you give the cobalt(II) nitrate equation, not the copper(II) equation.

parts.problemMd:
Using complex ions formed by Cu<sup>2+</sup> with ligands selected from H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>, Cl<sup>–</sup>, C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>, construct an equation for each of the following.

i) A ligand substitution reaction with no change in the coordination number or the charge on the complex ion.

[2]

ii) A ligand substitution reaction with both a change in the coordination number and the charge on the complex ion.

[2]

iii) A ligand substitution reaction with no change in the coordination number but a change in the charge on the complex ion.

[2]

iv) A ligand substitution reaction with the greatest increase in entropy.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
Equations for each type of ligand substitution by Cu<sup>2+</sup> (ligands available: H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>, Cl<sup>–</sup>, C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>):

i) No change in coordination number or charge:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub> → [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O → [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing

ii) Change in both coordination number and charge:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 4Cl<sup>–</sup> → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> Only octahedral → tetrahedral reactions via Cl<sup>–</sup> substitution are accepted
> 
> Reverse reactions are not accepted (entropically unfavourable).

iii) Change in charge but no change in coordination number:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + 3C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> → [Cu(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>4–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + Cl<sup>–</sup> → [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>Cl]<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing
> 
> Full Cl<sup>–</sup> substitution is not accepted

iv) Greatest increase in entropy:

[Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> → [Cu(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

**OR**

[Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> → [Cu(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 4NH<sub>3</sub>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct chemical species
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing

> **[exam-tip]**
> Read each sub-part carefully and identify exactly what must change and what must stay the same before writing your equation.
> 
> For part iv, entropy increases most when the fewest ligand molecules replace the greatest number of ligands.
> 
> One EDTA<sup>4–</sup> (hexadentate) replaces six monodentate ligands, releasing six water molecules and greatly increasing the number of moles of products.

**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows a reaction pathway involving various copper(II) species.

![Flow diagram of reactions converting solid CuSO₄ through intermediates A–D to CuO, Cu(s) and [CuCl₄]³⁻, using H₂O, NH₃, Na₂CO₃, heat and conc. HCl](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/6-2-3a-h-copper-carbonate-reaction-scheme.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) Using the information in Fig. 3.1, construct the equation including state symbols to form compound **C** and other products.

[2]

ii) State the type of reaction that occurs when compound **C** is converted into copper(II) oxide.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation, including state symbols, to form compound C:

CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) → CuCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for all state symbols correct

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The type of reaction when compound C is converted into copper(II) oxide:
> 
> - Thermal decomposition / thermolysis **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Decomposition' alone is not accepted; 'thermal' must be specified

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i: all species are soluble except copper(II) carbonate (all Group 1 salts are soluble), so CuCO<sub>3</sub> is the precipitate. Compound C is CuCO<sub>3</sub> (s).
> 
> For part ii: copper(II) carbonate breaks down on heating to form copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide. This is thermal decomposition. If you write 'decomposition' alone, you must include 'thermal' to gain the mark.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 3.1 shows a reaction pathway involving various copper(II) species.

Complex A is the hexaaquacopper(II) ion [Cu(H2O)6]2+, formed when copper(II) sulfate dissolves in water. Complex D is [CuCl4]2-, formed when concentrated hydrochloric acid provides excess Cl- ions for ligand substitution.

The oxidation number of copper in [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> is +1.

i) State the electronic configuration of a Cu<sup>+</sup> ion.

[1]

ii) Deduce the role of copper metal in the formation of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> from the complex **D**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The electronic configuration of a Cu<sup>+</sup> ion:
> 
> - 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The role of copper metal in the formation of [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> from complex D:
> 
> - A reducing agent **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ground state electron configuration of Cu is 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>1</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> (copper is an exception to aufbau filling: the 4s<sup>1</sup> 3d<sup>10</sup> arrangement is more stable than 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>9</sup>). When Cu forms Cu<sup>+</sup>, the 4s<sup>1</sup> electron is removed, leaving the stable [Ar] 3d<sup>10</sup> configuration.
> 
> In the reaction [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2–</sup> + Cu → [CuCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>3–</sup> + Cu<sup>+</sup>, copper metal loses an electron and is oxidised. Because it causes reduction of the complex, it acts as a reducing agent. Remember: reducing agents are themselves oxidised.

parts.problemMd:
Iron(II) gluconate, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>FeO<sub>14</sub>, is the active ingredient in some brands of iron supplements.

A student carries out an experiment to determine the mass of iron(II) gluconate in one tablet of an iron supplement, using the method below.

1. The student crushes two tablets and dissolves the powdered tablets in dilute sulfuric acid
2. The student makes up the solution from step 1 to 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> in a volumetric flask.
3. The student then titrated 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> portions of the solution obtained in step 2 with 0.00200 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> potassium manganate(VII).

The student obtains a mean titre of 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup>.

In this titration, 1 mole of manganate(VII) ions reacts with 5 moles of iron(II) ions.

Calculate the mass, in mg, of iron(II) gluconate in **one** tablet. Show your working and give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of iron(II) gluconate in one tablet:

- List the known values:

  - volume of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup>
  - concentration of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 0.00200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>
  - mole ratio MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> : Fe<sup>2+</sup> = 1:5
- Calculate the moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>:

moles = $\frac{13.50}{1000}$ x 0.00200

moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> = 2.70 x 10<sup>–5</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the aliquot:

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 2.70 x 10<sup>–5</sup> x 5

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–4</sup> mol

- Scale to the full solution:

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–4</sup> x 10

moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>FeO<sub>14</sub> and the mass in both tablets:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (12 x 12.0) + (22 x 1.0) + 55.8 + (14 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 445.8

mass in 2 tablets = 1.35 x 10<sup>–3</sup> x 445.8

mass in 2 tablets = 0.60183 g

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by 2 for one tablet and convert to mg:

mass in 1 tablet = $\frac{0.60183}{2}$ x 1000

mass in 1 tablet = **301 mg**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> = 2.70 x 10<sup>–5</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–4</sup> mol **AND** in 250 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1.35 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub> = 445.8 **AND** mass in 2 tablets = 0.60183 g
> 
> 1 mark for final answer = 301 mg
> 
> Allow error carried forward if any error is correctly carried forward through subsequent steps

> **[exam-tip]**
> Take care with the *M*<sub>r</sub> calculation:
> 
> (12 x 12.0) + (22 x 1.0) + 55.8 + (14 x 16.0) = 445.8.
> 
> A common error is calculating the mass of Fe only rather than the mass of C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>FeO<sub>14</sub>, which gives 37.7 mg.
> 
> Remember the student crushed two tablets in step 1, so divide the total mass by 2 to get the mass per tablet. Convert from g to mg (x 1000) before rounding to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

A student carries out an experiment to determine the mass of iron(II) gluconate in one tablet of an iron supplement, using the method below.

1. The student crushes two tablets and dissolves the powdered tablets in dilute sulfuric acid
2. The student makes up the solution from step 1 to 250.0 cm^3^ in a volumetric flask.
3. The student then titrated 25.0 cm^3^ portions of the solution obtained in step 2 with 0.00200 mol dm^−3^ potassium manganate(VII).

The student obtains a mean titre of 13.50 cm^3^.

The typical concentration of a potassium manganate(VII) solution used in redox titrations is 0.0200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

Use the information in part (a) to explain, quantitatively, why the student replaced this with a 0.00200 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> potassium manganate(VII) solution for this titration.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The student used 0.00200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> instead of 0.0200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> because:
> 
> - A 0.0200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> potassium manganate(VII) solution would produce a titre of 1.35 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - This would be hard to measure accurately from a burette
> **OR**
> This would have a high (percentage) error / uncertainty **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks you to use the **information** in part (a) (the data given in the experiment), not your calculated answer. The 0.00200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> solution gives a 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup> titre. Since 0.0200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> is ten times more concentrated, it would require only 13.50 ÷ 10 = 1.35 cm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> A titre of 1.35 cm<sup>3</sup> is too small to measure accurately with a standard 50 cm<sup>3</sup> burette as it would have a very high percentage error.

parts.problemMd:
Some iron supplements contain iron(II) sulfate or iron(II) fumarate.

**Table 4.1** shows the information taken from the labels of two iron supplements, **A** and **B**.

**Table 4.1**

| **Iron supplement** | **Iron compound** | **Mass of iron compound in one tablet / mg** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Iron(II) sulfate, FeSO<sub>4</sub> | 180 |
| **B** | Iron(II) fumarate, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> | 210 |

State which iron supplement, **A** or **B**, would provide the greater mass of iron per tablet. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine which supplement provides the greater mass of iron per tablet:

- Calculate the mass of Fe in supplement **A**:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of FeSO<sub>4</sub> = 55.8 + 32.1 + (4 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of FeSO<sub>4</sub> = 151.9

mass of Fe in **A** = $\frac{55.8}{151.9}$ x 180

mass of Fe in **A** = 66.1 mg

- Calculate the mass of Fe in supplement **B**:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> = (4 x 12.0) + (2 x 1.0) + 55.8 + (4 x 16.0)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> = 169.8

mass of Fe in **B** = $\frac{55.8}{169.8}$ x 210

mass of Fe in **B** = 69.0 mg

**[1 mark]**

Supplement **B** provides the greater mass of iron per tablet (69.0 mg > 66.1 mg) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for mass of Fe in **A** = 66 mg **AND** mass of Fe in **B** = 69 mg (both correct)
> 
> Accept values to 3 sf: A = 66.1 mg, B = 69.0 mg
> 
> 1 mark for supplement **B** identified as providing the greater mass of iron per tablet

> **[exam-tip]**
> Iron fumarate contains iron as Fe<sup>2+</sup>: the fumarate ion (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>) pairs with Fe<sup>2+</sup>, giving iron(II) fumarate.
> 
> Calculate the mass of iron (not the mass of the compound) in each tablet. The *M*<sub>r</sub> values needed are FeSO<sub>4</sub> = 151.9 and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>2</sub>FeO<sub>4</sub> = 169.8.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction between ethanedioic acid, H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, and sodium hydroxide, NaOH.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction between ethanedioic acid and sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> (COOH)<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → (COONa)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanedioic acid (H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) may also be written as (COOH)<sub>2</sub>. It is a diprotic acid, so it reacts with 2 moles of NaOH to form the salt sodium ethanedioate / sodium oxalate (Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) and water.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The equation for the reaction between ethanedioic acid and sodium hydroxide:

H2C2O4 + 2NaOH → Na2C2O4 + 2H2O

OR

(COOH)2 + 2NaOH → (COONa)2 + 2H2O

15.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) requires 10.30 cm<sup>3</sup> of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of NaOH for complete neutralisation, using phenolphthalein as the indicator.

15.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of the same H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) required 12.35 cm<sup>3</sup> of potassium manganate(VII), KMnO<sub>4</sub>, solution for complete oxidation to carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid.

Calculate the concentration of the H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) solution.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentration of the H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> solution:

- Calculate the moles of NaOH:

moles of NaOH = $\frac{0.25\times10.30}{1000}$

moles of NaOH = 2.575 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (mole ratio H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> : NaOH = 1:2, from the equation in the previous part):

moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{2.575\times10^{-3}}{2}$

moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 1.2875 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>:

concentration = $\frac{1.2875\times10^{-3}}{15.00} \times 1000$

concentration of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = **0.0858 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of NaOH = 2.575 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 1.2875 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol (using 1:2 mole ratio)
> 
> 1 mark for concentration = 0.0858 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried foward as long as the error is carried forward correctly

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the equation from the previous part (H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O) to find the mole ratio: 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> reacts with 2 moles of NaOH.
> 
> The volume of KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution (12.35 cm<sup>3</sup>) given in the problem context is used to calculate the KMnO<sub>4</sub> concentration in a separate part. This calculation only requires the NaOH titration data.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

15.00 cm^3^ of the same H~2~C~2~O~4~ (aq) required 12.35 cm^3^ of potassium manganate(VII), KMnO~4~, solution for complete oxidation to carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid.

Construct the full redox equation, including state symbols, for this redox titration.
parts.solutionMd:
To construct the full redox equation for the KMnO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> titration:

- Construct the two half-equations:

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 8H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5e<sup>–</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**

H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 2e<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Combine the half-equations (multiply reduction x 2, oxidation x 5; cancel H<sup>+</sup> and e<sup>–</sup>):

2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) + 6H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + 5H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> (aq) → 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 8H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 10CO<sub>2</sub> (g) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> If state symbols are absent or incorrect, a maximum of 1 mark is deducted overall

> **[exam-tip]**
> The colour change at the end-point of a KMnO<sub>4</sub> redox titration is from purple (MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>) to very pale pink / colourless (Mn<sup>2+</sup>).
> 
> To derive the half-equations:
> 
> - MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> is reduced from +7 to +2 (gains 5 electrons per Mn)
> - H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is oxidised to CO<sub>2</sub> (loses 2 electrons per molecule)
> - Add H<sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O to balance charge and atoms.
> 
> To combine:
> 
> - Multiply the reduction half-equation by 2 and the oxidation half-equation by 5 so that both sides have 10 electrons.
> - Then cancel the 10e<sup>–</sup> and 10H<sup>+</sup> that appear on both sides.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

15.00 cm^3^ of H~2~C~2~O~4~ (aq) requires 10.30 cm^3^ of a 0.25 mol dm^-3^ solution of NaOH for complete neutralisation, using phenolphthalein as the indicator.

15.00 cm^3^ of the same H~2~C~2~O~4~ (aq) required 12.35 cm^3^ of potassium manganate(VII), KMnO~4~, solution for complete oxidation to carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid.

moles of H~2~C~2~O~4~ = 1.2875 x 10^-3^ mol

2MnO~4~^–^ (aq) + 6H^+^ (aq) + 5H~2~C~2~O~4~ (aq) → 2Mn^2+^ (aq) + 8H~2~O (l) + 10CO~2~ (g)

Calculate the concentration of the potassium manganate(VII), KMnO<sub>4</sub>, solution.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the concentration of the KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution:

- Calculate the moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> using the 5:2 mole ratio (H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> : MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>) from the full equation:

moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 1.2875 x 10<sup>-3</sup> x $\frac{2}{5}$

moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 5.15 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration of KMnO<sub>4</sub>:

concentration = $\frac{5.15\times10^{-4}\times1000}{12.35}$

concentration of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = **0.0417 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub> = 5.15 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol (using 5:2 mole ratio)
> 
> 1 mark for concentration = 0.0417 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Allow error carried forward if a different consistent value for moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is used

> **[exam-tip]**
> From the full equation 2MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + 6H<sup>+</sup> + 5H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> → 2Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 8H<sub>2</sub>O + 10CO<sub>2</sub>, the mole ratio of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> to MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> is 5:2. Multiply the moles of H<sub>2</sub>C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> by 2/5 to get the moles of KMnO<sub>4</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The d-orbitals of a transition element are involved in the formation of complexes.

Explain what is meant by the term degenerate orbitals.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Degenerate orbitals are:
> 
> - Orbitals that are all at the same energy level
> **OR**
> Orbitals that are equal in energy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although questions specifically on the definition of degenerate orbitals are uncommon in exams, understanding degeneracy is essential for explaining why transition element complexes are coloured as it underpins the whole d-orbital splitting concept.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the shape of the d<sub>xy</sub> orbital.

![dxy orbital showing four lobes arranged between the x and y axes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-3-colour-of-complexes/assets/008-dxy-orbital-showing-four-lobes-arranged-between-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

The d<sub>xz</sub> orbital has a similar shape but the lobes are between the x-axis and z-axis and the d<sub>yz</sub> orbital has a similar shape but the lobes are between the y-axis and z-axis.

i) State the difference in the spatial alignment of a d<sub>xy</sub> orbital compared to a d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital.

[1]

ii) Sketch the shape of a d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital on the axes provided in Fig. 1.2.

![Three-dimensional coordinate axes diagram showing x, y and z axes intersecting at the origin, with z vertical, x horizontal and y slanting between them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-3-colour-of-complexes/assets/009-three-dimensional-coordinate-axes-diagram-showin.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The difference in spatial alignment between a d<sub>xy</sub> orbital and a d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital is:
> 
> - The lobes of a d<sub>xy</sub> orbital point between the x and y axes
> **AND**
> The lobes of a d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital point along the x and y axes **[1 mark]**

ii) The shape of a d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital is:

![dz2 orbital showing two lobes extending along the z-axis and a ring of electron density in the xy-plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-3-colour-of-complexes/assets/010-dz2-orbital-showing-two-lobes-extending-along-th.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for two lobes along the z-axis
> 
> 1 mark for a ring / hoop / doughnut of electron density in the xy-plane

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is more common to be asked to draw the shapes of orbitals or to identify an orbital from a diagram than to describe the difference in spatial alignment. The key distinction is direction: d<sub>xy</sub> lobes point between the axes, whereas d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> lobes point along them. The d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital is unique in having two lobes along z plus a ring of electron density in the xy-plane.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The d-orbitals of a transition element are involved in the formation of complexes.

Degenerate orbitals are:
- Orbitals that are all at the same energy level
OR
Orbitals that are equal in energy

State what causes the d-orbitals in a transition element ion to become non-degenerate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The d-orbitals in a transition element ion become non-degenerate when:
> 
> - Dative covalent / coordinate bonds form between the transition element ion and ligands
> **OR**
> Ligands bond to / surround the transition element ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The splitting of the degenerate d-orbitals into two sets of non-degenerate d-orbitals is caused by the dative covalent bonding of ligands to the central metal ion. The extent of the splitting depends on the number, type, and size of the ligands present.

parts.problemMd:
The splitting of degenerate d-orbitals gives two sets of non-degenerate d-orbitals at different energy levels.

Complete Table 1.1 to show which d-orbitals have higher energy and which have lower energy in octahedral and tetrahedral complexes.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **Higher energy** | **Lower energy** |
|---|---|---|
| **Octahedral** |   |   |
| **Tetrahedral** |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|   | **Higher energy** | **Lower energy** |
|---|---|---|
| **Octahedral** | d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup>  and d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> | d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub> and d<sub>yz</sub> |
| **Tetrahedral** | d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub> and d<sub>yz</sub> | d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup>  and d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all d-orbitals correctly assigned for octahedral complexes
> 
> 1 mark for all d-orbitals correctly assigned for tetrahedral complexes

> **[exam-tip]**
> You only need to remember the energy assignments for one geometry because they are reversed in the other. In octahedral complexes, d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub>-y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> and d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> have higher energy; in tetrahedral complexes these same orbitals have lower energy, with d<sub>xy</sub>, d<sub>xz</sub> and d<sub>yz</sub> taking the higher energy positions.

parts.problemMd: Define the term transition element.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A transition element is:
> 
> - (A d-block element that can) form one or more stable ions with an incomplete d subshell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a standard definition you are required to know. Note that zinc and scandium are not transition elements: Zn<sup>2+</sup> has a full 3d subshell (d<sup>10</sup>) and Sc<sup>3+</sup> has an empty 3d subshell (d<sup>0</sup>), so neither meets the definition.

parts.problemMd:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, acts as a monodentate ligand in many transition element complexes.

i) Define the term monodentate ligand.

[2]

ii) Aqueous silver ions, Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq), react with aqueous ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub> (aq), to form a linear complex.

State the formula of this complex. Include its charge.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A monodentate ligand is defined as:
> 
> - A species / molecule / ion that forms one dative covalent / coordinate bond to a central metal ion **[1 mark]**
> - Using a lone pair of electrons to form the bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The formula of this complex, including its charge, is:
> 
> - [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Monodentate ligands form only one coordinate bond to the central metal ion. Common examples include:
> 
> - Water (H<sub>2</sub>O)
> - Ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>)
> - Chloride ions (Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> - Cyanide ions (CN<sup>-</sup>).
> 
> The linear [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> complex forms because Ag<sup>+</sup> adopts linear geometry with two coordinate bonds. Since NH<sub>3</sub> carries no charge, the overall charge of the complex equals the charge on the silver ion.

parts.problemMd:
There are two isomeric complex ions with the formula [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>. One is green and the other is violet.

i) State the type of stereoisomerism shown by these two complex ions.

[1]

ii) Explain why these complex ions are coloured, and why their colours are different.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of stereoisomerism shown is:
> 
> - Cis-trans / geometrical (stereoisomerism) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) These complex ions are coloured and have different colours because:
> 
> - Ligands split the d-orbitals into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels **[1 mark]**
> - Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The observed colour is the complement of the colour of light absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The two isomers have different spatial arrangements of ligands, giving different d-orbital splitting energies (Δ*E*), so different wavelengths of light are absorbed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four marking points for colour are always the same:
> 
> 1. d-orbital splitting by ligands
> 2. Visible light absorbed / electron promoted
> 3. Complementary colour observed
> 4. Different spatial arrangement of ligands → different Δ*E* → different wavelength absorbed.
> 
> Learn these four points and you will always score full marks on this type of question.
> 
> ![Cis and trans isomers of [Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ showing the two different spatial arrangements of chloride ligands around the octahedral chromium centre](assets/002-cis-and-trans-isomers-of-cr-nh3-4cl2-showing-the.jpeg)

Ethane-1,2-diamine, H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is represented as en. Nickel forms the complex ion [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, in which it is surrounded octahedrally by six nitrogen atoms.

Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

![Blank three-dimensional octahedral framework for drawing the two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)3]2+](assets/003-blank-three-dimensional-octahedral-framework-for.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The two stereoisomers of [Ni(en)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are:

![Optical isomers of [Ni(en)3]2+ showing three bidentate en ligands in a left-handed propeller arrangement around the nickel centre and a right-handed propeller arrangement around the nickel centre](assets/004-optical-isomers-of-ni-en-3-2-showing-three-biden.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct first stereoisomer
> 
> 1 mark for a second correct stereoisomer that is the non-superimposable mirror image of the first
> 
> "en" notation is acceptable in place of the full structural formula H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>

> ![Alternative representations of ethane-1,2-diamine, a bidentate ligand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-3-colour-of-complexes/assets/005-alternative-representations-of-ethane-1-2-diamin.png)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethane-1,2-diamine is a bidentate ligand because each NH<sub>2</sub> group can donate a lone pair to the central metal ion. parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Ethane-1,2-diamine, H₂NCH₂CH₂NH₂, is represented as en.

Ethane-1,2-diamine is a useful reagent in organic chemistry.

i) Explain why ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base.

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction of ethane-1,2-diamine with an excess of hydrochloric acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base because:
> 
> - The nitrogen atoms have lone pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - These lone pairs accept protons / are donated to protons (from the acid) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction with excess hydrochloric acid is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → ClH<sub>3</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts protons using a lone pair of electrons. Ethane-1,2-diamine has two NH<sub>2</sub> groups, each with a lone pair on nitrogen, so it can accept two protons in total. With excess HCl, both amino groups are protonated. You can also write the ionic equation: H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → (H<sub>3</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>)<sup>2+</sup>

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the geometry and colours of transition element complexes.

Explain why transition elements have variable oxidation states but Group 1 elements do not.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Transition elements have variable oxidation states but Group 1 elements do not because:
> 
> - In transition elements, the 4s and 3d subshells are close in energy / successive ionisation energies increase gradually **[1 mark]**
> - In Group 1 elements, the second electron is removed from a much lower energy level / there is a large increase in ionisation energy between the first and second ionisation energies **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should be able to explain variable oxidation states in terms of successive ionisation energies. For transition elements, the small differences between ionisation energies mean that several oxidation states are energetically accessible. For Group 1 elements, the second ionisation energy is far higher than the first because the electron is removed from a stable noble gas core, so only the +1 oxidation state is observed.

parts.problemMd:
Transition element compounds are often coloured. For example, [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is green.

Explain why transition element complexes are coloured.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Transition element complexes are coloured because:
> 
> - Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels **[1 mark]**
> - Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital **[1 mark]**
> - The observed colour is the complement of the colour of light absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The wavelength of light absorbed depends on the size of the d-orbital splitting energy (Δ*E*), which depends on the identity and number of ligands **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These four marking points come up every time a question asks why transition element complexes are coloured. Learn them in order:
> 
> 1. d-orbital splitting by ligands
> 2. Visible light absorbed / electron promoted
> 3. Complementary colour observed
> 4. Different ligands give different Δ*E*, hence different colours.
> 
> If the question only asks why the complex is coloured (not why different complexes have different colours), points 1–3 are sufficient.

parts.problemMd:
Zinc and cobalt ions react with water to form the complexes [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

i) Explain why water is able to act as a ligand in forming these complexes.

[2]

ii) State the geometry of the [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex ion.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Water is able to act as a ligand because:
> 
> - Oxygen has a lone pair of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Which it donates to form a dative covalent / coordinate bond with the metal ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The geometry of [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:
> 
> - Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand must be able to donate a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate bond with the central metal ion — it acts as a Lewis base. Water uses the lone pairs on the oxygen atom for this purpose. With six water ligands, [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> adopts an octahedral geometry to place the six coordinate bonds as far apart as possible.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Transition element complexes are coloured because:

- Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels
- Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital
- The observed colour is the complement of the colour of light absorbed
- The wavelength of light absorbed depends on the size of the d-orbital splitting energy (ΔE), which depends on the identity and number of ligands

Explain why solutions containing [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are colourless.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> [Zn(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is colourless because:
> 
> - The Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion has a completely full 3d subshell (d<sup>10</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - No d-d electron transitions can occur / no electrons can be promoted between d-orbitals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Zinc is not a transition element because Zn<sup>2+</sup> has the electron configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>, which is a full 3d subshell.
> 
> For a complex to be coloured, d-orbital splitting must occur and an electron must be able to move between the two sets.
> 
> With a completely full d subshell, this is impossible, so no visible light is absorbed and the solution appears colourless. Contrast this with Co<sup>2+</sup>, which has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>7</sup> (a partially filled 3d subshell) and can absorb visible light.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain why aqueous nickel(II) ions, Ni<sup>2+</sup>(aq), are green.

[4]

ii) Explain why aqueous scandium(III) ions, Sc<sup>3+</sup>(aq), are colourless.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Aqueous Ni<sup>2+</sup> ions are green because:
> 
> - Ligands cause the d-orbitals to split into two sets of non-degenerate energy levels **[1 mark]**
> - Visible light is absorbed when an electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher energy d-orbital **[1 mark]**
> - Ni<sup>2+</sup> has a partially filled 3d subshell, so d-d electron transitions can occur **[1 mark]**
> - The observed colour (green) is the complement of the colour of light absorbed **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Aqueous Sc<sup>3+</sup> ions are colourless because:
> 
> - Sc<sup>3+</sup> has an empty 3d subshell (d<sup>0</sup>), so no d-d electron transitions can occur **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Scandium is not a transition element because Sc<sup>3+</sup> has the electron configuration [Ar], it has no 3d electrons at all.
> 
> Without any electrons in the d-orbitals, no d-d transitions are possible and no visible light is absorbed, so Sc<sup>3+</sup> solutions are colourless.
> 
> Nickel(II) has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>8</sup>, which is a partially filled 3d subshell, so it can form coloured complexes.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to aqueous copper(II) ions causes a change in the colour of the solution.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Adding excess aqueous ammonia to aqueous copper(II) ions causes a colour change because:
> 
> - (Four of the) water ligands are replaced by ammonia ligands / ligand exchange occurs **[1 mark]**
> - The d-orbital splitting energy (Δ*E*) between the two sets of d-orbitals changes because it depends on the identity of the ligand **[1 mark]**
> - A different wavelength / frequency of light is absorbed, so a different colour is observed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> First recognise that adding excess ammonia causes ligand exchange: water ligands in [Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are replaced by ammonia ligands to form [Cu(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>2</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.
> 
> Different ligands cause different extents of d-orbital splitting, so the energy gap changes. Since a different wavelength of light is absorbed, the complementary colour seen changes, and the solution appears a deeper blue.

parts.problemMd:
The [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup> complex ion contains iron and cyanide ligands.

i) Deduce the oxidation state of iron in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup>. Show your working.

[1]

ii) Draw the arrangement of electrons in the 3d and 4s subshells of the iron ion in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup>, using arrow-in-box notation.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To deduce the oxidation state of iron in [Fe(CN)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>4-</sup>:

Fe + (6 x -1) = -4

Fe = +2 **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for +2 with working shown (CN<sup>-</sup> = -1 stated or implied; Fe + 6(-1) = -4 seen)

ii) The arrangement of electrons in the 3d and 4s subshells of the Fe<sup>2+</sup> ion is:

![Fe2+ orbital box diagram showing the 3d subshell with six electrons arranged as three pairs in the lower three boxes and empty 4s subshell, with [Ar] noble gas core notation](assets/001-fe2-orbital-box-diagram-showing-the-3d-subshell-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for six electrons correctly arranged in the 3d subshell with empty 4s and [Ar] noble gas core notation

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the oxidation state, recall that each CN<sup>-</sup> ligand carries a -1 charge. With six CN<sup>-</sup> ligands, total charge from ligands = 6 x (-1) = -6. The overall complex charge is -4, so: Fe + (-6) = -4, giving Fe = +2.
> 
> For the orbital diagram, Fe<sup>2+</sup> has the configuration [Ar]3d<sup>6</sup> — the 4s subshell is empty because electrons are removed from 4s before 3d. Include [Ar] at the start to indicate the noble gas core.

parts.problemMd:
Cobalt is a transition element with atomic number 27.

Complete the electronic configurations of a Co atom and a Co<sup>2+</sup> ion.

Co atom   1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>  ..................................

Co<sup>2+</sup> ion   1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup>  ..................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The electronic configurations of a Co atom and a Co<sup>2+</sup> ion are:
> 
> - Co atom: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup>
> **OR**
> 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 4s<sup>2</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Co<sup>2+</sup> ion: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although the Periodic Table suggests electrons fill in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, the correct filling order is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 3d, 4s. The 3d orbital is slightly lower in energy than 4s, so 3d fills before 4s.
> 
> You can check your answer by adding up all the electrons:
> 
> 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 7 + 2 = 27
> 
> When writing the Co<sup>2+</sup> ion configuration, remember that 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons. Co<sup>2+</sup> has 25 electrons, so the 4s electrons are removed first, giving 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>6</sup> 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>6</sup> 3d<sup>7</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
When concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to a solution containing [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, a ligand exchange reaction occurs.

Draw a three-dimensional diagram to show the shape of the complex ion formed. Include the overall charge.

overall charge ......................................
parts.solutionMd:
The complex ion formed is the tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion:

![Three-dimensional tetrahedral diagram of [CoCl4]2- with cobalt at the centre and four chloride ligands at the corners, showing correct 3D bonds](assets/001-tetrahedral-cocl4-2-complex-with-cobalt-at-the-c.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional tetrahedral diagram with four chloride ligands and 3D bonds shown
> 
> 1 mark for correct overall charge: 2- / [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, all six water ligands are replaced by four chloride ions. Chloride ions are larger than water molecules, so the coordination number changes from 6 to 4, and the geometry changes from octahedral to tetrahedral.
> 
> The overall charge: Co<sup>2+</sup> + 4(Cl<sup>-</sup>) = +2 + 4(-1) = -2, giving [CoCl<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2-</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Co<sup>2+</sup> ions exist as [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex ions in aqueous solution.

Complete the three-dimensional diagram to show the shape of this complex. State the geometry. On your diagram, state the bond angle.

![Blank three-dimensional octahedral diagram of [Co(H2O)6]2+ with cobalt at the centre and positions for six water ligands to be added](assets/010-blank-three-dimensional-octahedral-diagram-of-co.png)

geometry ..................................................
parts.solutionMd:
The completed three-dimensional diagram of [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> is:

![Three-dimensional octahedral diagram of [Co(H2O)6]2+ with six water ligands and bond angles of 90 degrees and 180 degrees labeled on the diagram](assets/011-three-dimensional-octahedral-diagram-of-co-h2o-6.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional octahedral structure showing six water ligands **AND** correct 2+ overall charge
> 
> 1 mark for stating octahedral geometry
> 
> 1 mark for stating a bond angle of 90° on the diagram (allow 180°)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Complexes with six ligands always form an octahedral geometry. The bond angles in an octahedral complex are 90° between adjacent ligands and 180° between opposite ligands.

parts.problemMd:
When aqueous ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub> (aq), is added to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq), dropwise at first and then in excess, two distinct chemical reactions occur. For each reaction, state the expected observations and construct an equation.

i) Addition of a few drops of NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)

observation .............................................................................

equation ..................................................................................

[2]

ii) Addition of an excess of NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)

observation .............................................................................

equation ..................................................................................

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Observations and equation for addition of a few drops of NH<sub>3</sub> (aq):
> 
> - Observation: blue / blue-green precipitate **[1 mark]**
> - [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq)

> [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) ⇌ Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**

> 
> - Observation: (straw) yellow / brown solution **[1 mark]**
> - Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>4</sub>(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 6NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq)
> **OR**
> Co(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 6NH<sub>3</sub> (aq) ⇌ [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>-</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Cobalt(II) and copper(II) are the two transition metals commonly tested for ligand substitution reactions with aqueous ammonia.
> 
> Cobalt(II) undergoes complete substitution with six water ligands replaced by six ammonia ligands, forming [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>. In contrast, copper(II) undergoes partial substitution with only four of the six water ligands replaced.
> 
> The [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> complex is unstable in air and readily oxidises to form a blue [Co(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> solution. You may be asked about this in a follow-on question.

parts.problemMd:
EDTA<sup>4-</sup> is a hexadentate ligand. When a solution of EDTA<sup>4-</sup> is added to a solution containing [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, a new complex is formed. The formula of this complex is [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup>.

i) Explain what is meant by the term hexadentate ligand.

[2]

ii) State the type of reaction occurring here.

[1]

iii) Write an expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, of [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> in this reaction.

[1]

iv) The numerical value of the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> is 7.7 x 10<sup>4</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup> at 298 K.

Deduce what this value indicates about the stability of [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> compared to [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The meaning of the term hexadentate ligand:
> 
> - A ligand that can donate six lone pairs of electrons (to a central metal atom / ion) **[1 mark]**
> - To form six dative (covalent) / coordinate bonds **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / replacement / displacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The stability constant expression for [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup>] / ([[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>][[EDTA]<sup>4-</sup>]) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) The value of *K*<sub>stab</sub> indicates that:
> 
> - [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> is (very) stable / more stable than [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A ligand is a species that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal atom or ion to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond. The prefix tells you how many lone pairs it can donate: mono (1), bi (2), and so on up to hexa (6).
> 
> Since all six water ligands in [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> are replaced by one EDTA<sup>4-</sup> ligand, this is a ligand exchange reaction. The equation is:
> 
> [Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4-</sup> ⇌ [CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> The *K*<sub>stab</sub> expression follows from this equation in the same way as any equilibrium expression. Water is not included because it is the solvent:
> 
> *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[CoEDTA]<sup>2-</sup>] / ([[Co(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>][[EDTA]<sup>4-</sup>])
> 
> The greater the value of *K*<sub>stab</sub>, the more stable the complex ion is relative to the aquo complex it replaced.

parts.problemMd:
Several platinum complexes, including oxoplatin, iproplatin, ormaplatin and satraplatin, are used as anti-cancer drugs. The central platinum ions in the four complexes shown in **Fig. 1.1** all have the same geometry and oxidation state.

![Structural diagrams of four platinum anti-cancer drug complexes: oxoplatin, iproplatin, ormaplatin and satraplatin](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-4-stereoisomerism-in-transition-element-complexes/assets/004-structural-diagrams-of-four-platinum-anti-cancer.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the oxidation state of the platinum ion and the geometry of these complexes.

oxidation state of the platinum ion ..................................................

geometry of the complexes ..................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The oxidation state and geometry of the platinum complexes are:
> 
> - Oxidation state of the platinum ion = +4 **[1 mark]**
> - Geometry of the complexes = Octahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To deduce the oxidation state of platinum, use oxoplatin as it contains familiar ligands. The charge contributions are:
> 
> - OH<sup>-</sup> contributes -1
> - Cl<sup>-</sup> contributes -1
> - NH<sub>3</sub> contributes 0 (neutral ligand)
> 
> Since the overall charge on the complex is 0:
> 
> Pt + 2(-1) + 2(-1) + 2(0) = 0
> 
> Pt - 4 = 0
> 
> Pt = +4
> 
> All four complexes have 6 coordinate bonds, so the geometry must be octahedral.
