parts.problemMd:
i) Some transition elements and their compounds behave as catalysts. Explain why transition elements behave as catalysts.

[2]

ii) Catalysis can be classified as heterogeneous or homogeneous. Complete Table 1.1 by placing **one **tick (`✓`) in each row to indicate the type of catalysis in each reaction.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **type of catalysis** |   |
|---|---|---|
| **reaction** | **heterogeneous** | **homogeneous** |
| Fe in the Haber process |   |   |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the I<sup>–</sup> / S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reaction |   |   |
| NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> |   |   |

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Transition elements are able to act as catalysts because:
> 
> - Transition elements have more than one stable oxidation state **[1 mark]**
> - There are vacant d-orbitals that can accept lone pairs from reactant molecules
> **OR**
> They can form dative bonds with ligands **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed Table 1.1:

|   | **type of catalysis** |   |
|---|---|---|
| **reaction** | **heterogeneous** | **homogeneous** |
| Fe in the Haber process | `\checkmark` |   |
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> in the I<sup>–</sup> / S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reaction |   | `\checkmark` |
| NO<sub>2</sub> in the oxidation of SO<sub>2</sub> |   | `\checkmark` |

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for all three rows correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), the two key properties that allow transition elements to act as catalysts are their ability to adopt multiple oxidation states (allowing them to act as both electron donors and acceptors in reaction cycles) and their vacant d-orbitals (which allow reactant molecules to form coordinate bonds with the metal).
> 
> For part (ii), a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from its reactants. Iron in the Haber process is a solid while the reactant gases N<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> are in the gas phase.
> 
> A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants. Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions and the I<sup>–</sup>/S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>8</sub><sup>2–</sup> reactants are all aqueous. NO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>2</sub> are both gases.

parts.problemMd:
A solution containing a mixture of Sn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and Sn<sup>4+</sup> (aq) is added to a solution containing a mixture of Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) and Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq).

Table 2.2 lists electrode potentials for some electrode reactions of these ions.

**Table 2.2**

| **electrode reaction** | ***E***<sup>**ɵ**</sup>** / V** |
|---|---|
| Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.44 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 3e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe | –0.04 |
| Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> | +0.77 |
| Sn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Sn | –0.14 |
| Sn<sup>4+</sup> + 2e<sup>–</sup> ⇌ Sn<sup>2+</sup> | +0.15 |

*E*<sup>ɵ</sup> data from the table can be used to predict the reaction that takes place when the two solutions are mixed.

i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Calculate *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for this reaction:
> 
> - Sn<sup>2+</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → Sn<sup>4+</sup> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required.
> 
> ii) The standard cell potential:
> 
> - *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = 0.77 – 0.15 = **+0.62 V** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the equation, compare the *E*<sup>ɵ</sup> values: Sn<sup>2+</sup>/Sn<sup>4+</sup> (+0.15 V) is less positive than Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+0.77 V). The less positive electrode acts as the anode (oxidation), so Sn<sup>2+</sup> is oxidised to Sn<sup>4+</sup>. The Fe<sup>3+</sup> half-equation runs in the forward direction (reduction). Balance electrons: 2 moles of Fe<sup>3+</sup> are reduced per mole of Sn<sup>2+</sup> oxidised.
> 
> For *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub>, use:
> 
> *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>reduction</sub> – *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>oxidation</sub>:
> 
> *E*<sup>ɵ</sup><sub>cell</sub> = (+0.77) – (+0.15) = +0.62 V

parts.problemMd:
Hexaaquairon(III) ions are pale violet. They form a colourless complex with fluoride ions, F<sup>–</sup>, as shown in equilibrium **1**, and a deep-red complex with thiocyanate ions, SCN<sup>–</sup>, as shown in equilibrium **2**.

equilibrium **1:**

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + F<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

violet ⇌ colourless

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

equilibrium **2:**

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> + SCN<sup>–</sup> ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O

violet ⇌ deep-red

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>

The following two experiments are carried out.

Experiment 1: A few drops of KSCN (aq) are added to 5 cm<sup>3</sup> of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq), followed by a few drops of KF (aq).

Experiment 2: A few drops of KF (aq) are added to 5 cm<sup>3</sup> of Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq), followed by a few drops of KSCN (aq).

i) State and explain the sequence of colour changes you would observe in each of Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.

[4]

ii) State the type of reaction occurring during the experiments in **(d)(i)**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The colour changes observed are:
> 
> Experiment 1:
> 
> - Violet to deep-red (adding KSCN forms the thiocyanate complex) **[1 mark]**
> - Deep-red to colourless (adding KF displaces the thiocyanate complex) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Experiment 2:
> 
> - Violet to colourless (adding KF forms the fluoride complex), remaining colourless on addition of KSCN **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup> > *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup>
> **OR**
> 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> > 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup>, so the fluoride complex is more stable and displaces the thiocyanate complex **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The type of reaction:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> In Experiment 2, the fluoride complex is not displaced by SCN<sup>–</sup> because the F<sup>–</sup> complex has the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> value.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through each experiment step by step.
> 
> Experiment 1: the pale violet [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> turns deep-red when KSCN is added, forming [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>SCN]<sup>2+</sup>. When KF is then added, the solution becomes colourless because the fluoride complex ([Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>F]<sup>2+</sup>, *K*<sub>stab</sub> = 2.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>) is more stable than the thiocyanate complex (*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>) and displaces it.
> 
> Experiment 2: the pale violet solution turns colourless when KF is added. When KSCN is then added, there is no colour change. The fluoride complex has the larger *K*<sub>stab</sub> value and cannot be displaced by SCN<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> For part (ii), any reaction in which one ligand replaces another is called ligand exchange or ligand substitution.

parts.problemMd:
Solutions of iron(III) salts are acidic due to the equilibrium shown.

[Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+ </sup>(aq) ⇌ [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>5</sub>(OH)]<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq)

K<sub>a</sub> = 8.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>

Calculate the pH of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> FeCl<sub>3 </sub>solution. Show your working.

pH = ..........................................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the pH of a 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> FeCl<sub>3</sub> solution:

- Find [H<sup>+</sup>]:

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> × [Fe<sup>3+</sup>]

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 8.9 × 10<sup>–4</sup> × 0.25

[H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 2.225 × 10<sup>–4</sup>

[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\sqrt{2.225\times10^{-4}}$

[H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.0149 mol dm<sup>–3 </sup>**[1 mark]**

- Calculate pH:

pH = –log(0.0149)

pH = **1.83** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = 0.0149 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> (accept 0.01492)
> 
> 1 mark for pH in the range 1.8–1.83

> **[exam-tip]**
> For this weak acid calculation, use:
> 
> [H<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = *K*<sub>a</sub> × [HA]
> 
> This assumes [H<sup>+</sup>] equals [A<sup>–</sup>] (both produced in equal amounts) and that the equilibrium concentration of the weak acid equals the initial concentration, since the degree of dissociation is small.
> 
> Here, [Fe(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> acts as the weak acid, so [HA]<sub>initial</sub> = 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. Take the square root to find [H<sup>+</sup>], then use pH = –log[H<sup>+</sup>].

parts.problemMd: Define the term ligand.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A ligand is a molecule or ion that:
> 
> - Contains a lone pair of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Donates a lone pair to a central metal ion to form a coordinate / dative (covalent) bond **[1 mark]**
> 
> A ligand must be described as a molecule or ion, not just a species
> 
> Stating only 'donates electrons' without specifying a lone pair is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A complete definition requires two elements: that the ligand possesses a lone pair of electrons, and that it donates that lone pair to the metal ion to form a coordinate bond.

parts.solutionMd:
i) To calculate the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, and its units:

- Recall that the overall stability constant is the product of the stepwise constants:

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = *K*<sub>1</sub> x *K*<sub>2</sub> x *K*<sub>3</sub> x *K*<sub>4</sub>

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = 1.78 x 10<sup>4</sup> x 4.07 x 10<sup>3</sup> x 9.55 x 10<sup>2</sup> x 1.74 x 10<sup>2</sup>

*K*<sub>stab</sub> = **1.20 x 10**<sup>**13**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> 
> 1 mark for units dm<sup>12</sup> mol<sup>-4</sup>

> The overall *K*<sub>stab</sub> equals the product of all stepwise stability constants: *K*<sub>stab</sub> = *K*<sub>1</sub> x *K*<sub>2</sub> x *K*<sub>3</sub> x *K*<sub>4</sub>.
>

parts.solutionMd:

> The stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, is:

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

|   | Ag<sup>+</sup> | NH<sub>3</sub> | ⇌ | [Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)]<sup>+</sup> |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| change / mol dm<sup>–3</sup> | −0.4998 | −0.4998 |   | +0.4998 |

parts.problemMd:
The complex [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> is significantly more stable than the complex [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>.

By considering the ligand exchange reaction between [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>, explain this difference in stability in terms of entropy changes.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in stability in terms of entropy changes:
> 
> - [Ni(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup> + EDTA<sup>4–</sup> ⇌ [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup> + 6NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - The number of particles / moles of species increases from 2 (on the left) to 7 (on the right), so entropy increases / Δ*S* is positive **[1 mark]**
> - The positive Δ*S* makes Δ*G* more negative (via Δ*G* = Δ*H* − *T*Δ*S*), making the ligand exchange more feasible / the EDTA complex more stable **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The chelate effect: polydentate ligands like EDTA displace multiple monodentate ligands in a single exchange step, increasing the total number of particles in solution and therefore increasing entropy.
> 
> Even if the enthalpy changes are similar, the more positive Δ*S* for EDTA displacement makes Δ*G* more negative, favouring formation of [Ni(EDTA)]<sup>2–</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
When chromium(III) sulfate dissolves in water, a violet solution containing the [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> ion forms.

i) State the bond angles found in this complex ion.

[1]

ii) Explain why the chromium(III) complex ion is coloured.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The bond angle is:
> 
> - 90° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> is octahedral as six identical water ligands arranged symmetrically around the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion. All six ligand-metal-ligand bond angles between adjacent ligands are 90°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The chromium(III) complex ion is coloured because:
> 
> - The water ligands cause the 3d orbitals to split into two energy levels of different energies **[1 mark]**
> - Light / radiation in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum is absorbed **[1 mark]**
> - The absorbed energy promotes electrons from the lower 3d energy level to the higher 3d energy level **[1 mark]**
> - The complementary colour / violet light is transmitted / observed **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'Green light is transmitted' is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> In an isolated transition metal atom the five 3d orbitals are degenerate (equal energy). When a complex ion forms, the ligands split the 3d orbitals into two energy levels. Light of a wavelength matching this energy gap is absorbed, promoting an electron to the higher level. The remaining complementary colour is transmitted and observed.
> 
> A common error is to state that colour arises because electrons 'return to their ground state and emit light', but this describes emission spectra (flame tests), not complex ion colour.
> 
> Also note: the question specifies [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, which appears violet, not green. Stating the wrong transmitted colour will lose the final mark.

ii) Write an expression for the stability constant, *K*<sub>stab</sub>, of [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> in this reaction.

[1]

iii) The numerical value of the *K*<sub>stab</sub> of [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is 2.51 × 10<sup>23</sup> in this reaction.

Suggest what this indicates about the position and entropy of the equilibrium.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction occuring is:
> 
> - Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement / replacement **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The stability constant expression for [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>stab</sub> = [[Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup>] / ([[Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>][EDTA<sup>4–</sup>]) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Identify the product ([Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup>) and the two reactants ([Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>) from the equation given in the question. Write the product concentration in the numerator and the reactant concentrations in the denominator. Water is excluded as the solvent.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The large value of *K*<sub>stab</sub> for [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> indicates:
> 
> - The equilibrium lies far to the right / [Cr(EDTA)]<sup>–</sup> is more stable than [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>
> **OR**
> The forward reaction is very feasible / spontaneous / goes to completion **[1 mark]**
> - Δ*S*<sub>system</sub> is positive / entropy increases **[1 mark]**
> - The number of moles / particles increases from 2 (reactants) to 7 (products)
> **OR**
> 2 moles of reactants form 7 moles of products **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explaining only the entropy change without addressing the position of equilibrium is not accepted for full marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> A large *K*<sub>stab</sub> means the equilibrium strongly favours products.
> 
> The entropy change follows from the ligand exchange equation: 2 species on the left (the hexaaqua complex and EDTA<sup>4–</sup>) produce 7 on the right (1 Cr-EDTA complex + 6 water molecules), so the number of particles increases and Δ*S* is positive.
> 
> This is the chelate effect: replacing six monodentate ligands with one hexadentate ligand in a single step greatly increases entropy and drives the reaction forward.

parts.problemMd:
Chromium(III) picolinate, shown in Fig. 1.2, is a neutral complex that can be prepared from the weak acid, picolinic acid.

![Structural formula of chromium(III) picolinate showing a Cr3+ ion coordinated to three picolinate ligands in an octahedral arrangement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/004-structural-formula-of-chromium-iii-picolinate-sh.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Chromium(III) picolinate is used in tablets as a nutritional supplement for chromium.

i) Draw the structure of the ligand in chromium(III) picolinate.

[1]

ii) A typical tablet of chromium(III) picolinate contains 200 μg of chromium.

Calculate the mass, in g, of chromium(III) picolinate in a typical tablet. Give your answer to three significant figures. Show your working.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of the ligand in chromium(III) picolinate is:

![Structure of the picolinate ligand showing a pyridine ring with a deprotonated carboxylate group (COO–) at the 2-position, and a lone pair on the nitrogen for coordination](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/28-chemistry-of-transition-elements/28-5-stability-constants-kstab/assets/005-structure-of-the-picolinate-ligand-showing-a-pyr.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the picolinate ligand: pyridine ring with deprotonated carboxylate (COO<sup>–</sup>) at position 2, without a negative charge on the nitrogen
> 
> The negative charge on the nitrogen is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The picolinate ligand is picolinic acid (pyridine-2-carboxylic acid) after deprotonation of the COOH group.
> 
> Three of nitrogen's five valence electrons are used in bonding within the pyridine ring, leaving a lone pair that forms the coordinate bond with Cr<sup>3+</sup>.
> 
> The nitrogen does not carry a formal negative charge, only the carboxylate oxygen does.

ii) To calculate the mass, in g, of chromium(III) picolinate in a typical tablet:

- State the *M*<sub>r</sub> of chromium(III) picolinate:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = 418.0

- Calculate moles of chromium (1 μg = 10<sup>–6</sup> g):

n(Cr) = $\frac{200\times10^{-6}}{52.0}$

n(Cr) = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate mass of chromium(III) picolinate:

mass = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> x 418.0

mass = **1.61 x 10**<sup>**–3**</sup> g **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *M*<sub>r</sub>(chromium(III) picolinate) = 418.0 **AND** moles of chromium = 3.85 x 10<sup>–6</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass = 1.61 x 10<sup>–3</sup> g (to 3 s.f.)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The *M*<sub>r</sub> of chromium(III) picolinate requires care: the picolinate ligand has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 122.1, and three coordinate to the Cr<sup>3+</sup> ion (plus one proton lost per ligand), giving *M*<sub>r</sub> = 52.0 + (3 x 122.0) = 418.0. Remember 1 μg = 10<sup>–6</sup> g.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **L** is a complex with the empirical formula CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>3</sub>

The formula of compound **L** contains one chloride ion and a complex ion **M**, which has two stereoisomers.

i) Deduce the formula of complex ion **M**.

[1]

ii) Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two stereoisomers of complex ion **M**.

[2]

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **L** has the empirical formula CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>3</sub> and contains one ionically-bonded chloride ion. Removing this gives complex ion **M** the composition CrN<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> with a 1+ charge. The N<sub>4</sub>H<sub>12</sub> portion is four NH<sub>3</sub> ligands, giving the formula [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup>.

ii) The three-dimensional diagrams showing the two stereoisomers of complex ion **M** are:

![Three-dimensional diagrams of cis-[Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ and trans-[Cr(NH3)4Cl2]+ showing correct wedge-dash notation with 1+ charges indicated on both isomers](assets/006-three-dimensional-diagrams-of-cis-cr-nh3-4cl2-an.png)

**[2 marks]**

> 
> 1 mark for the second isomer drawn as the other geometric isomer (*cis* or *trans*), correctly labelled, with 1+ charge shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>]<sup>+</sup> is octahedral and exists as *cis* (both Cl adjacent, 90° apart) and *trans* (both Cl opposite, 180° apart) isomers. Draw each with 2 'out wedges', 2 'in wedges', and 2 bonds in the plane of the paper.

parts.problemMd:
The structural formulae of four different organic compounds are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Structural formula** | **IUPAC name** |
|---|---|
| C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> |   |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO |   |
| CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> |   |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |   |

Complete Table 1.1 by stating the systematic (IUPAC) name for each compound.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Structural formula** | **IUPAC name** |
|---|---|
| C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **methylbenzene** |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO | **Final answer:** **pentanal** |
| CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **dimethylamine** |
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H | **Final answer:** **2-aminopropanoic acid** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for methylbenzene
> 
> 1 mark for pentanal
> 
> 1 mark for dimethylamine
> 
> 1 mark for 2-aminopropanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> For C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> tells you this is a benzene ring
> - The five hydrogen atoms in the structure tell you that one hydrogen atom has been substituted, in this case for a CH<sub>3</sub> group
> - Therefore it is methylbenzene
> 
> For CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO:
> 
> - The CHO group at the end of the molecule indicates the compound is an aldehyde
> - There are five carbon atoms in the straight chain, so the name is pentanal
> 
> For CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub>:
> 
> - The NH atom indicates that this is an amine
> - There are two CH<sub>3</sub> groups bonded to the nitrogen atom, so dimethyl- should be in the name
> - Therefore the name is dimethylamine
> 
> For CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H:
> 
> - This compound is an amino acid
> - There are three carbon atoms in the chain with a carboxylic acid group, CO<sub>2</sub>H
> - This group takes priority so is named last: propanoic acid
> - There is also a NH<sub>2</sub> group (amine group) bonded to the second carbon
> - Therefore the name is 2-aminopropanoic acid

> - HCl is eliminated **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An addition-elimination reaction involves two molecules joining together with the simultaneous loss of a small molecule. In this case:
> 
> - Addition: water adds across the C=O bond
> - Elimination: HCl is lost
> 
> Other named mechanisms to know:
> 
> - Free-radical substitution
> - Electrophilic addition

> - Electrophilic substitution

**[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The reaction pathway for the formation of an N-substituted amide is shown in a three-step synthesis in Fig. 2.1. In step 1, the major product of the reaction is formed.

The IUPAC names of compounds **W** and **X**:
- **W** is propene
- **X** is 2-chloropropane

5.0 g of compound **W** was used to produce compound **X**. The percentage yield was 64%.

i) Calculate the mass, in grams, of compound **X**. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. Show your working.

[3]

ii) State **two** reasons why the percentage yield of the reaction is not 100%.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of compound **X**:

- List the known values:

  - mass of W = 5.0 g
  - M<sub>r</sub> of W (propene) = 42
  - M<sub>r</sub> of X (2-chloropropane) = 78.5
  - percentage yield = 64%
- Calculate the moles of compound **W**:

n(W) = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}}$

n(W) = $\frac{5.0}{42}$

n(W) = 0.119 mol **[1 mark]**

- Mole ratio W : X = 1 : 1, so n(X) theoretical = 0.119 mol

- Calculate the theoretical mass of compound **X**:

mass(X) = n(X) x M<sub>r</sub>(X)

mass(X) = 0.119 x 78.5

mass(X) = 9.34 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the actual mass of compound **X** using the percentage yield:

actual mass = theoretical mass x $\frac{\mathrm{percentage} \mathrm{yield}}{100}$

actual mass = 9.34 x $\frac{64}{100}$

actual mass = **6.0 g** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward in steps 2 and 3 if a correct method is used with an incorrect moles value from step 1.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100.
> 
> Give your answer to the number of decimal places specified. Take care to use an unrounded intermediate value where possible: 5.0 / 42 x 78.5 x 0.64 = 5.98... g, which rounds to 6.0 g (1 dp).

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Two reasons why the percentage yield is not 100%:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - By-products are formed in this reaction
> - Reaction has not gone to completion
> - Alternative chemical pathways exist
> - Formation of intermediates
> 
> **[2 marks]**

[2]

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The product of the reaction between CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO and HCN is:

- 2-hydroxypentanenitrile

![Structure of 2-hydroxypentanenitrile showing the hydroxy group at carbon-2 and the nitrile group extending from carbon-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-1-formulas-functional-groups-and-the-naming-of-organic-compounds/assets/008-structure-of-2-hydroxypentanenitrile-showing-the.png)

> 
> 1 mark for the correct name: 2-hydroxypentanenitrile

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Changes in shape and chirality during the formation of the organic product:
> 
> Shape:
> 
> - The CHO / aldehyde group changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral (the CHOHCN / hydroxynitrile group) **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O bond breaks, forming two single bonds (to OH and CN groups)
> **AND**
> The carbon atom is now surrounded by 4 single bonding pairs, resulting in a tetrahedral shape **[1 mark]**
> 
> Chirality:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO / butanal has no chiral centres
> **AND**
> The organic product / 2-hydroxypentanenitrile has one chiral centre **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O bond breaks, forming two single bonds to OH and CN groups
> **AND**
> The carbon atom now has four different atoms or groups of atoms attached **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO is the aldehyde butanal, which has no chiral centres because no carbon has four different atoms or groups attached.
> 
> The aldehyde carbon has a trigonal planar shape due to the C=O double bond.
> 
> Aldehydes undergo an addition reaction with HCN to form hydroxynitrile compounds. The product here is 2-hydroxypentanenitrile (note that the CN group adds a carbon to the chain, making it five carbons rather than four).
> 
> After the reaction, the former carbonyl carbon has four different groups attached (H, OH, CN, and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>-), so it becomes a chiral centre.

> - Methyl butanoate **[1 mark]**

This question is about benzene.

Describe and explain the shape of benzene.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape of benzene can be described and explained as follows:

> - Hybridisation of carbon atoms: sp<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> π bonds formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the plane of the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon in benzene forms three σ bonds using its sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals: one to each neighbouring ring carbon and one to a hydrogen atom. These bonds lie in the plane of the ring at 120° to each other.
> 
> Each carbon also has one unhybridised p orbital pointing perpendicular to the ring plane. These p orbitals overlap sideways with the p orbitals on neighbouring carbons to form the π system. Because all six p orbitals overlap equally, the π electrons are delocalised across the whole ring rather than fixed between specific carbon pairs.
> 
> A key consequence of this delocalisation is that all six C–C bond lengths in benzene are equal, with a value between a C–C single bond (0.154 nm) and a C=C double bond (0.134 nm). Students sometimes lose the third mark by describing either σ or π bond formation but not both.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can be nitrated by warming it with a mixture of concentrated sulfuric acid and concentrated nitric acid.

The mechanism for the reaction is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Reaction mechanism showing nitration of benzene: benzene ring attacked by nitronium ion, forming sigma complex, then deprotonation to give nitrobenzene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/004-reaction-mechanism-showing-nitration-of-benzene-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) Name the mechanism of this nitration reaction.

[1]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction between H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and HNO<sub>3</sub> that generates the electrophile for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism of this nitration reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mechanism is electrophilic because the attacking species, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, is electron-deficient and attacks the electron-rich benzene ring. It is substitution rather than addition because the hydrogen atom is replaced by the NO<sub>2</sub> group, preserving the aromaticity of the ring. Addition would break the delocalised π system and is strongly disfavoured.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> The two-step representation: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> followed by H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O is accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this equation, concentrated sulfuric acid acts as an acid, donating a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) to nitric acid. The protonated nitric acid (H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) is unstable and loses water to form the nitronium ion, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. It is this NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion that acts as the electrophile and attacks the benzene ring in the mechanism shown in Fig. 1.1.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can be used to synthesise (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid which is a drug that can be used to treat chronic inflammation of the intestines.

i) Draw the structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid.

[1]

ii) One of the intermediate products made during the synthesis of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid is the molecule shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Chemical structure of 4‑nitrotoluene: a benzene ring with a methyl group at the top and a nitro group at the opposite, para position](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/005-chemical-structure-of-4-nitrotoluene-a-benzene-r.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Give the systematic name of the molecule shown in Fig. 1.2.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid is:

![Structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid showing a benzene ring with an amino group at the para position and a CH2COOH group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/006-structure-of-4-aminophenyl-ethanoic-acid-showing.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of (4-aminophenyl)ethanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work through the name systematically to build up the structure:
> 
> - "ethanoic acid" indicates a –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group attached to a benzene ring (phenylethanoic acid)
> - "4-amino" indicates an –NH<sub>2</sub> group at the para (4-) position of the ring, directly opposite the –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group
> 
> Start by drawing phenylethanoic acid, with the –CH<sub>2</sub>COOH group attached to C-1 of the benzene ring:
> 
> Then add the –NH<sub>2</sub> group at C-4 to give the final structure:

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The systematic name of the molecule shown in Fig. 1.2 is:
> 
> - 4-nitromethylbenzene **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecule in Fig. 1.2 is methylbenzene with a nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) substituted onto the ring. When naming, take the carbon bearing the methyl group as C-1. The nitro group is directly opposite, at C-4, giving the name 4-nitromethylbenzene.

parts.problemMd:
Noradrenaline, shown in Fig. 1.3, is a hormone and neurotransmitter which contains a benzene ring. It is released during stress to stimulate the heart and increase blood pressure.

![Chemical structure of noradrenaline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/007-chemical-structure-of-noradrenaline.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

Name three functional groups in the noradrenaline molecule in addition to the arene group.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Three functional groups in noradrenaline in addition to the arene group are:
> 
> - Phenol **[1 mark]**
> - (Secondary) alcohol **[1 mark]**
> - (Primary) amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Noradrenaline contains three functional groups in addition to the arene group:
> 
> 1. Phenol: the –OH group attached directly to the benzene ring. This is a separate functional group from alcohol and must be named specifically as phenol.
> 2. Secondary alcohol: the –OH group attached to a carbon that is bonded to two other carbon atoms. Because the central carbon has two C–C bonds, it is a secondary alcohol, not a primary one.
> 3. Primary amine: the –NH<sub>2</sub> group, where the nitrogen is bonded to one carbon chain (one R group) and two hydrogen atoms.
> 
> A common error is to name the phenol –OH as an alcohol. In CIE mark schemes, phenol and alcohol are distinct functional groups and cannot be substituted for each other.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, undergoes electrophilic substitution.

i) State what is meant by the term electrophile.

[1]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction between benzene and concentrated nitric acid.

[1]

iii) Identify the electrophile in this reaction.

[1]

iv) Write an equation to show how this electrophile is generated.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The meaning of the term electrophile:
> 
> - A species that accepts / receives an electron pair / electron pair acceptor / electron-deficient species **[1 mark]**
> 
> Answers referring only to positive charge without mention of electron pairs are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key distinction between an electrophile and a nucleophile is the direction of the electron pair: electrophiles accept pairs, nucleophiles donate them.
> 
> Electrophiles do not need to carry a full positive charge. A partial positive charge (δ+) is sufficient; for example, the carbon in a polar C–X bond can act as an electrophile.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the reaction between benzene and concentrated nitric acid:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is called nitration and produces nitrobenzene, a pale yellow liquid.
> 
> Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst, so it does not appear in the overall equation; it is regenerated at the end of the mechanism.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The electrophile in this reaction:
> 
> - NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> / the nitronium ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The electrophile is the nitronium ion, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, not nitric acid itself. Nitric acid must first react with concentrated sulfuric acid to generate NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> before the substitution reaction can proceed.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iv) The equation showing how this electrophile is generated:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base in this step, accepting a proton from concentrated sulfuric acid. This is unusual for nitric acid, which is normally an acid, but it occurs because concentrated sulfuric acid is a stronger acid.
> 
> The HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ion can donate a proton back at the end of the mechanism, regenerating H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. This explains why sulfuric acid is described as a catalyst.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene is a highly unsaturated molecule.

i) Explain why benzene undergoes substitution reactions rather than addition reactions.

[3]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction of benzene with chlorine. State the conditions required for this reaction.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The electrons in benzene are delocalised across all six carbon atoms in the ring
> - Delocalisation confers extra stability to the benzene ring
> - Addition reactions would disrupt / break the delocalised electron system
> - Disrupting delocalisation would require more energy than is released, making addition energetically unfavourable
> - Substitution reactions preserve the delocalised / aromatic ring structure
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Answers referring to benzene having localised double bonds are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stability gained through delocalisation is sometimes called the delocalisation energy or resonance energy. It is this extra stability that makes addition reactions thermodynamically unfavourable compared to substitution reactions, as addition would destroy the aromatic system.
> 
> When explaining this in the exam, link your points clearly: delocalised electrons give stability, and addition would destroy this stability. Saying only "benzene is stable" without explaining why does not gain the mark.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The equation for the reaction of benzene with chlorine, and the conditions required:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + HCl **[1 mark]**
> - AlCl<sub>3</sub> as a catalyst, anhydrous conditions **[1 mark]**
> 
> FeCl<sub>3</sub> / iron(III) chloride is accepted as an alternative catalyst
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The aluminium chloride catalyst is sometimes called a halogen carrier. It polarises the Cl–Cl bond to generate a Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile, which then attacks the benzene ring.
> 
> Anhydrous conditions are essential because AlCl<sub>3</sub> reacts vigorously with water. If moisture is present, the catalyst is destroyed and the reaction will not proceed.

parts.problemMd:
An aromatic organic compound with molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub> reacts with bromine in the presence of UV light to produce a compound with molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Br.

i) Name the type of reaction.

[1]

ii) Draw the structures of the reactant and product.

[2]

iii) Suggest the formula of one other organic product that could form in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction is:
> 
> - Free radical substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The clue here is the presence of UV light, which provides the energy needed to initiate free radical substitution. This reaction occurs at the methyl group (side chain), not on the benzene ring itself. Bromine reacts with alkyl hydrogens under UV light, not with the delocalised ring.

ii) The structures of the reactant and product are:

![Structural diagrams showing methylbenzene as the reactant and (bromomethyl)benzene as the product of free radical substitution with bromine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/003-structural-diagrams-showing-methylbenzene-as-the.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the reactant: methylbenzene / toluene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the product: (bromomethyl)benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub> corresponds to methylbenzene: a benzene ring with one methyl group. The degree of unsaturation is 4, consistent with a benzene ring.
> 
> When UV light initiates the reaction, a bromine radical abstracts a hydrogen from the methyl group, not from the ring. The benzene ring is too stable to undergo addition or radical substitution under these conditions.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) One other organic product that could form is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBr<sub>2</sub> / C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CBr<sub>3</sub> / C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br<sub>3</sub>
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub> / C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>14</sub>
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> HBr is not accepted as it is an inorganic product

> **[exam-tip]**
> Further substitution can occur with excess bromine and UV light, where one or two more hydrogen atoms in the methyl group can be replaced, giving C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHBr<sub>2</sub> and C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CBr<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> The final alternative product, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, forms when two benzyl radicals combine in the termination step.

parts.problemMd:
Propanal reacts with potassium cyanide, followed by dilute acid, to form the hydroxynitrile CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN.

State the systematic name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(OH)CN is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxybutanenitrile **[1 mark]**
> 
> The 'e' at the end of butane must be included; '2-hydroxybutannitrile' is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The name is built in three steps: identify the parent chain (4 carbons including the CN carbon = butane), add the nitrile suffix keeping the 'e' (butane + nitrile = butanenitrile), then number the hydroxy group from the nitrile end (OH is on C-2 = 2-hydroxy).
> 
> The most common error is dropping the 'e' to write '2-hydroxybutannitrile', which is not accepted.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propanal reacts with potassium cyanide, followed by dilute acid, to form the hydroxynitrile CH~3~CH~2~CH(OH)CN.

Name the mechanism for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic addition **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both words are required for the mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both words, nucleophilic and addition, must be present. Writing only one will not gain the mark.
> 
> This mechanism applies whenever a nucleophile attacks the C=O group of an aldehyde or ketone. The addition part reflects that the nucleophile adds across the C=O double bond rather than substituting an existing group.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Propanal reacts with potassium cyanide, followed by dilute acid, to form the hydroxynitrile CH3CH2CH(OH)CN.

The mechanism for this reaction is: Nucleophilic addition

Explain why propanal undergoes this type of mechanism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Propanal undergoes this mechanism because:
> 
> - The C=O bond is polar
> **OR**
> O is more electronegative than C
> **OR**
> C is δ+ and O is δ−  **[1 mark]**
> - Nucleophiles / CN<sup>-</sup> are electron pair donors 
> **AND** 
> They are attracted to the electron-deficient C<sup>δ+</sup> carbon **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These two marks are sequential: the first establishes why the carbon is susceptible to attack (polar C=O bond, δ+ carbon), and the second explains why a nucleophile is attracted to it (electron pair donors are drawn to δ+ centres).
> 
> For the second mark, both parts are required: you must state that CN<sup>-</sup> / nucleophiles are electron pair donors, and that they are attracted to the δ+ carbon. Stating only one of these will not gain the mark.

parts.problemMd:
Under suitable conditions, 3-nitrobenzaldehyde can be formed by the reaction of benzaldehyde with appropriate reagents.

i) State the name of the mechanism, and the reagents and conditions, for the formation of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde.

mechanism ................................................................................

reagents ................................................................................

conditions ................................................................................

[3]

ii) Draw the fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde. On your diagram, draw a circle around each functional group.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism, reagents and conditions for this nitration reaction are:
> 
> - Mechanism: electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**
> - Reagents: concentrated nitric acid
> **AND**
> Concentrated sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: heat / reflux
> **AND**
> Temperature in the range 25–60 °C **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This reaction is a nitration, which is a type of electrophilic aromatic substitution in which a nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) replaces a hydrogen atom on the benzene ring.
> 
> Both acids are required. The sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst by protonating the nitric acid to generate the nitronium ion (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), which is the electrophile in the mechanism.
> 
> The temperature must be controlled carefully. Too high a temperature leads to polynitration, where more than one nitro group is added to the ring.
> 
> When numbering the carbon atoms, count the benzene carbon bearing the aldehyde group as C-1. The –CHO group is an electron-withdrawing meta-director, so the nitro group is added at C-3.

ii) The fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde with the functional groups circled is:

![The fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde with circles around the aldehyde group, nitro group, and benzene ring](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/001-the-fully-displayed-formula-of-3-nitrobenzaldehy.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct fully displayed formula of 3-nitrobenzaldehyde
> 
> 1 mark for all three functional groups correctly circled

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three functional groups to circle are:
> 
> - The aldehyde group (–CHO)
> - The nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>)
> - The benzene ring
> 
> The benzene ring is the most commonly missed functional group. It counts as a functional group in its own right.
> 
> Take care with the nitro group in the fully displayed formula. It contains two N–O bonds: one N=O double bond and one N–O single bond, with the oxygen bearing a negative charge. Make sure the correct number of bonds is shown before circling.

parts.problemMd:
Benzaldehyde, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHO, is the simplest aromatic aldehyde with a characteristic smell of almonds or cherries.

i) State the hybridisation of the carbon atom in the aldehyde group and predict the C–C=O bond angle.

hybridisation ................................................................................

bond angle ................................................................................

[2]

ii) A student suggests that a molecule of benzaldehyde is not planar because there is free rotation around the C–C bond connecting the benzene ring to the aldehyde group.

Explain why the student is incorrect.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The hybridisation and C–C=O bond angle in benzaldehyde are:
> 
> - Hybridisation: sp<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - C–C=O bond angle: 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The carbon atom in the aldehyde group (–CHO) has three groups attached: the ring carbon, the hydrogen, and the oxygen (via the double bond, which counts as one group). Three groups around a central atom corresponds to sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation and a trigonal planar arrangement, giving bond angles of 120°.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) To explain why the student is incorrect:
> 
> - The p-orbital on the carbon atom of the aldehyde group overlaps / delocalises with the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - This gives the C–C bond partial double bond character, which restricts rotation **[1 mark]**
> 
> Writing π orbital instead of p-orbital in the first marking point is accepted
> 
> The statement that lone pairs on the oxygen atom delocalise into the ring is not accepted for the first marking point.
> 
> References to hydrogen bonding or van der Waals' forces are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The student's error is treating the C–C bond connecting the ring to the aldehyde group as a simple single bond, like those found in alkanes. In benzaldehyde, this is not the case.
> 
> The p-orbital on the carbonyl carbon (the C of –CHO) is parallel to the p-orbitals of the benzene ring. These orbitals overlap sideways, extending the delocalised π system across the C–C bond. This gives the C–C bond partial double bond character, which restricts rotation and holds the molecule in a planar conformation.
> 
> A common error is to state that lone pairs on the oxygen delocalise into the ring. This is what happens in phenol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH), not benzaldehyde. In benzaldehyde, it is the p-orbital on the carbonyl carbon that overlaps with the ring, not lone pairs on oxygen.

parts.problemMd:
Methylbenzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of an AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst.

i) Draw the structure of the major organic product of this reaction.

[1]

ii) Deduce the total number of σ and π bonds in one molecule of this organic product.

σ bonds ..............................

π bonds ..............................

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The major organic product of this reaction is:

![Structure of 4-methylacetophenone, the major organic product of the Friedel-Crafts acylation of methylbenzene with ethanoyl chloride, showing the acetyl group at the para position](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-2-characteristic-organic-reactions/assets/002-structure-of-4-methylacetophenone-the-major-orga.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the major organic product, with the acetyl group (CH<sub>3</sub>CO–) at the 4/para position of the methylbenzene ring
> 
> The 2/ortho product is not accepted as the major product.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a Friedel-Crafts acylation. The ethanoyl chloride reacts with the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst to form the acylium ion (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>):
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>
> 
> The CH<sub>3</sub> group on methylbenzene is an electron-donating ortho/para director, so substitution occurs at the ortho or para positions. The para product is the major product because the ortho positions have greater steric hindrance from the adjacent ring hydrogens.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The total number of σ and π bonds in one molecule of the organic product is:
> 
> - σ bonds = 20
> **AND**
> π bonds = 4 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every covalent bond contains a sigma bond, including the sigma component of every double bond.
> 
> To count sigma bonds: count every bond in the structure. 4-methylacetophenone has 20 bonds in total, so there are 20 sigma bonds.
> 
> To count pi bonds: count each double bond once. Using a Kekulé structure, the benzene ring contains 3 C=C double bonds, plus 1 C=O double bond in the acetyl group, giving 4 pi bonds in total.

name: Shapes of Aromatic Organic Molecules; σ & π Bonds
section: 29. An Introduction to A Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd: Draw the displayed formula of benzene.
parts.solutionMd:
The displayed formula of benzene is:

![Kekulé structure of benzene with alternating single and double bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/004-kekul-structure-of-benzene-with-alternating-sing.png)

**OR**

![Delocalised structure of benzene with a circle inside a regular hexagon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/005-delocalised-structure-of-benzene-with-a-circle-i.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct displayed formula of benzene showing all six C–H bonds and all six C–C bonds. Both the Kekulé structure and the delocalised (circle) representation are accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The fully displayed formula must show all atoms and all bonds. For benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), draw all six C–H bonds and all six C–C bonds explicitly.
> 
> You can draw benzene as a hexagon with alternating single and double bonds (Kekulé structure) or as a regular hexagon with a circle inside to represent the delocalised π electrons.

parts.problemMd: State the bond angle in a benzene molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in benzene is:
> 
> - 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom in benzene is bonded to three other atoms, creating three regions of electron density. These arrange in a trigonal planar geometry, giving bond angles of 120°. There are no lone pairs on the carbon atoms to distort this angle.

parts.problemMd: State the type of hybridisation of the carbon atoms in benzene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of hybridisation of the carbon atoms in benzene is:
> 
> - sp<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation means that one s orbital and two p orbitals combine to form three sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals arranged at 120° to each other in a plane. Each carbon in benzene also has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to this plane, which participates in the delocalised π system.
> 
> Compare with sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon (e.g. methane), where all four orbitals hybridise to give a tetrahedral geometry with 109.5° bond angles.

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic (IUPAC) name for compounds W, X and Y.

![Three substituted benzene compounds labelled W, X and Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/001-three-substituted-benzene-compounds-labelled-w-x.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic (IUPAC) names for compounds W, X and Y are:
> 
> - W = 4-chloromethylbenzene **[1 mark]**
> - X = 3-nitrobenzoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Y = propylbenzene **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The benzene ring is the main functional group in compounds W and Y, so the suffix is -benzene.
> 
> In W, the prefixes chloro- and methyl- are needed. The methyl group assumes position 1 and the chloro- group is given a position in relation to this, i.e. 4.
> 
> In Y, the prefix propyl- is used to represent the –CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> group.
> 
> For compound X, the benzene ring has the –COOH group attached, so its suffix is benzoic acid. It also has the NO<sub>2</sub> group attached, so the prefix nitro- is needed, and its position is given in relation to the –COOH group.

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic (IUPAC) name for compound Z.

![Structural formula of 2,4-dibromophenol labelled compound Z](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/002-structural-formula-of-2-4-dibromophenol-labelled.jpeg)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic (IUPAC) name for compound Z is:
> 
> - 2,4-dibromophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The benzene ring contains an –OH group, so the main stem is phenol.
> 
> Starting from the OH group (on carbon 1, as this is the dominant functional group) and counting anticlockwise, there are two bromine atoms on carbons 2 and 4. This is the lowest numbered version as counting clockwise would give 4 and 6.

parts.problemMd: State the bond angle in a benzene molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in benzene is:
> 
> - 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom in benzene is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and bonded to three other atoms. The three areas of electron density arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving a trigonal planar arrangement and a bond angle of 120°.

parts.problemMd:
In benzene, each of the carbon atoms is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised.

i) Describe how neighbouring carbon atoms form σ bonds.

[1]

ii) Neighbouring carbon atoms also form π bonds. Describe how these π bonds are formed.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) σ bonds between neighbouring carbon atoms are formed by:
> 
> - End-on / axial overlap of sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised orbitals **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) π bonds between neighbouring carbon atoms are formed by:
> 
> - Sideways / lateral overlap of adjacent p orbitals (above and below the plane of the ring) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom has three sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised orbitals (formed from one s and two p orbitals), arranged at 120° to each other in a plane. These sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals overlap end-on with the sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals of neighbouring carbon atoms and the s orbital of the hydrogen atom, forming σ bonds.
> 
> Each carbon atom also has one unhybridised p orbital, perpendicular to the plane of the molecule. These p orbitals overlap sideways with adjacent p orbitals, forming π bonds. The resulting electrons become delocalised around the ring.

parts.problemMd:
State the systematic (IUPAC) name for each of the following aromatic compounds.

![Two aromatic compounds labelled X and Y](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-3-shapes-of-aromatic-organic-molecules--and--bonds/assets/003-two-aromatic-compounds-labelled-x-and-y.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic (IUPAC) names are:
> 
> - compound X: 1-chloro-2-methylbenzene **[1 mark]**
> - compound Y: 3,5-dichlorophenylamine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name compound X, the chloro and methyl groups are listed in alphabetical order, with the methyl group at position 1.
> 
> To name compound Y, the dominant functional group is the amine group. When bonded directly to a benzene ring, this gives the parent name phenylamine. The two chloro groups are at positions 3 and 5.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the benzene ring is planar.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The benzene ring is planar because:
> 
> - All carbon atoms in C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> / benzene are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - Forming a trigonal planar / triangular planar arrangement
> **AND**
> (With) bond angles of 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hybridisation explains the shape of molecules. sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation produces three equivalent orbitals arranged at 120° in a plane, giving a trigonal planar geometry. Since all six carbon atoms in benzene are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised, the entire ring lies in one plane.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

compound X: 1-chloro-2-methylbenzene

Compound X can be formed from benzene in a two-step reaction.

State the reagents and conditions required for each step.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> - step 1 reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - step 1 conditions: anhydrous **[1 mark]**
> - step 2 reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> and AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - step 2 conditions: anhydrous **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For benzene to react, a powerful electrophile must be generated. The delocalised π system is very stable and will only react with powerful electrophiles. AlCl<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid catalyst (halogen carrier) by generating an electrophilic species from the reagent.
> 
> Step 1 is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation: benzene reacts with CH<sub>3</sub>Cl / AlCl<sub>3</sub> to form methylbenzene.
> 
> Step 2 is a Friedel-Crafts halogenation: methylbenzene reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> / AlCl<sub>3</sub> to form compound X as a mixture of 2- and 4-chloromethylbenzene.
> 
> Anhydrous conditions are essential: water hydrolyses AlCl<sub>3</sub>, destroying its catalytic activity.

parts.problemMd: State the bond angle in a benzene molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The bond angle in benzene is:
> 
> - 120° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon atom in benzene is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and bonded to three other atoms. The three areas of electron density arrange themselves as far apart as possible, giving a trigonal planar arrangement and a bond angle of 120°.

parts.problemMd: Explain why benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, does not react with aqueous bromine, whereas hexene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, reacts readily.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Hexene reacts with aqueous bromine but benzene does not because:
> 
> - The π bond in hexene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> contains localised electrons / an area of high electron density **[1 mark]**
> - The π bond in hexene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> induces a partial positive (δ+) and partial negative (δ–) in the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule **[1 mark]**
> - The δ+ Br / bromine atom is attracted to the π bond in hexene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, forming a carbocation intermediate **[1 mark]**
> - The carbocation intermediate attracts the δ– Br / bromine atom **[1 mark]**
> - In benzene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, there are no localised electrons / areas of high electron density, so it cannot polarise the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule
> **OR**
> In benzene / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, the electrons are delocalised with no areas of high electron density, so it cannot polarise the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with halogen molecules because the localised π bond has high electron density that readily polarises the Br<sub>2</sub> molecule. Benzene's delocalised electrons cannot do this as a halogen carrier such as AlBr<sub>3</sub> is needed to generate a sufficiently powerful electrophile for benzene to react.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene reacts with liquid bromine in the presence of a suitable catalyst.

State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene's delocalised π electron system is very stable. Unlike alkenes, it does not undergo electrophilic addition (which would disrupt the stabilising ring), but instead undergoes electrophilic substitution, which restores the delocalised ring after each step.

name: Isomerism: Optical
section: 29. An Introduction to A Level Organic Chemistry

parts.problemMd:
Hydroxypropanoic acid has two position isomers.

i) Draw the structural formulae of the two position isomers of hydroxypropanoic acid and state the systematic name of each.

[2]

ii) State which of these isomers exhibits optical isomerism.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The two position isomers of hydroxypropanoic acid are:

3-hydroxypropanoic acid:

![Structural formula of 3-hydroxypropanoic acid with the hydroxyl group on C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/011-structural-formula-of-3-hydroxypropanoic-acid-wi.png)

2-hydroxypropanoic acid:

![Structural formula of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid with the hydroxyl group on C2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/012-structural-formula-of-2-hydroxypropanoic-acid-wi.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct name and structure of 3-hydroxypropanoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for the correct name and structure of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The isomer that exhibits optical isomerism is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxypropanoic acid
> **OR**
> Lactic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two position isomers differ only in the location of the –OH group: C2 in 2-hydroxypropanoic acid and C3 in 3-hydroxypropanoic acid. The –OH cannot sit on the same carbon as the –COOH group, so only two positions are possible.
> 
> To identify the optically active isomer, look for a carbon carrying four different groups (the chiral centre). In 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, C2 carries –H, –OH, –CH<sub>3</sub>, and –COOH: four different groups, so it is chiral. In 3-hydroxypropanoic acid, C3 carries two H atoms, so it cannot be a chiral centre.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the structures of three amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, cysteine and aspartate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/013-structural-formulae-of-glycine-cysteine-and-aspa.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Identify the amino acid in Fig. 1.1 that does not exhibit optical isomerism.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The amino acid in Fig. 1.1 that does not exhibit optical isomerism is:
> 
> - Glycine / Gly **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An optically active compound contains a chiral centre: a carbon bonded to four different atoms or groups. Of the three amino acids in Fig. 1.1, glycine is the only one where the central carbon carries two hydrogen atoms. Because two of its substituents are identical, glycine has no chiral centre and does not exhibit optical isomerism.

parts.problemMd:
Serine, shown in Fig. 1.2, exhibits optical isomerism.

![Structural formula of serine showing the chiral centre](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/014-structural-formula-of-serine-showing-the-chiral-.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two optical isomers of serine.
parts.solutionMd:
The two optical isomers of serine are:

![Three-dimensional diagrams of the two optical isomers of serine shown as non-superimposable mirror images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/015-three-dimensional-diagrams-of-the-two-optical-is.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

>

>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The chiral centre in serine is the central carbon, which carries –H, –NH<sub>2</sub>, –COOH, and –CH<sub>2</sub>OH. Place this carbon at the centre of your diagram and draw four bonds arranged tetrahedrally: two standard bonds in the plane of the page, one wedge bond (coming towards you) and one dash bond (going away from you).
> 
> The second optical isomer is the mirror image of the first. The simplest way to generate it is to keep two groups in the same position and swap the other two. The key check is that no rotation of one structure should allow it to be superimposed onto the other.

parts.problemMd:
Leucine is an optically active amino acid with the molecular formula (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)COOH.

Draw the displayed formula of leucine.
parts.solutionMd:
The displayed formula of leucine is:

![Displayed formula of leucine showing all bonds including C–C, C–H, O–H and N–H bonds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/001-displayed-formula-of-leucine-showing-all-bonds-i.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct fully-displayed formula of leucine with all bonds shown, including the O–H bond in the carboxylic acid group and the N–H bonds in the amino group

> **[exam-tip]**
> A displayed formula shows every bond in the molecule as a line. The most commonly missed bonds are the O–H in the –COOH group and both N–H bonds in the –NH<sub>2</sub> group. Check your diagram includes all of these before moving on.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Leucine is an optically active amino acid with the molecular formula (CH~3~)~2~CHCH~2~CH(NH~2~)COOH.

Leucine exists as stereoisomers.

i) Explain what is meant by the term stereoisomerism.

[2]

ii) Describe how the two optical isomers of leucine can be distinguished.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The meaning of the term stereoisomerism:
> 
> - Molecules with the same structural formula / same atoms bonded to each other in the same order **[1 mark]**
> - But with a different arrangement of atoms in space **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The two optical isomers of leucine can be distinguished:
> 
> - By passing plane-polarised light through solutions of each isomer / by using a polarimeter **[1 mark]**
> - Each optical isomer / enantiomer rotates the plane of polarised light in opposite directions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the definition of stereoisomerism, two points are needed:
> 
> 1. The molecules have the same structural formula (the same atoms bonded in the same order)
> 2. They differ in the spatial arrangement of those atoms.
> 
> Saying only 'different arrangement' without specifying it is a spatial difference will not score the second mark.
> 
> For distinguishing optical isomers, focus on the one physical property that sets them apart: their effect on plane-polarised light. One enantiomer rotates the plane clockwise and the other rotates it anticlockwise. A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both, so the rotations cancel and there is no net effect on the light.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Leucine is an optically active amino acid with the molecular formula (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH(NH₂)COOH.

Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two optical isomers of leucine.
parts.solutionMd:
The two optical isomers of leucine are:

![Three-dimensional diagrams of the two optical isomers of leucine shown as non-superimposable mirror images](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/002-three-dimensional-diagrams-of-the-two-optical-is.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct three-dimensional diagram of one optical isomer of leucine, with the chiral carbon at the centre bearing four different groups shown using wedge-and-dash notation
> 
> 1 mark for the second optical isomer drawn as the non-superimposable mirror image of the first
> 
> Allow other valid orientations of the four groups provided the two structures are non-superimposable mirror images of each other

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find the chiral centre in leucine, identify the carbon with four different groups attached. In leucine, this is the carbon bearing –H, –NH<sub>2</sub>, –COOH, and –CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> Place the chiral carbon at the centre of your diagram. Use two standard bonds in the plane of the page, one wedge bond coming towards you, and one dash bond going away from you. Attach the four different groups to the ends of these bonds.
> 
> To draw the second isomer, reflect the first in a mirror. The two structures must be non-superimposable: no rotation should make one identical to the other.

**Extract:**

Leucine is an optically active amino acid with the molecular formula (CH~3~)~2~CHCH~2~CH(NH~2~)COOH.

State the systematic (IUPAC) name of leucine.
