parts.problemMd:
Propranolol is an optically active drug. Its structure is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Skeletal formula of propranolol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-propranolol.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

i) Deduce the molecular formula of propranolol.

[1]

ii) On Fig. 2.1, indicate the chiral centre with an asterisk (*).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The molecular formula of propranolol is:
> 
> - C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>21</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> C<sub>16</sub>H<sub>21</sub>O<sub>2</sub>N **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To count atoms in a skeletal formula, go through carbon by carbon. In a skeletal formula, each line end and intersection represents a carbon, and H atoms on carbon are implied (not shown). The fused ring system in propranolol has carbons shared between the two rings, so be careful not to count those shared carbons twice.

ii) The chiral centre of propranolol is:

![Skeletal formula of propranolol with an asterisk indicating the chiral centre on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-propranolol-with-an-asterisk.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying the chiral centre as the carbon attached to the –OH group, with four different groups (–H, –OH, –OCH<sub>2</sub>– chain, and –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)– chain).

> **[exam-tip]**
> To identify the chiral centre, look for the only carbon bonded to four different groups. The carbon attached to the –OH group carries –H, –OH, the –OCH<sub>2</sub>– chain, and the –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)– group: all four are different, making it the chiral centre. Other carbons in propranolol either form part of the aromatic ring or carry identical substituents.

parts.problemMd: Explain why a racemic mixture of propranolol has no effect on plane-polarised light.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A racemic mixture of propranolol has no effect on plane-polarised light because:
> 
> - A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of each enantiomer / optical isomer **[1 mark]**
> - The rotation of plane-polarised light by each enantiomer is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, so the effects cancel out **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key word here is 'equal': a racemic mixture has a 50:50 ratio of the two enantiomers. One enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light clockwise by a given angle; the other rotates it anticlockwise by the same angle. Because the amounts are equal, these rotations exactly cancel, giving no net rotation.
> 
> If the mixture were not a 50:50 ratio (for example, if it contained more of one enantiomer), it would still rotate plane-polarised light and would not be described as a racemic mixture.

parts.problemMd: Explain why it is often important that chiral drugs, such as propranolol, are administered as a single pure enantiomer rather than as a racemic mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> It is often important because:
> 
> - Each enantiomer has / may have different biological activity / interacts differently with biological receptors **[1 mark]**
> - One enantiomer may have unwanted / harmful side effects
> **OR**
> Administering a single enantiomer increases the potency / effectiveness of the drug **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties in achiral environments, but biological receptors are chiral. This means the two enantiomers of a drug can interact very differently with receptors in the body. In some drugs, one enantiomer provides the therapeutic benefit while the other is inactive or causes side effects. By administering the pure active enantiomer, the required dose is lower and the risk of side effects is reduced.

parts.problemMd:
Chiral catalysts are often used in the manufacturing process of drugs.

i) State the purpose of using a chiral catalyst in drug synthesis.

[1]

ii) State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a chiral catalyst.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The purpose of using a chiral catalyst in drug synthesis:
> 
> - To ensure that only one enantiomer is produced / formed **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) One advantage and one disadvantage of using a chiral catalyst:
> 
> One advantage:
> 
> - Only small amounts of catalyst are needed
> **OR**
> The catalyst can be reused / recycled **[1 mark]**
> 
> One disadvantage:
> 
> - Chiral catalysts are expensive / costly to produce **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The advantages and disadvantages of a chiral catalyst follow the same pattern as any catalyst: small quantities are required and the catalyst is not consumed in the reaction, so it can be recovered and reused. The specific purpose in chiral synthesis is selectivity: only one enantiomer is formed, avoiding the need to separate a racemic mixture afterwards.
> 
> Enzymes are biological chiral catalysts. They can achieve very high enantiomeric purity but may require carefully controlled reaction conditions (pH, temperature, aqueous environment) that are not always practical for industrial synthesis.

parts.problemMd:
Two isomers of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

![Structural formulae of propanal (compound A, an aldehyde) and propanone (compound B, a ketone)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/003-structural-formulae-of-propanal-compound-a-an-al.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

i) State the systematic (IUPAC) name of compound **A** and of compound **B**.

[2]

ii) State the name of the mechanism for the reaction between compound **A** and HCN.

[1]

iii) Describe the mechanism for the reaction between compound **A** and HCN. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and partial charges in your diagram.

[4]

iv) State the systematic name of the organic product formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic (IUPAC) names of compounds **A** and **B** are:
> 
> - **A**: propanal **[1 mark]**
> - **B**: propanone **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic addition **[1 mark]**

iii) The mechanism for the reaction between compound **A** and HCN is:

![Nucleophilic addition mechanism showing the cyanide ion attacking the carbonyl carbon of propanal, with curly arrows for electron movement, formation of the alkoxide intermediate, and protonation to give 2-hydroxybutanenitrile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/004-nucleophilic-addition-mechanism-showing-the-cyan.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow drawn from the lone pair of :CN<sup>-</sup> to the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon atom of compound A
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow drawn from the C=O bond to the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct negatively charged intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and CN bonded to the former carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow drawn from the lone pair of O<sup>-</sup> to an H<sup>+</sup> ion, forming the final product
> 
> HCN alone is not accepted as the nucleophile. The cyanide ion (:CN<sup>-</sup>) is the nucleophile.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iv) The systematic name of the organic product is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxybutanenitrile **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound A is an aldehyde (the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain); compound B is a ketone (the carbonyl group is internal). Both can undergo nucleophilic addition with HCN.
> 
> For the mechanism in part iii), the nucleophile is the cyanide ion CN<sup>-</sup>, which attacks the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon of the C=O group. Your diagram must show:
> 
> - The lone pair on :CN<sup>-</sup> with a curly arrow going to the δ<sup>+</sup> carbon.
> - → A curly arrow from the C=O bond going to the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen (forming O<sup>-</sup>).
> - → The complete intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and CN bonded to the former carbonyl carbon.
> - → A curly arrow from the lone pair on O<sup>-</sup> going to H<sup>+</sup>, forming the final –OH group.
> 
> For part iv), the product is a hydroxynitrile. The –CN group becomes part of the carbon chain (extending it by one carbon), so the parent chain is 4 carbons long. The –OH is on C2 and the nitrile is the principal functional group: 2-hydroxybutanenitrile.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two isomers of C~3~H~6~O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

**Fig. 3.1**

Compound **A**: propanal (an aldehyde)
Compound **B**: propanone (a ketone)

Compound **B** also reacts with HCN.

i) State the systematic name of the organic product formed.

[1]

ii) Explain why the organic product in b(i) does not exhibit optical isomerism.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic name of the organic product:
> 
> - 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The product does not exhibit optical isomerism because:
> 
> - The central carbon of the product is bonded to two identical methyl / –CH<sub>3</sub> groups **[1 mark]**
> - Optical isomerism requires a chiral centre; this compound has no carbon bonded to four different groups **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When propanone (compound B) reacts with HCN, the product is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. The central carbon (C2) carries –OH, –CN, and two –CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Because two of its substituents are identical, C2 is not a chiral centre, and the compound cannot exhibit optical isomerism.
> 
> This contrasts with the product from compound A (propanal), where C2 after HCN addition carries –H, –OH, –CN, and –CH<sub>3</sub>: four different groups, giving a chiral centre and therefore a pair of optical isomers.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two isomers of C~3~H~6~O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

**Fig. 3.1**

Compound A is propanal (an aldehyde) and compound B is propanone (a ketone).

Explain why the reaction between compound **A** and HCN produces a racemic mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reaction between compound A and HCN produces a racemic mixture because:
> 
> - Compound A / the carbonyl group is planar
> **OR**
> The carbonyl carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The nucleophile / CN<sup>-</sup> ion can attack from above or below the plane of the carbonyl group with equal probability **[1 mark]**
> - A chiral centre is created with four different groups attached, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key is the geometry of the carbonyl group. The carbonyl carbon in compound A is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised and the molecule is planar around that carbon. This means the incoming nucleophile (CN<sup>-</sup>) can approach from either side of the plane with equal probability. Attack from above gives one enantiomer; attack from below gives the mirror image. Since both are equally probable, equal amounts of each enantiomer form, giving a racemic mixture.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two isomers of C~3~H~6~O are shown below in Fig. 3.1.

Compound A is propanal (an aldehyde) and compound B is propanone (a ketone).

The reaction between compound A and HCN produces a racemic mixture because:
- Compound A / the carbonyl group is planar OR The carbonyl carbon is sp^2^ hybridised
- The nucleophile / CN^-^ ion can attack from above or below the plane of the carbonyl group with equal probability
- A chiral centre is created with four different groups attached, giving equal amounts of both enantiomers

Explain why the racemic mixture formed in this reaction has no effect on plane-polarised light.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The racemic mixture has no effect on plane-polarised light because:
> 
> - It contains a 50:50 / equal mixture of each enantiomer / optical isomer **[1 mark]**
> - The rotation of plane-polarised light by each enantiomer is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, so the effects cancel out
> **OR**
> Half of the mixture rotates the plane of polarised light clockwise and half rotates it anticlockwise, giving zero net rotation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light by the same angle but in opposite directions. Because the racemic mixture contains exactly equal amounts of both, the clockwise rotation from one enantiomer is exactly cancelled by the anticlockwise rotation of the other. The overall effect on the light is zero.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the chemistry of limonene.

- The other enantiomer is responsible for a lemon smell

Draw three-dimensional diagrams to show the two optical isomers of limonene.

|   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The three-dimensional diagrams of the two optical isomers of limonene are:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

This question is about the chemistry of limonene.

Limonene is a naturally occurring hydrocarbon found in citrus fruits, with the molecular formula C~10~H~16~.

Limonene exists as a pair of enantiomers:

- One enantiomer is responsible for a strong orange smell
- The other enantiomer is responsible for a lemon smell

Suggest why receptors in the human nose can distinguish between the orange and lemon enantiomers of limonene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Receptors in the human nose can distinguish between the enantiomers of limonene because:
> 
> - Each enantiomer has a different three-dimensional shape / structure **[1 mark]**
> - Receptors in the human nose have a specific three-dimensional shape
> **OR**
> Receptors in the human nose are stereospecific **[1 mark]**
> - Only one enantiomer fits a given receptor / the two enantiomers fit different receptors **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question draws on the concept of molecular shape complementarity, the same principle as enzyme-substrate specificity in biology. Enantiomers have the same physical properties such as melting and boiling points, but different three-dimensional arrangements, which is why they interact differently with chiral environments such as receptors.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Limonene is a naturally occurring hydrocarbon found in citrus fruits, with the molecular formula C~10~H~16~.

Limonene can undergo full hydrogenation to form menthane as shown.

![Equation showing limonene reacting with two molecules of hydrogen gas to form menthane by complete hydrogenation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/29-an-introduction-to-a-level-organic-chemistry/29-4-isomerism-optical/assets/009-equation-showing-limonene-reacting-with-two-mole.png)

For the complete hydrogenation of an impure sample of 3.00 g of limonene at room temperature and pressure, 870 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen was required.

Calculate, showing your working, the percentage purity of limonene.

percentage purity = ........................ %
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage purity of the limonene sample:

- Convert the volume of H<sub>2</sub> and calculate moles of H<sub>2</sub>:

870 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.870 dm<sup>3</sup>

moles H<sub>2</sub> = $\frac{0.870}{24.0}$

moles H<sub>2</sub> = 0.03625 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Use the molar ratio to find moles of limonene (limonene : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 2):

moles limonene = $\frac{0.03625}{2}$

moles limonene = 0.018125 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate M<sub>r</sub> of limonene and the mass of pure limonene:

M<sub>r</sub> (limonene) = (12.0 x 10) + (1.0 x 16) = 136 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

mass of limonene = 0.018125 x 136

mass of limonene = 2.465 g

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage purity:

$\text{percentage purity} = \frac{\text{mass of pure limonene}}{\text{total mass of impure sample}} \times 100$

percentage purity = $\frac{2.465}{3.00}$ x 100

percentage purity = **82.2%**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct moles of H<sub>2</sub> = 0.03625 mol (accept 0.0363 or 0.0362) **AND** correct unit conversion 870 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.870 dm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct moles of limonene = 0.018125 mol
> 
> 1 mark for correct mass of limonene = 2.465 g
> 
> 1 mark for correct percentage purity = 82.2%
> 
> Allow error carried forward from any step within the calculation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Retrieve the molar volume at RTP (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>-1</sup>) from the Data Booklet; it is not provided in the question.
> 
> Show all steps clearly: convert the volume of H<sub>2</sub> to dm<sup>3</sup>, use the 1:2 molar ratio from the equation to find moles of limonene, calculate the mass of pure limonene using M<sub>r</sub>, and then apply the percentage purity formula.

parts.problemMd:
The final step of the multi-step synthetic conversion of limonene to menthol is shown.

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr<sub>3</sub>, and bromoethane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br, to form ethylbenzene.

Construct an equation for the formation of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> species.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the formation of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> species is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + AlBr<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> The aluminium bromide acts as a Lewis acid, accepting a bromide ion from bromoethane to generate the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> carbocation electrophile and the AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> ion.
> 
> Always ensure the halogen in the catalyst matches the halogenoalkane: AlBr<sub>3</sub> with bromoalkanes, AlCl<sub>3</sub> with chloroalkanes.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr~3~, and bromoethane, CH~3~CH~2~Br, to form ethylbenzene.

State the name of the mechanism for the formation of ethylbenzene from benzene and aluminium bromide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of the mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than addition because substitution allows the delocalised π system to be restored. Addition would permanently break the ring's delocalisation, destroying the extra stability this provides.
> 
> Do not confuse the mechanism name (electrophilic substitution) with the reaction type (Friedel-Crafts alkylation). Both describe aspects of this reaction but are not interchangeable.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr3, and bromoethane, CH3CH2Br, to form ethylbenzene.

Describe the mechanism for the conversion of benzene into ethylbenzene using the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the conversion of benzene into ethylbenzene is:

![Electrophilic substitution mechanism showing a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C+ of the ethyl carbocation, the carbocation intermediate with a horseshoe partial delocalisation and positive charge, and a curly arrow from the C–H bond restoring the ring with loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/016-electrophilic-substitution-mechanism-showing-a-c.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the π system of the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion (arrow must start from the ring, not from inside it)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure: horseshoe opening towards the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, positive charge inside the ring system, with CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub> and H both attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring, restoring the delocalised π system, with H<sup>+</sup> shown as lost

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common errors in electrophilic substitution mechanisms:
> 
> - Starting the first curly arrow from inside the ring rather than from the ring circle
> - Placing the positive charge on the wrong carbon in the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile. It must be on the terminal carbon
> - Drawing the horseshoe extending past carbons 2 and 6 in the intermediate
> - Omitting H<sup>+</sup> in the final step

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene can react with aluminium bromide, AlBr~3~, and bromoethane, CH~3~CH~2~Br, to form ethylbenzene.

The equation for the formation of the CH~3~CH~2~^+^ species is:
CH~3~CH~2~Br + AlBr~3~ → CH~3~CH~2~^+^ + AlBr~4~^–^

State why anhydrous conditions are required for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Anhydrous conditions are required because:
> 
> - Water reacts with / hydrolyses the AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst, preventing formation of the electrophile **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow: water would deactivate / destroy the catalyst

> **[exam-tip]**
> AlBr<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid that is rapidly destroyed by water. Even trace moisture reacts with the catalyst before it can generate the CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile, so the reaction cannot proceed. Anhydrous solvents and glassware are essential for all Friedel-Crafts reactions.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation for the reaction of benzene with concentrated nitric acid to form nitrobenzene and water.
parts.solutionMd:
An equation for the reaction is:

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct formulas for the reactants: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> and HNO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for correct formulas for the products: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an electrophilic substitution reaction. A nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) replaces one hydrogen atom on the benzene ring.
> 
> The reaction requires a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at a temperature between 25 and 60 °C. The concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts as a catalyst and is regenerated at the end.

parts.problemMd:
The structure of methylbenzene is shown below in Fig. 2.1.

![Skeletal formula of methylbenzene showing a hexagonal benzene ring with a methyl (CH~3~) group attached](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/035-skeletal-formula-of-methylbenzene-showing-a-hexa.jpeg)

**Fig. 2.1**

Draw the skeletal formulae of the two isomers of chloromethylbenzene formed from the reaction of methylbenzene and Cl<sub>2</sub> in the presence of AlCl<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
The two isomers of chloromethylbenzene are:

![Skeletal formulae of 2-chloromethylbenzene with Cl at the 2-position and 4-chloromethylbenzene with Cl at the 4-position relative to the methyl group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/036-skeletal-formulae-of-2-chloromethylbenzene-with-.jpeg)

> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 4-chloromethylbenzene

parts.problemMd: State the type of reaction that benzene will typically undergo.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Benzene typically undergoes:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than addition because substitution restores the delocalised π system. Addition would permanently break the ring's extra stability.
> 
> The three types of substitution to know are: free radical (alkanes + halogens), electrophilic (benzene ring reactions), and nucleophilic (halogenoalkanes + nucleophiles).

parts.problemMd: State the name of the mechanism that benzene will undergo if reacted with bromine in the presence of a halogen carrier to form bromobenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the name of the mechanism that benzene will undergo if reacted with bromine in the presence of a halogen carrier to form bromobenzene, C~6~H~5~Br.

Construct an equation to show how the halogen carrier generates the Br<sup>+</sup> ion in order to allow the reaction in part **(a)** to occur.
parts.solutionMd:
An equation showing the generation of the Br<sup>+</sup> ion is:

AlBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

**OR**

FeBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants: AlBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> or FeBr<sub>3</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for correct products: AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup> or FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + Br<sup>+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The halogen carrier acts as a Lewis acid, accepting one bromine atom from Br<sub>2</sub> to generate the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile. AlBr<sub>3</sub> and FeBr<sub>3</sub> are equally acceptable.
> 
> The catalyst is regenerated at the end when the complex ion reacts with the H<sup>+</sup> lost from the ring:

parts.problemMd: Explain why Friedel-Crafts acylation gives a mono-substituted product, while Friedel-Crafts alkylation may give a mixture of poly-substituted products.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Friedel-Crafts acylation gives only a mono-substituted product because:
> 
> - The acyl product contains an electron-withdrawing –COR group, which deactivates the benzene ring towards further electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**
> - In alkylation, the product contains an electron-donating alkyl group, which activates the ring and allows further substitution to occur (polyalkylation) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The acyl group withdraws electron density from the ring through the C=O bond, making the ring less reactive towards electrophiles. An alkyl group donates electron density into the ring by the inductive effect, increasing reactivity and making poly-substitution more likely.
> 
> This is a key practical advantage of acylation: it always gives a single, predictable mono-substituted product.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The aluminium chloride catalyst reforms because:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> is produced during electrophilic substitution when the benzene ring is restored **[1 mark]**
> - H<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> → HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> is consumed when it accepts Cl<sup>–</sup> to generate the acylium ion, forming AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>. The H<sup>+</sup> lost from the ring in the final step then reacts with AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> to regenerate AlCl<sub>3</sub> and release HCl. The catalyst is therefore reformed and can participate in further reaction cycles.

> Step 1 is electrophilic substitution (nitration). Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> generates the NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile. Keep the temperature below 55 °C to prevent di-nitration.
> 
> Step 2 reduces −NO<sub>2</sub> to −NH<sub>2</sub>. Only Fe or Sn with concentrated HCl are acceptable reducing agents for this step for this specification.

parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for reaction 2 (electrophilic aromatic substitution) is:

![Electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism of methylbenzene bromination showing curly arrow attack on ring from Br+, arenium ion intermediate with horseshoe delocalisation, and H+ elimination to restore aromaticity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/010-electrophilic-aromatic-substitution-mechanism-of.jpeg)

> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the benzene π system to the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium ion intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation extending over more than half of the ring but not past carbons 2 and 6; positive charge shown on ring; H shown at the substitution position

> **[exam-tip]**

> 
> - Forgetting to show the H atom at the ring carbon being substituted
> - Drawing the horseshoe delocalisation incorrectly. It must extend over more than half the ring but must not include the carbon bearing the incoming group
> - Omitting H<sup>+</sup> as the eliminated species in the final step
> - Misplacing the positive charge on the arenium ion intermediate

parts.problemMd:
Benzene reacts with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid.

Describe the structure and bonding of a benzene molecule, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>. In your answer, refer to:

- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- the bond angles within the ring
- how the *σ* and *π* bonds are formed.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The structure and bonding of a benzene molecule can be described as:
> 
> - The carbon atoms are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The molecule is planar (or a flat hexagon)
> **AND**
> the bond angle is 120° **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bonds are formed by the head-on (or end-on) overlap of (sp<sup>2</sup>) orbitals **[1 mark]**
> - The π bonds (or delocalised system) are formed by the sideways overlap of p-orbitals (creating electron density above and below the plane of the ring) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When describing benzene, avoid drawing or implying **alternating double bonds**. Examiners are looking for the idea of a **delocalised π system** spread over all six carbon atoms, not localised C=C bonds.
> 
> A good way to check your answer is to mention **both** the planar structure **and** the π electron cloud above and below the ring. Together, these explain benzene’s unusual stability compared with alkenes.

parts.problemMd:

i) Construct an equation to show the generation of the electrophile.

[1]

ii) Name and draw the fully labelled mechanism for the formation of nitrobenzene.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An equation to show the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the formation of nitrobenzene is:

![Benzene ring undergoes nitration with NO2+, forms an intermediate with NO2 and H+, resulting in nitrobenzene and hydrogen ion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/001-benzene-ring-undergoes-nitration-with-no2-forms-.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct name of mechanism: electrophilic substitution
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the delocalised π-system of the benzene ring to the NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> ion (arrow must start from the ring circle and point to the N atom or + charge)
> 
> 1 mark for correct structure of the intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation opening towards the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon **AND** positive charge clearly inside the horseshoe/ring system **AND** H and NO<sub>2</sub> attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C−H bond back into the ring to restore delocalisation, showing loss of H<sup>+</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In nitration mechanisms, the most common lost marks are due to curly arrows starting in the wrong place. Always start the arrow from the benzene ring circle or a C−C bond, never from a carbon atom itself.
> 
> In the intermediate, check that only one carbon is sp<sup>3</sup>, with both H and NO<sub>2</sub> attached, and that the positive charge is inside the ring, not on the NO<sub>2</sub> group.
> 
> When the final arrow is drawn, it must clearly show re-formation of the delocalised π system and the loss of H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
i) State the relative order of increasing acidity for ethanol, phenol, and ethanoic acid.

ii) Identify the electronic effect of the alkyl group that makes the ethoxide ion less stable than the phenoxide ion.

[1]

iii) Describe the distribution of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion that makes it the most stable of these three conjugate bases.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of increasing acidity is:
> 
> - Ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The electronic effect of the alkyl group that makes the ethoxide ion less stable than the phenoxide ion is:
> 
> - Positive inductive effect
> **OR**
> +*I* effect
> **OR**
> Electron-donating effect **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The distribution of the negative charge in the ethanoate ion that makes it the most stable of these three conjugate bases is:
> 
> - Charge is spread equally over both oxygen atoms
> **OR**

> The negative charge / π-electrons are delocalised over the COO<sup>−</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd: Predict the major product formed when phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The major product is:
> 
> - 4-nitrophenol
> **OR**
> 2-nitrophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
Benzene can be converted into 3-chlorobenzoic acid in a multi-step synthesis.

Suggest a **three-step** synthetic route for this conversion. In your answer, identify the reagents and conditions for each step and draw the structures of the intermediate compounds formed.
parts.solutionMd:
One suitable three-step synthetic route for the conversion of benzene into 3-chlorobenzoic acid is:

**Step 1** — Friedel-Crafts alkylation to give methylbenzene:

![Chemical structure of methylbenzene (toluene), showing a hexagonal benzene ring with a circle inside and a CH3 group attached](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/002-chemical-structure-of-methylbenzene-toluene-show.png)

Reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl (or CH<sub>3</sub>Br) with AlCl<sub>3</sub> (or FeBr<sub>3</sub>) catalyst

**Step 2** — Oxidation of the methyl side chain to give benzoic acid:

![Chemical structure of benzoic acid, showing a hexagonal benzene ring connected to a COOH group](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/003-chemical-structure-of-benzoic-acid-showing-a-hex.png)

Reagents: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat; then acidify

**Step 3** — Electrophilic chlorination of the ring to give 3-chlorobenzoic acid:

Reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> with AlCl<sub>3</sub> (or FeCl<sub>3</sub>) catalyst

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for step 1 reagents: CH<sub>3</sub>Cl / CH<sub>3</sub>Br **AND** AlCl<sub>3</sub> / FeBr<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure of methylbenzene (toluene)
> 
> 1 mark for step 2 reagents: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, heat, then acidify
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate structure of benzoic acid
> 
> 1 mark for step 3 reagents: Cl<sub>2</sub> **AND** AlCl<sub>3</sub> / FeCl<sub>3</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of the steps matters. If chlorination is done while the ring has a −CH<sub>3</sub> group, the methyl group directs substitution to the 2- and 4-positions.
> 
> Oxidising the side chain first gives −COOH, which is a meta-director, so chlorination then gives the 3-chloro product.

parts.problemMd:
The nitration of benzene forms the basis for the synthesis of dyes and explosives.

i) Construct an equation for the generation of the electrophile.

[1]

ii) State which reactant is acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base and justify your answer.

[1]

iii) Identify the conjugate acid in the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the generation of the electrophile is:
> 
> - 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reactant acting as a Brønsted-Lowry base and the justification are:
> 
> - Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> It accepts a proton from sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is not accepted as the Brønsted-Lowry base.
> 
> iii) The conjugate acids in the reaction are:
> 
> - H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **AND**
> NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> accepts H<sup>+</sup> from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, so HNO<sub>3</sub> is the base.
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> donates the proton, making it the acid.
> 
> The intermediate H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> decomposes immediately to H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>. Both are conjugate acids because each formed by gaining H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:

ii) The mechanism for step 1 is:

![Friedel-Crafts acylation mechanism showing a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C+ of the acylium ion, the carbocation intermediate with horseshoe partial delocalisation and positive charge, and a curly arrow from the C–H bond restoring the ring with loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/005-friedel-crafts-acylation-mechanism-showing-a-cur.png)

> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the π system of the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the acylium ion (arrow must start from the ring, not inside it)

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

i) The reagents required for the production of compound A are:

- CH~3~CH~2~COCl / propanoyl chloride

The acylium ion (CH~3~CH~2~CO^+^) is generated when propanoyl chloride reacts with AlCl~3~:

CH~3~CH~2~COCl + AlCl~3~ → CH~3~CH~2~CO^+^ + AlCl~4~^–^

Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for the structure of the catalyst once the electrophile has been generated in part **(b)**.

parts.problemMd: Explain why benzene can generally only undergo substitution reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because:
> 
> - Addition requires breaking the delocalised π system to form new bonds **[1 mark]**
> - Breaking the delocalised π system requires significant energy input **[1 mark]**
> - The C–H bond at the ring is not part of the delocalised π system **[1 mark]**
> - Substituting H leaves the delocalised π system intact **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzene's delocalised π system gives it extra stability. Addition would permanently destroy this, which is energetically unfavourable. Substitution replaces only the H atom (not part of the π system), so the ring's full delocalisation is restored after reaction.

Fig. 2.1

parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the formation of the ketone is:

![Electrophilic substitution mechanism for Friedel-Crafts acylation showing acylium ion attack on benzene ring, arenium ion intermediate, and regeneration of AlCl3 catalyst](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/015-electrophilic-substitution-mechanism-for-friedel.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the C<sup>+</sup> of the acylium ion (the + must be on the carbon of the acylium group)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium ion intermediate: horseshoe delocalisation extending over more than half of the ring but not past carbons 2 and 6; positive charge on ring; acylium group and H shown at the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C−H bond back to the ring to restore delocalisation
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from an Al−Cl bond in AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> to the Cl atom (showing Cl<sup>−</sup> leaving)
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the Cl<sup>−</sup> to the H atom on the ring carbon, showing H<sup>+</sup> removal and regeneration of AlCl<sub>3</sub> **AND** HCl shown as a product

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common errors in Friedel-Crafts acylation mechanisms:
> 
> - The first arrow must start touching the ring, not start inside it
> - The horseshoe in the intermediate must cover more than half the ring, with the gap at the carbon bearing the acylium group
> - The positive charge in the intermediate must be on the ring carbon (not on the acylium group)
> - In the final step, AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> acts as a Brønsted base, removing H<sup>+</sup> from the ring to regenerate AlCl<sub>3</sub> and form HCl

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction, reagent and conditions are:
> 
> - Type of reaction: reduction / hydrogenation / addition **[1 mark]**
> - Reagent and conditions: H<sub>2</sub>
> **AND**
> Ni / Pt catalyst **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The bond angles and explanation are:
> 
> - Benzene = 120°
> **AND**
> Cyclohexane = 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

SO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → SO<sub>3</sub>H<sup>+</sup> + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>

i) Describe the mechanism for the reaction of benzene with SO<sub>3</sub>H<sup>+</sup> ions in Fig. 3.3. Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.

![Partially drawn electrophilic substitution mechanism for the reaction of benzene with SO3H+ showing blank spaces for curly arrows, the intermediate, and the product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/020-partially-drawn-electrophilic-substitution-mecha.png)

**Fig. 3.3**

[3]

ii) Construct an equation to show how the H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst is reformed.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed mechanism is:

![Completed sulfonation mechanism showing a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the sulfur of SO3H+, the carbocation intermediate with partial delocalisation and positive charge, and loss of H+ to give benzenesulfonic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/021-completed-sulfonation-mechanism-showing-a-curly-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the benzene ring to the sulfur atom of SO<sub>3</sub>H<sup>+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct intermediate: horseshoe, positive charge inside the ring, with SO<sub>3</sub>H and H both attached to the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring, restoring the delocalised π system, with H<sup>+</sup> shown as lost
> 
> ii) The equation to show how the catalyst is reformed is:
> 
> - HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This mechanism follows exactly the same pattern as nitration and halogenation of benzene, the only difference is the electrophile. The positive charge in the intermediate must be on the carbon atom bonded to the sulfur, not on the SO<sub>3</sub>H group.

> The H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst is regenerated when the H<sup>+</sup> produced in the final step reacts with HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>. This mirrors how AlCl<sub>3</sub> is regenerated in Friedel-Crafts reactions.

3-aminobenzoic acid can be synthesised from methylbenzene in three steps as shown in Fig. 3.4.

parts.solutionMd:
i) The structures of **M** and **N** are:

![Skeletal formulae of intermediates M (benzoic acid, benzene ring with COOH group) and N (3-nitrobenzoic acid, benzene ring with COOH and NO2 groups at the 3-position)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/30-hydrocarbons/30-1-arenes/assets/023-skeletal-formulae-of-intermediates-m-benzoic-aci.png)

> 1 mark for the correct structure of M: benzoic acid (benzene ring with –COOH group)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of N: 3-nitrobenzoic acid (benzene ring with –COOH and –NO<sub>2</sub> at the 3-position)
> 
> ii) The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> - Step 1: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> / hot MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>, heat under reflux (then acidify) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of steps matters. Oxidising the methyl group first gives a –COOH group, which is an electron-withdrawing meta-director, which directs the nitro group to the 3-position in step 2. parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of an aluminium bromide, AlBr3, catalyst to form bromobenzene. Fig. 1.1 shows an incomplete mechanism for the generation of the Br+ electrophile.

A lone pair of electrons from the δ– bromine atom is donated to AlBr3, forming a coordinate bond. This draws electrons away from the other bromine atom, making it electron-deficient and generating the Br+ electrophile.

The intermediate then loses a proton, restoring the delocalised electron system.

Construct an equation to show how the AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst is regenerated.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the regeneration of the AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst is:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> + [AlBr<sub>4</sub>]<sup>–</sup> → HBr + AlBr<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst is consumed in the first step to generate the Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile. It is regenerated when the H<sup>+</sup> ion produced during the substitution step reacts with [AlBr<sub>4</sub>]<sup>–</sup>. The overall equation for the reaction is:
> 
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br + HBr

parts.problemMd:
Methylbenzene can react with chlorine under different conditions to give the monochloro derivatives **F** and **G**, shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Diagram of aromatic reactions: methylbenzene converts to 4-chloromethylbenzene (F) via reaction 1 and to chloromethylbenzene (G) via reaction 2.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/020-diagram-of-aromatic-reactions-methylbenzene-conv.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

State the reagents and conditions for each reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each reaction are:
> 
> - Reaction 1: Cl<sub>2</sub> **AND** AlCl<sub>3</sub> / FeCl<sub>3</sub> / Fe / Al **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction 2: Cl<sub>2</sub> **AND** ultraviolet / UV light **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Halogenation of alkylarenes occurs in two different ways depending on the conditions:
> 
> - In the aromatic ring: requires a halogen carrier. For chlorination, the carrier must be a chloride compound, such as AlCl<sub>3</sub>, FeCl<sub>3</sub>, Fe, or Al. Bromide carriers (e.g. AlBr<sub>3</sub>) would not generate the Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile needed.
> - In the side chain: requires ultraviolet (UV) light to initiate homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, generating chlorine radicals.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Methylbenzene can react with chlorine under different conditions to give the monochloro derivatives **F** and **G**, shown in Fig. 2.1.

{align=center} **Fig. 2.1**

State the name of the mechanism for each reaction in Fig. 2.1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mechanism for each reaction is:
> 
> - Reaction 1: electrophilic substitution **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction 2: free radical substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In reaction 1, the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst generates the Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile, which attacks the electron-rich benzene ring in an electrophilic substitution reaction.
> 
> In reaction 2, UV light causes homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, producing chlorine radicals that react with the methyl side chain in a free radical substitution reaction.
> 
> Both are substitution reactions because a hydrogen atom is replaced by chlorine, but the mechanisms are completely different.

parts.problemMd:
2-bromopentane is a halogenoalkane and bromobenzene is a halogenoarene.

State which compound is more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> - 2-bromopentane **[1 mark]**

> Halogenoarenes are much less reactive than halogenoalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution. In bromobenzene, the lone pair on the bromine atom is partially delocalised into the benzene ring, which strengthens the C–Br bond significantly compared to the average C–Br bond.

parts.problemMd: The average bond enthalpy of a C–Br bond is 276 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. Suggest whether the bond enthalpy of the C–Br bond in bromobenzene is greater or less than the average bond enthalpy and state what this means about the strength of the C–Br bond in bromobenzene.

> 
> - Greater **[1 mark]**
> - The C–Br bond in bromobenzene is stronger than a typical C–Br bond **[1 mark]**

> This question has two parts: state whether the bond enthalpy is greater or less, then state what this means about bond strength. One mark is available for each.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd: Explain why halogenoalkanes such as bromopropane are more reactive than halogenoarenes such as bromobenzene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why halogenoalkanes are more reactive than halogenoarenes towards nucleophilic substitution:
> 
> - The C–Br bond in halogenoalkanes / bromopropane is polar: δ+ C atom and δ– Br atom **[1 mark]**
> - Nucleophiles can attack the δ+ carbon atom **[1 mark]**
> - One of the lone pairs of electrons on the bromine in bromobenzene is delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A complete answer contrasts both compounds: in halogenoalkanes, the polar C–Br bond is open to nucleophilic attack at the δ+ carbon; in halogenoarenes, lone pair donation from Br into the ring creates partial double-bond character that strengthens the C–Br bond and prevents nucleophilic substitution.

Cl<sub>2</sub> + AlCl<sub>3</sub> → Cl<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Construct the equation for the electrophilic substitution of benzene:

Cl<sup>+</sup> + C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Cl + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Construct the equation showing regeneration of the catalyst:

H<sup>+</sup> + AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> → HCl + AlCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

**AND**

This completes the catalytic cycle: AlCl<sub>3</sub> is consumed in step 1 but regenerated in step 3, so the overall amount of AlCl<sub>3</sub> is unchanged.

Use these ideas to suggest the structures of the intermediate compounds **Y** and **Z** in the following synthesis of 4-chlorophenylamine.

parts.solutionMd:
The structures of Compounds **Y** and **Z** are:

Compound **Y** (chlorobenzene):

![Structure of chlorobenzene showing a benzene ring with a Cl substituent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/002-structure-of-chlorobenzene-showing-a-benzene-rin.png)

Compound **Z** (4-chloronitrobenzene):

![Structure of 4-chloronitrobenzene showing a benzene ring with Cl at position 4 and a NO2 group at position 1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/31-halogen-compounds/31-1-halogen-compounds/assets/003-structure-of-4-chloronitrobenzene-showing-a-benz.png)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order matters: chlorination must occur before nitration so that the –Cl group directs the –NO<sub>2</sub> into the 4-position
> 
> To decide which step comes first, work backwards from the final product (4-chlorophenylamine) and consider the directing effects:
> 
> The –Cl group is 2,4-directing, so if chlorination occurs first, nitration is directed to the 4-position. This gives 4-chloronitrobenzene (Compound Z). Reduction of the –NO<sub>2</sub> group then gives 4-chlorophenylamine.

Fig. 3.1 shows two reactions of methylbenzene.

The three chloro-compounds **A**, **B** and **C** vary in their ease of hydrolysis.

i) Place a tick in the box in Table 3.1 corresponding to the correct relative rates of hydrolysis. [the symbol '>' means 'faster than'].

**Table 3.1**

|   | Place **one** tick only in this column |
|---|---|
| **A** > **B** > **C** |   |
| **A** > **C** > **B** |   |
| **B** > **A** > **C** |   |
| **B** > **C** > **A** |   |
| **C** > **B** > **A** |   |
| **C** > **A** > **B** |   |

[1]

ii) Suggest an explanation for these differences in reactivity.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The correct order of ease of hydrolysis:
> 
> - **C** > **B** > **A** **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The explanation for the differences in reactivity:
> 
> - Compound **C** (acyl chloride) is most reactive: the carbon atom is highly δ+ due to bonding to two electronegative atoms (Cl and =O)
> **OR**
> an addition-elimination mechanism is possible **[1 mark]**
> - Compound **A** (aryl chloride) is least reactive: a lone pair on the Cl atom is delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character and making it very strong **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrolysis involves nucleophilic attack by OH<sup>–</sup> on the carbon atom. Ease of hydrolysis depends on how accessible and electron-deficient that carbon is:
> 
> Compound **C** (acyl chloride) is most reactive: the carbon is highly δ+ (bonded to two electronegative groups: Cl and C=O), and an addition-elimination mechanism is available.
> 
> Compound **B** (chloroalkyl benzene) is intermediate: the C–Cl bond is polar and accessible, but the carbon is less activated than in an acyl chloride.
> 
> Compound **A** (aryl chloride) is least reactive: the lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the benzene ring π system, creating partial double-bond character that significantly strengthens the C–Cl bond.

Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for nucleophilic addition-elimination is:

![Nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism for the reaction of propan-2-ol with ethanoyl chloride, showing curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, and tetrahedral intermediate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/32-hydroxy-compounds/32-1-alcohols/assets/005-nucleophilic-addition-elimination-mechanism-for-.webp)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the O–H oxygen to the δ+ carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the δ– carbonyl oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for a correct tetrahedral intermediate structure
> 
> 1 mark for correct curly arrows on the intermediate showing loss of Cl<sup>-</sup> and restoration of the C=O bond

> **[exam-tip]**
> This mechanism is nucleophilic addition-elimination. There are two stages:
> 
> 1. Addition: the lone pair on the oxygen of propan-2-ol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the C=O breaks to form a tetrahedral intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and Cl still attached.
> 2. Elimination: the C–Cl bond breaks (Cl<sup>-</sup> leaves); the C=O re-forms as electrons from O<sup>-</sup> move back onto carbon.
> 
> Curly arrows must start from a lone pair or a bond and point towards a positive or partial-positive centre. Show all δ+ and δ– on the C=O and C–Cl bonds clearly before drawing your arrows.

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Explain why phenol acts as a weak acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol acts as a weak acid because:
> 
> - The lone pair on the oxygen atom delocalises into the benzene / aromatic π system **[1 mark]**
> - This weakens the O–H bond / stabilises the phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - The H<sup>+</sup> ion can be donated / released more easily **[1 mark]**
> 
> Phenol is a weak acid, so the equilibrium C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> lies to the left; accept references to partial dissociation

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenol is a weak acid because it only partially dissociates in aqueous solution. The explanation requires three linked ideas:
> 
> 1. Delocalisation: the lone pair on oxygen spreads into the ring π system.
> 2. Effect on O–H bond: this weakens the O–H bond and stabilises the phenoxide ion formed when H<sup>+</sup> leaves.
> 3. Result: H<sup>+</sup> can be released, but the equilibrium lies to the left, making phenol weak rather than strong.
> 
> Do not describe phenol as fully dissociating — that would make it a strong acid. The stability of the phenoxide ion, provided by delocalisation, is the key driving factor.

parts.problemMd:
Phenol behaves as a weak acid.

[1]

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of phenol with sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + NaOH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
>

>

> **[exam-tip]**
> These are acid–base reactions:
> 
> Acid + base → salt + water (phenol + NaOH)
> 
> Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas (phenol + Na)
> 
> The product in both reactions is sodium phenoxide, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>. The phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) forms an ionic bond with Na<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
Explain why phenol is a weak acid.

You should include an equation in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol acts as a weak acid because:
> 
> - Phenol can donate the H atom from the O–H group to form the phenoxide ion **[1 mark]**
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The phenoxide ion is stable because the negative charge is delocalised (spread) over the entire ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids donate protons. Although phenol is a weak acid, it can still lose the H from the –OH group to form the phenoxide ion. The equilibrium lies to the left (phenol is not fully ionised), making it weakly acidic.

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain how the acidities of ethanol and phenol compare with that of water.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A comparison of the acidities of ethanol and phenol with that of water:
> 
> - Ethanol is less acidic than water **[1 mark]**
> - The ethyl group is electron-donating, concentrating more negative charge on the oxygen atom of the ethoxide ion **[1 mark]**
> - Phenol is more acidic than water **[1 mark]**
> - The phenoxide ion is more stable than hydroxide because the negative charge is delocalised over the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The order of acidity (least to most acidic): ethanol < water < phenol
> 
> In phenol, the phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) has its charge spread over the benzene ring via delocalisation. This reduces the tendency to accept H<sup>+</sup> back, making phenol more acidic than water.
> 
> In ethanol, the ethoxide ion (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>) has charge concentrated on oxygen because the ethyl group is electron-donating. The higher charge density means H<sup>+</sup> is more strongly attracted back, making ethanol less acidic than water.

> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of **G**: HO–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>2</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Further substitution of **G** to form HO–C<sub>6</sub>HBr<sub>3</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub> **OR** HO–C<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>4</sub>–NH<sub>2</sub> is accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rodinol is a weak acid (phenol group) and a base (amine group):
> 
> - Reaction with NaOH: the phenol –OH is deprotonated to give compound E (sodium 4-aminophenoxide) and water
> - Reaction with HCl: the –NH<sub>2</sub> is protonated to give compound F (4-aminophenol hydrochloride)
> 
> When rodinol reacts with excess aqueous bromine, both the –OH and –NH<sub>2</sub> groups are activating, directing electrophiles to positions 2 and 6. The most likely product (compound G) is 4-amino-2,6-dibromophenol, but further bromination is also possible and accepted.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactions of phenol and benzene.

Explain the difference in bromination of phenol and benzene. In your answer, include structures of any organic products formed in the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The structure of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is:

![2,4,6-tribromophenol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/32-hydroxy-compounds/32-2-phenol/assets/027-2-4-6-tribromophenol.jpeg)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 2,4,6-tribromophenol
> 
> The difference in bromination of phenol and benzene, including structures of any organic products formed:
> 
> - Phenol has a lone pair on the oxygen atom that (partially) delocalises into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> 
> - The π electrons of benzene are delocalised over the ring **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Phenol has a higher electron density in the ring than benzene **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Benzene cannot polarise the Br–Br bond
> **OR**
> Phenol can polarise the Br–Br bond (allow: δ<sup>+</sup> Br or Br<sup>+</sup> electrophile) **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Bromination of benzene requires a halogen carrier catalyst such as FeBr<sub>3</sub> / AlBr<sub>3</sub> and pure bromine **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to form 2,4,6-tribromophenol **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question covers a lot of content. Break your answer into sections:
> 
> **Bromination of phenol**:
> 
> - The lone pair on the oxygen atom delocalises into the π ring, increasing electron density.
> - This allows phenol to polarise the Br–Br bond and react with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.
> 
> **Bromination of benzene**:
> 
> - The π electrons are delocalised but the electron density is lower than in phenol.
> - Benzene cannot polarise Br–Br on its own and requires pure bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst (FeBr<sub>3</sub> or AlBr<sub>3</sub>), giving bromobenzene.
> 
> **Directing effects**:
> 
> - The –OH group is an activating group that directs electrophiles to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, which is why three bromine atoms are substituted in phenol but only one in benzene.

A mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol can be formed via the pathway shown in Fig. 1.1.

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the reagents **and** conditions required for reaction **1**.

[1]

ii) Calculate the mass, in grams, of phenol required to form 30 g of 2-nitrophenol assuming a 35% yield. Give your answer to three significant figures and show your working.

mass = ............... g

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for reaction **1** are:
> 
> - Dilute HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> Room temperature **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the mass of phenol required to produce 30 g of 2-nitrophenol at 35% yield:

- State the M<sub>r</sub> values:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrophenol = 139.0

*M*<sub>r</sub> of phenol = 94.0

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass of 2-nitrophenol produced at 100% yield:

mass at 100% yield = $\frac{30}{35} \times 100$

mass at 100% yield = 85.71 g

- Calculate the moles of 2-nitrophenol:

moles = $\frac{85.71}{139.0}$

moles = 0.617 mol

**[1 mark]**

moles of phenol = 0.617 mol

mass = 0.617 x 94.0 = **58.0 g**

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The tricky part of this calculation is working back from the actual yield to find the theoretical mass at 100% yield. Rearrange the percentage yield formula: theoretical mass = actual mass ÷ % yield x 100.

parts.problemMd:
Phenol reacts with sodium to form a salt and hydrogen gas in an acid-base reaction.

Explain why phenol behaves as a weak acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Phenol behaves as a weak acid because:
> 
> - The O–H bond breaks; H<sup>+</sup> is donated and the phenoxide ion, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>, is formed **[1 mark]**
> - A lone pair on the oxygen atom (partially) delocalises into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - This stabilises the phenoxide ion / the negative charge is delocalised (spread) over the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the ring is the key difference between phenol and simple alcohols. It weakens the O–H bond compared to alcohols, making phenol acidic. However, phenol is still a weak acid because the equilibrium lies to the left, so it does not fully ionise in water.
> 
> The formula of the phenoxide ion is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup>. The dissociation equation is:
> 
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup>
> 
> You may also be asked to calculate the pH of a phenol solution from a given concentration using the K<sub>a</sub> expression.

parts.problemMd: State the relative acidities of benzoic acid and phenol. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative acidities of benzoic acid and phenol are:
> 
> - Benzoic acid is a stronger acid than phenol **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O group in benzoic acid withdraws electron density from the O–H bond (negative inductive effect) **[1 mark]**
> - This weakens the O–H bond, making it easier to release H<sup>+</sup> / the proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stronger an acid, the more easily it donates a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). In benzoic acid, the adjacent C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond, stabilising the benzoate anion and making proton release easier.
> 
> In phenol, the oxygen lone pair is donated into the benzene ring, which reduces the electron density available on the oxygen. However, phenol has no carbonyl group to further weaken the O–H bond, so it is a weaker acid than benzoic acid (though stronger than aliphatic alcohols).

parts.problemMd:
State the relative order of acidity of benzoic acid, phenylmethanol and 4-methylphenol shown in Fig. 1.1, starting with the most acidic. Explain your reasoning.

![Structural formulae of three organic compounds: benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH), phenylmethanol (C₆H₅CH₂OH), and 4-methylphenol (4-CH₃-C₆H₄-OH)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/006-structural-formulae-of-three-organic-compounds-b.jpeg)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of acidity and reasoning are:
> 
> - Benzoic acid > 4-methylphenol > phenylmethanol **[1 mark]**
> - The benzoate ion is stabilised by delocalisation of negative charge over two electronegative oxygen atoms 
> **OR**
> The C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond **[1 mark]**
> - The 4-methylphenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - The alkoxide ion of phenylmethanol is destabilised by the electron-donating CH<sub>2</sub> group 
> **OR**
> The alkyl group donates electron density to the oxygen, making it less stable **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The relative acidity depends on the stability of the conjugate base (the anion formed after losing H<sup>+</sup>). The more stable the anion, the more readily the compound donates a proton.
> 
> The benzoate ion is particularly stable because the negative charge is delocalised over two electronegative oxygen atoms. The phenoxide ion is less stable as the charge is delocalised into carbon atoms in the ring. The alkoxide ion from phenylmethanol is destabilised by the electron-donating effect of the benzyl group.

![Chemical structure of the Nylon 6,6 repeat unit showing the amide linkage –NH–CO– connecting a hexamethylene diamine chain and an adipoyl chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-1-carboxylic-acids/assets/005-chemical-structure-of-the-nylon-6-6-repeat-unit-.png)

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation for the formation of the ester from methanol and propanoic acid is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> The first part of the ester name comes from the alcohol: methanol gives the methyl- group. The second part comes from the carboxylic acid: propanoic acid gives the -propanoate group. The ester formed is methyl propanoate.
> 
> During the reaction, a water molecule is lost and an ester linkage (-COO-) forms between the two groups. This type of reaction is a condensation reaction.
> 
> In the structural formula, the -CO- portion comes from the carboxylic acid and the -O- portion comes from the alcohol, giving CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>.

parts.problemMd: Name and outline a mechanism for the reaction between methanol and propanoyl chloride to form methyl propanoate.
parts.solutionMd:
The name and mechanism for the reaction between methanol and propanoyl chloride to form methyl propanoate:

Name = (nucleophilic) addition-elimination

![Nucleophilic addition step of addition-elimination mechanism: curly arrow from methanol lone pair to δ+ carbonyl carbon of propanoyl chloride, and curly arrow from C=O bond to O, giving tetrahedral intermediate with negatively charged O and positively charged methanol oxygen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/004-nucleophilic-addition-step-of-addition-eliminati.png)

**[5 marks]**

> 1 mark for naming the mechanism: (Nucleophilic) Addition-elimination
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the oxygen (of the OH) to the carbon atom of C=O **AND **δ+ on C of C=O and δ− on O of C=O
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from C=O bond to the O of the C=O bond
> 
> 1 mark for three correct curly arrows in the second stage **AND **a lone pair on the O atom
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of the ion including the two charges

> **[exam-tip]**
> The alcohol acts as a nucleophile in this reaction. The lone pair on the oxygen of methanol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon, and an HCl molecule is eliminated in the second step.
> 
> Make sure your curly arrows are clear and double-headed. The first mechanism mark requires both the curly arrow from the lone pair **AND **the partial charges (δ+ on C and δ− on O of C=O) to be shown.
> 
> The mechanism is called addition-elimination because the nucleophile first adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate, and then the chloride ion is eliminated.

parts.problemMd: State **two** advantages of using propanoyl chloride over propanoic acid in the preparation of esters in industry.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two advantages of using propanoyl chloride over propanoic acid in the preparation of esters in industry:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The reactions with acyl chlorides are quicker / faster
> - The acyl chloride reactions go to completion / are irreversible / do not form an equilibrium mixture
> - A higher yield of ester is obtained
> - No catalyst is required
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A reaction that forms an equilibrium mixture will result in a lower yield of product, because the reverse reaction continuously converts products back into reactants. Acyl chlorides avoid this problem as they react irreversibly, producing a higher yield in a shorter time.

parts.problemMd:
Methanoic acid, HCO<sub>2</sub>H, has a similar acid strength to propanoic acid.

Describe a chemical test to distinguish between these two acids. Name the acid which gives a positive result in this test and describe the observations that would be made.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A chemical test to distinguish between the two acids, and the expected observations, are:
> 
> Any **one** of the following sets (1 mark for the chemical test and 1 mark for the acid/observation):
> 
> Set 1:
> 
> - Chemical test: Tollens' reagent
> - Acid/observation: Methanoic acid gives a silver mirror / black precipitate / grey solid
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Set 2:
> 
> - Chemical test: Fehling's solution
> - Acid/observation: Methanoic acid gives a red / orange precipitate / solid
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution both react with methanoic acid because the carbonyl carbon has a hydrogen directly bonded to it, as shown in the displayed formulae.
> 
> ![Displayed formulae of methanoic acid (left, H-C(=O)-OH) and propanoic acid (right, CH3CH2COOH), showing that methanoic acid has a hydrogen directly bonded to its carbonyl carbon, unlike propanoic acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/002-displayed-formulae-of-methanoic-acid-left-h-c-o-.jpeg)
> 
> This allows methanoic acid to behave like an aldehyde and act as a reducing agent.
> 
> Propanoic acid does not give a positive result because, although its carbon is doubly bonded to oxygen, it does not have a hydrogen directly attached to the carbonyl carbon.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
i) The product of the first step:

![Displayed formula of propanoyl chloride (CH3CH2COCl), the acyl chloride product of reacting propanoic acid with PCl5, showing C=O and C-Cl bonds at the terminal carbon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-2-esters/assets/003-displayed-formula-of-propanoyl-chloride-ch3ch2co.jpeg)

> ii) The reagents and conditions needed for each step are:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The ester phenyl propanoate, C~2~H~5~CO~2~C~6~H~5~, can be made from phenol and propanoic acid in a two step synthesis.

Acyl chlorides react faster and irreversibly, giving a higher yield. The esterification of acyl chlorides proceeds via an addition-elimination mechanism, which is why the reaction goes to completion.

parts.problemMd:
Esters are responsible for various sweet, flowery and fruity smells. Some confectionery products use synthetic esters to achieve their aroma.

A student reacted acids and alcohols together to form ethyl methanoate (raspberry essence) and ethyl butanoate (pineapple essence).

Construct word and symbol equations to show the reactions that would produce these esters.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The word and symbol equations for the formation of ethyl methanoate (raspberry essence) and ethyl butanoate (pineapple essence) are:
> 
> - Ethanol + methanoic acid → ethyl methanoate + water
> **AND**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + HCOOH → HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol + butanoic acid → ethyl butanoate + water
> **AND**
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember that acid + alcohol → ester + water.
> 
> The alcohol gives the alkyl part of the ester name (ethanol = ethyl-) and the acid gives the carboxylate part (methanoic acid = -methanoate; butanoic acid = -butanoate).

parts.problemMd:
Octyl ethanoate can be manufactured or extracted from oranges and grapefruits. It is a flammable ester with a boiling point of 211 <sup>o</sup>C, a flash point of 86 <sup>o</sup>C and a density of 0.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

A student reacted an acid and an alcohol in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to make an immiscible sample of octyl ethanoate. They added warm, aqueous sodium carbonate solution to remove any excess acid.

i) Explain why distillation would **not** work to safely obtain the octyl ethanoate.

[2]

ii) Describe the equipment that the student could use to safely obtain their octyl ethanoate and explain how this equipment would work.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Distillation would not allow the student to safely obtain their octyl ethanoate because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The ester / octyl ethanoate is flammable
> **AND**
> it could ignite using a Bunsen burner / its flash point is below its boiling point
> - The high boiling point of the ester / octyl ethanoate
> **AND**
> means that the aqueous portion would boil off / would leave behind any dissolved materials in the ester / octyl ethanoate
> - There is a risk that the ester / octyl ethanoate could distil across with the water
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> ii) The equipment that the student could use to safely obtain their octyl ethanoate is:
> 
> - A separating funnel **[1 mark]**
> - (Because) the ester / octyl ethanoate does not dissolve in water
> **OR**
> (Because) the ester / octyl ethanoate forms an organic layer
> **OR**
> (Because) the ester / octyl ethanoate floats on top of the other chemicals **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question gives you a lot of information about octyl ethanoate: it is flammable (flash point 86 °C), has a high boiling point (211 °C), and has a density of 0.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, meaning it is less dense than water and immiscible with it.
> 
> The flash point (86 °C) is well below the boiling point (211 °C), so the ester would ignite before it could be distilled safely using a Bunsen burner.
> 
> To safely purify the octyl ethanoate, focus on its low density and immiscibility with water. A separating funnel allows the organic layer to be separated from the aqueous layer without any heating.

i) The equation for the reaction between propan-2-ol and ethanoic acid, showing the structure of the organic product:

parts.problemMd:
