> **[exam-tip]**
> The compound in Fig. 1.1 is an acyl chloride. To name an acyl chloride, take the name of the parent carboxylic acid and replace "-ic acid" with "-oyl chloride". The longest chain (including the carbonyl carbon) has four carbons, so the parent acid is butanoic acid, giving **butanoyl chloride**.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoyl chloride reacts with ethanol to form ethyl ethanoate as shown in Fig. 1.2.

![Reaction equation showing ethanoyl chloride reacting with ethanol to form ethyl ethanoate and HCl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/005-reaction-equation-showing-ethanoyl-chloride-reac.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) State the name of the other product formed in this reaction.

[1]

ii) This reaction can be described as an esterification reaction or an acylation reaction.

Explain why this reaction can also be described as a condensation reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

> i) The name of the other product formed:
> 
> - Hydrogen chloride / HCl **[1 mark]**
>

> 
> - A small molecule / hydrogen chloride / HCl is eliminated **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A condensation reaction is one in which two molecules join together and a small molecule is eliminated.
> 
> When an acyl chloride reacts with an alcohol, HCl is the small molecule eliminated. Compare this with the direct esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol, where water (H<sub>2</sub>O) is eliminated instead.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoyl chloride can also react with ammonia to form ethanamide.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl
> **OR**
> CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both equations are accepted by CIE. When excess ammonia is present, the HCl produced immediately reacts with a second NH<sub>3</sub> molecule to form ammonium chloride, NH<sub>4</sub>Cl. The equation using 2NH<sub>3</sub> is the more complete answer when excess ammonia is specified.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

> **[exam-tip]**
> The by-products SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl tell you which reagent was used. SOCl<sub>2</sub> (thionyl chloride) produces SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl as by-products:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + SOCl<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl + SO<sub>2</sub> + HCl
> 
> The other reagents that convert carboxylic acids to acyl chlorides are PCl<sub>5</sub> (by-products: POCl<sub>3</sub> + HCl) and PCl<sub>3</sub> (by-product: H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>3</sub>).

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
i) State the names of the two products formed when propanoyl chloride undergoes hydrolysis.

[2]

ii) State the name of the mechanism by which hydrolysis occurs.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two products formed when propanoyl chloride undergoes hydrolysis are:
> 
> - Propanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - HCl / hydrochloric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Addition-elimination / nucleophilic addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The hydrolysis of an acyl chloride always produces the corresponding carboxylic acid and HCl. Water acts as the nucleophile, attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon atom, before HCl is eliminated.
> 
> For higher-mark questions, you may be asked to draw the full mechanism for this reaction.

parts.problemMd: Explain why propanoyl chloride will more readily undergo hydrolysis compared to 2-chloropropane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason propanoyl chloride hydrolyses more readily is:
> 
> - The carbonyl carbon is bonded to two highly electronegative atoms (oxygen and chlorine) / the carbonyl carbon is highly electron-deficient (δ+) **[1 mark]**
> - It strongly attracts nucleophiles / is highly susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water **[1 mark]**
> 
> 'The C-Cl bond is weaker' is not accepted without reference to the electron-deficient carbonyl carbon

> **[exam-tip]**
> In 2-chloropropane, the carbon bonded to chlorine is attached to only one electronegative atom. In propanoyl chloride, the carbonyl carbon is attached to both oxygen and chlorine. This creates a much larger δ+ charge on the carbonyl carbon, making it far more susceptible to nucleophilic attack by water.
> 
> Note that the C-Cl bond in an acyl chloride is indeed weaker than in an alkyl chloride, but this alone is not the accepted explanation here. The answer must reference the electron deficiency of the carbonyl carbon and its susceptibility to nucleophilic attack.

parts.problemMd:
Acyl chlorides are commonly used carboxylic acid derivatives.

Ethanoyl chloride reacts with an excess of ammonia.

A student proposes the following equation to represent the reaction:

CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + NH<sub>3</sub>  →  CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + HCl

Correct and explain the student's error.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct equation for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with excess ammonia is:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>COCl + 2NH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub> + NH<sub>4</sub>Cl **[1 mark]**
> 
> The student's equation is incorrect because:
> 
> - The excess ammonia reacts with the HCl produced, because ammonia is a base
> **AND**
> Ammonium chloride is formed as the second product (not hydrogen chloride) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The student's equation would have been correct if ethanoyl chloride reacted with a single equivalent of ammonia only. The use of excess ammonia means a second molecule of NH<sub>3</sub> acts as a base and reacts with the HCl produced, forming NH<sub>4</sub>Cl as the ionic salt product.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain why butanoic acid is a weaker acid than 2-chlorobutanoic acid.

[2]

ii) Draw the skeletal formula for 2-chlorobutanoic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Butanoic acid is a weaker acid than 2-chlorobutanoic acid because:
> 
> - The chlorine atom withdraws electron density from the –COOH group **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) the O–H bond is weakened, making it easier for 2-chlorobutanoic acid to lose an H<sup>+</sup> ion **[1 mark]**

ii) The skeletal formula for 2-chlorobutanoic acid is:

![Skeletal formula of 2-chlorobutanoic acid with Cl substituent at the alpha carbon](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-2-chlorobutanoic-acid-with-c.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of 2-chlorobutanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acids ionise in water by losing an H<sup>+</sup> proton from the –OH group. The weaker the O–H bond, the more readily the proton is lost and the stronger the acid.
> 
> In 2-chlorobutanoic acid, the electronegative chlorine at C2 withdraws electron density from the nearby –COOH group through the sigma bonds (inductive effect). This weakens the O–H bond further compared to butanoic acid, making 2-chlorobutanoic acid a stronger acid.

> A chloro-substituted butanoic acid that is a stronger acid than 2-chlorobutanoic acid is:
> 
> - 2,2-dichlorobutanoic acid
> **OR**
> 2,3-dichlorobutanoic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The more chlorine atoms attached to the molecule, the greater the electron withdrawal from the –COOH group and the stronger the acid. Both 2,2-dichlorobutanoic acid and 2,3-dichlorobutanoic acid are valid answers, as each contains two chlorine atoms compared to one in 2-chlorobutanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
Butanoyl chloride can undergo hydrolysis.

Describe the mechanism for the hydrolysis of butanoyl chloride. Include charges, dipoles, lone pairs of electrons and curly arrows, as appropriate.
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism for the hydrolysis of butanoyl chloride is:

![Curly arrow mechanism diagram showing nucleophilic addition-elimination of water with butanoyl chloride to form butanoic acid and HCl](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/003-curly-arrow-mechanism-diagram-showing-nucleophil.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the oxygen atom of H<sub>2</sub>O to the δ+ carbonyl carbon **AND** δ+ shown on the carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen atom of the C=O group
> 
> 1 mark for all three curly arrows drawn correctly **AND** a lone pair shown on the oxygen atom of H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for a correct structure of the tetrahedral intermediate (including both charges)

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism. The water molecule acts as the nucleophile, with its lone pair attacking the δ+ carbonyl carbon. After the addition step forms the tetrahedral intermediate, the elimination step regenerates the C=O bond as HCl is eliminated to give butanoic acid.
> 
> Make sure your curly arrows are double-headed and you clearly show the δ+ on the carbonyl carbon.

parts.problemMd: State and explain the relative ease of hydrolysis for butanoyl chloride, chlorobenzene and 1-chlorobutane.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct order of ease of hydrolysis (most reactive first) is:
> 
> - Butanoyl chloride > 1-chlorobutane > chlorobenzene **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation for the order of butanoyl chloride and 1-chlorobutane:
> 
> - Butanoyl chloride has a carbon atom bonded to two electronegative atoms (oxygen and chlorine) **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) the carbonyl carbon is more strongly δ+ than the carbon in 1-chlorobutane, making it more susceptible to nucleophilic attack **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation for the position of chlorobenzene:
> 
> - A lone pair of electrons from the Cl atom overlaps with the delocalised π electrons in the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - (Therefore,) the C–Cl bond acquires partial double-bond character and is stronger / harder to break **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acyl chlorides can be hydrolysed readily at room temperature by water. Alkyl chlorides such as 1-chlorobutane require heating under reflux with aqueous alkali, because hydroxide ions are stronger nucleophiles than water and are needed to break the C–Cl bond.
> 
> Aryl chlorides such as chlorobenzene are the least reactive towards hydrolysis. One of the lone pairs on the Cl atom overlaps with the delocalised π system of the benzene ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character. This makes the C–Cl bond significantly stronger and much harder to break.

parts.problemMd:
A common method for esterification is to react an alcohol with an acyl chloride.

i) State the name of the mechanism for the reaction of butan-2-ol with ethanoyl chloride.

[1]

ii) Describe the mechanism for the reaction of butan-2-ol with ethanoyl chloride. Include charges, dipoles, lone pairs of electrons and curly arrows, as appropriate.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the reaction of butan-2-ol with ethanoyl chloride is:

![Curly arrow mechanism diagram showing nucleophilic addition-elimination of butan-2-ol with ethanoyl chloride to form an ester](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/33-carboxylic-acids-and-derivatives/33-3-acyl-chlorides/assets/007-curly-arrow-mechanism-diagram-showing-nucleophil.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the lone pair on the O of butan-2-ol to the C of the C=O, **AND** δ+ shown on the carbonyl carbon
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the O of the C=O group
> 
> 1 mark for O<sup>–</sup> on the former carbonyl O (with lone pair and negative charge) **AND** O<sup>+</sup> on butan-2-ol O **AND** a curly arrow from the lone pair of O<sup>–</sup> to the C–O bond
> 
> 1 mark for the correct ester product **AND** a curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to the Cl atom

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mechanism is nucleophilic addition-elimination. The oxygen lone pair from butan-2-ol attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon in the addition step. The subsequent elimination step regenerates the C=O group and HCl is lost.
> 
> Learn the general mechanism rather than memorising it for one specific reaction. If you understand what nucleophilic addition-elimination involves, you can apply it to any acyl chloride reaction.

parts.problemMd:
Acyl chlorides undergo various reactions with water, alcohols, ammonia and primary amines.

Ethanamide is the product of a chemical reaction.

State the necessary reactants and name the other product.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reactants required to make ethanamide using an acyl chloride are:
> 
> - Reactant: Ethanoyl chloride **[1 mark]**
> - Reactant: Ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Other product: ammonium chloride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To identify the reactants, look at the functional groups in the product. Ethanamide (CH<sub>3</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>) contains a carbonyl group (from an acyl chloride) and an amine group (from ammonia). The acyl chloride that produces the CH<sub>3</sub>CO– group is ethanoyl chloride (CH<sub>3</sub>COCl).
> 
> When an acyl chloride reacts with ammonia, the byproduct is ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl), because excess ammonia reacts with the HCl produced.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoyl chloride can react with primary aliphatic and aromatic amines to produce different amides.

i) Explain why ethanoyl chloride is more reactive towards ethylamine than phenylamine.

[2]

ii) Name the products of both reactions and classify the nitrogen in each product.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Ethanoyl chloride reacts more readily with ethylamine than phenylamine because:
> 
> - Ethylamine is a stronger nucleophile than phenylamine
> **OR**
> Phenylamine is a weaker nucleophile than ethylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The alkyl group in ethylamine donates electron density to N, making the lone pair more available for nucleophilic attack
> **OR**
> The N lone pair in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available for nucleophilic attack **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The products and classification of nitrogen are:
> 
> - N-ethylethanamide **[1 mark]**
> - N-phenylethanamide **[1 mark]**
> - The nitrogen in both products is secondary / 2° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): the reactivity of an amine as a nucleophile depends on how available the lone pair on N is. Alkyl groups (in ethylamine) donate electron density to N via the inductive effect, increasing lone pair availability. In phenylamine, the N lone pair is partially delocalised into the benzene π system, reducing its availability for nucleophilic attack.
> 
> For part (ii): when naming secondary amides from acyl chloride reactions, identify the chain attached to N (ethyl / phenyl) and the chain containing the carbonyl (ethan-). The product names take the form N-[alkyl/aryl]ethanamide. Both nitrogen atoms are secondary because N is bonded to two carbon atoms in the amide.

parts.problemMd:
Butylamine can be synthesised from 1-bromobutane.

State the reagents and conditions required for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions required for the conversion of 1-bromobutane into butylamine are:
> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanolic solvent / ethanol **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under pressure **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amines can be prepared by two main routes:
> 
> - The reaction of halogenoalkanes with excess ethanolic ammonia, heated under pressure
> - The reduction of nitriles using LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether
> 
> Make sure you know the reagents and conditions required for both of these reactions.

parts.problemMd: Explain why amines can act as bases.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Amines can act as bases because:
> 
> - They can accept a proton (H<sup>+</sup> ion) / donate the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom to a proton, forming a dative / coordinate bond **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A base is defined as a proton acceptor or electron-pair donor.
> 
> An amine accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup> ion) by donating its lone pair of electrons from the nitrogen atom to form a dative (coordinate) bond. This is why amines are classified as bases.

parts.problemMd:
Ethylamine acts as a base when it reacts with hydrochloric acid.

(i) Construct an equation for this reaction.

[1]

(ii) State the systematic name of the organic product formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of ethylamine with hydrochloric acid:
> 
> - CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HCl → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of the organic product:
> 
> - Ethylammonium chloride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The nitrogen atom in ethylamine accepts a proton (H<sup>+</sup> ion) from HCl by donating its lone pair of electrons to form a dative bond. This gives the nitrogen atom a positive charge in the product.
> 
> Amines react with HCl to form amine salts. The product must show the correct charges on the correct atoms.

parts.problemMd:
Amines react with acid chlorides to produce nitrogen-containing products.

i) State the name of the mechanism for the reaction between ethanoyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>COCl, and methylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.

[1]

ii) Describe the mechanism for this reaction. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

[4]

iii) State the systematic name of the compound formed in the reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism:
> 
> - (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the reaction between ethanoyl chloride and methylamine is:

![Nucleophilic addition-elimination mechanism between ethanoyl chloride and methylamine, showing lone pair on nitrogen attacking carbonyl carbon, tetrahedral intermediate with charges, and elimination of chloride to give N-methylethanamide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-1-primary-and-secondary-amines/assets/001-nucleophilic-addition-elimination-mechanism-betw.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from lone pair on N atom to δ+ C atom AND curly arrow from C=O bond to O atom, with correct dipole shown on C=O
> 
> 1 mark for correct tetrahedral intermediate with positive charge on N and negative charge on O
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from lone pair on O<sup>-</sup> atom to C-O bond AND curly arrow from C-Cl bond to Cl atom
> 
> 1 mark for correct product structure (N-methylethanamide)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The systematic name of the compound formed:
> 
> - *N*-methylethanamide **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An *N*-substituted amide is produced during the vigorous reaction between an amine and an acyl chloride.
> 
> Always show the lone pair on the nitrogen atom and the dipole on the C=O bond. The nitrogen atom in the intermediate carries a positive charge (it has four bonds) and the oxygen atom carries a negative charge.
> 
> The final step of the mechanism involves loss of H<sup>+</sup> as HCl, removed by the Cl<sup>-</sup> ion or another methylamine molecule. This step is not required in the mechanism.
> 
> The *N* in *N*-methylethanamide indicates that the methyl group is on the nitrogen atom. This is a condensation reaction, as two molecules combine to eliminate the small molecule HCl.

parts.problemMd:
Methylamine can be prepared from chloromethane.

i) State the reagents and conditions required for this synthesis.

[3]

ii) State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for the preparation of methylamine:
> 
> - Excess ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanolic solvent / ethanol **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under pressure **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The name of the mechanism:
> 
> - Nucleophilic substitution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Excess ammonia reduces the likelihood that the methylamine product will attack chloromethane. Because methylamine can itself act as a nucleophile, using excess ammonia prevents the formation of secondary and tertiary amines.
> 
> The excess ammonia also reacts with the HCl produced to form NH<sub>4</sub>Cl, removing it from the reaction mixture and preventing it from reacting with the methylamine.
> 
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction in which the nitrogen lone pair in ammonia attacks the carbon bearing the Cl, replacing Cl<sup>-</sup> as the leaving group.

parts.problemMd:
Chloroethane can also react with methylamine.

i) Draw the skeletal formula of the organic compound formed in this reaction.

ii) State the type of amine formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The type of amine formed is:
> 
> - Secondary amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a halogenoalkane reacts with a primary amine, a secondary amine is formed. The halogen is replaced by the nitrogen in the amine through nucleophilic substitution.
> 
> The product of chloroethane reacting with methylamine is N-methylethylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>). This is a secondary amine as the nitrogen atom has two alkyl groups (a methyl and an ethyl group) attached to it.

parts.problemMd:
Methylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, and dimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, are both soluble in water.

i) Suggest how, other than smell, the two solutions could be distinguished from one another.

[2]

ii) Explain your answer to part (i).

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A method to distinguish the two solutions:
> 
> - Use a pH meter **[1 mark]**
> - Dimethylamine produces a higher pH reading than methylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Explanation:
> 
> - The relative basicity depends on the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**
> - Dimethylamine is the stronger base
> **AND**
> the two alkyl groups donate electron density to the N atom (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Secondary amines such as dimethylamine are stronger bases than primary amines such as methylamine. This is because more alkyl groups on the nitrogen atom push electron density towards it, increasing the availability of the lone pair for accepting a proton.
> 
> In terms of base strength:
> 
> tertiary amines > secondary amines > primary amines > ammonia.

parts.problemMd:
The structural formulae of four isomeric amines, **A**–**D**, with the molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N are given in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

|   | **formula** | **systematic name** | **type of amine** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> | *N*-methylethanamine |   |
| **B** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N |   | tertiary |
| **C** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> |   |   |
| **D** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> |   |   |

Complete Table 2.1 to give the name and type of each amine. Each amine is primary, secondary, or tertiary.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

|   | **formula** | **systematic name** | **type of amine** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub> | *N*-methylethanamine | **Final answer:** **secondary** |
| **B** | (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N | **Final answer:** **trimethylamine / N,N-dimethylmethanamine** | tertiary |
| **C** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> | **Final answer:** **propan-1-amine / propylamine** | **Final answer:** **primary** |
| **D** | CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> | **Final answer:** **propan-2-amine / 2-aminopropane** | **Final answer:** **primary** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for A = secondary **AND **B = trimethylamine / N,N-dimethylmethanamine
> 
> 1 mark for C = propan-1-amine / propylamine **AND **primary
> 
> 1 mark for D = propan-2-amine / 2-aminopropane **AND **primary

> **[exam-tip]**
> (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N has three methyl groups on the nitrogen atom, making it a tertiary amine. It is commonly called trimethylamine; the IUPAC name is N,N-dimethylmethanamine.
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> is a propane chain with the amine group at carbon-1, making it a primary amine. Its IUPAC name is propan-1-amine.
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub> has the amine group at carbon-2, making it a primary amine. Its IUPAC name is propan-2-amine; 2-aminopropane is also accepted.
> 
> Primary amines have an –NH<sub>2</sub> group on one alkyl group. Secondary amines have an –NH group between two alkyl groups. Tertiary amines have three alkyl groups on the nitrogen.

parts.problemMd:
State the relative order of basicity of ammonia, hexylamine, and phenylamine. Explain your reasoning.

most basic  ......................... > ......................... > ......................... least basic
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of basicity (most basic to least basic) is:
> 
> - Hexylamine > ammonia > phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The hexyl / alkyl group is electron-donating (positive inductive effect)
> **AND**
> this increases the electron density on the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring
> **AND**
> this decreases the electron density on the nitrogen atom **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing the basicity of amines:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electrons (positive inductive effect), increasing the electron density on nitrogen. This makes the lone pair more available to accept a proton, so hexylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
> - In phenylamine, the lone pair on nitrogen delocalises into the benzene ring, reducing the electron density on nitrogen. This makes the lone pair less available, so phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia.

ii) Complete the mechanism of the reaction between hexylamine and ethanoyl chloride.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism:
>

parts.problemMd:
Three nitrogen-containing molecules, ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, and *N*-methylethanamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub>, are drawn below in Fig. 1.1.

![Three amine molecules: ammonia (NH3), phenylamine (C6H5NH2), and N-methylethanamine (CH3CH2NHCH3), shown as structural diagrams](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/017-three-amine-molecules-ammonia-nh3-phenylamine-c6.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the relative order of basicity of the three amine molecules shown in Fig. 1.1.

least basic ......................... < ......................... < ......................... most basic

[1]

ii) Explain your answer to part (i).

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of basicity, from least to most basic, is:
> 
> - Phenylamine < ammonia < *N*-methylethanamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The explanation for the order of basicity is:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electron density towards the N atom in *N*-methylethanamine / the methyl and ethyl groups have a positive inductive effect **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in *N*-methylethanamine is more available to accept a proton / bond with H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - In phenylamine, the lone pair on N overlaps with / becomes delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in phenylamine is therefore less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Base strength depends on the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom to accept H<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> For *N*-methylethanamine: two alkyl groups donate electron density towards N through the positive inductive effect, making the lone pair more available. This makes it the strongest base of the three.
> 
> For phenylamine: N is bonded directly to the benzene ring. The lone pair overlaps with the delocalised π electron system, partially withdrawing it from N and reducing its availability to bond with H<sup>+</sup>. This makes phenylamine the weakest base, weaker even than ammonia, which has no interaction with an aromatic ring system.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> - Below 10 °C / between 0 °C and 10 °C / ice-cold conditions **[1 mark]**

ii) The structure of the diazonium salt is:

![Structural formula of benzenediazonium chloride, showing a phenyl group bonded to two nitrogen atoms connected by a triple bond, with a positive charge on the terminal N atom and Cl minus as the counterion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/018-structural-formula-of-benzenediazonium-chloride-.png)

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Sodium hydroxide is required because:
> 
> - The reduction in strongly acidic conditions produces the protonated amine / 4-methylphenylammonium salt rather than the free amine **[1 mark]**
> - Aqueous sodium hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium salt / acts as a base to neutralise the acid and liberate the free amine **[1 mark]**

> To obtain the free amine, aqueous NaOH is added after the reduction step. It accepts the H<sup>+</sup> from the ammonium ion (acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base), releasing the neutral 4-methylphenylamine.

parts.problemMd:
When heated, phenylamine reacts with iodomethane to form compound **B**, *N*-methylphenylamine.

i) Describe the mechanism for the formation of the *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt from the reaction of phenylamine and iodomethane. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

[3]

ii) A further reaction occurs with an excess of iodomethane to form compound **C**, *N,N*-dimethylphenylamine.

Explain what this implies about the relative basicity of phenylamine and compound **B**.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The mechanism for the formation of the *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt is:

![Mechanism diagram showing nucleophilic substitution: the lone pair on the N atom of phenylamine attacks the delta positive carbon of iodomethane while the C-I bond breaks heterolytically, forming N-methylphenylammonium iodide salt with positive charge on N and I minus as a separate species](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-2-phenylamine-and-azo-compounds/assets/008-mechanism-diagram-showing-nucleophilic-substitut.jpg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the lone pair on N of phenylamine to the δ+ carbon of iodomethane
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the C–I bond to the I atom
> 
> 1 mark for correct product showing positive charge on the N atom **AND** I<sup>−</sup> / iodide ion as a separate species

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction. Phenylamine (the nucleophile, lone pair on N) attacks iodomethane (the electrophile, δ+ on C):
> 
> - One curly arrow from the lone pair on N to the δ+ carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>I
> - One curly arrow from the C–I bond to I
> - Product: *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt with positive charge on N and I<sup>−</sup> as a separate ion

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) This implies about the relative basicity:
> 
> - Compound **B** / *N*-methylphenylamine is a stronger base than phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The methyl group in compound **B** donates electron density towards the N atom / positive inductive effect of the methyl group **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in compound **B** is therefore more available to accept a proton than in phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both compounds contain a phenyl ring, so the delocalising effect of the ring on the N lone pair applies equally to both. The only structural difference is the methyl group in compound **B**.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since both phenylamine and compound **B** contain the phenyl ring, the delocalisation of the N lone pair into the π system applies equally to both. The only difference is the methyl group in compound **B**, which donates electron density towards N (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept H<sup>+</sup>. This makes compound **B** a stronger base, which explains why excess iodomethane is required to form compound **C**.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The acid-base indicator methyl red is an azo dye synthesised from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and phenylamine. Fig. 1.1 shows the first stages of this synthesis.

Synthesis scheme for methyl red showing: 2-nitrobenzaldehyde undergoes step 1 (oxidation) to give 2-nitrobenzoic acid, then step 2 (reduction) to give compound A (2-aminobenzoic acid), which undergoes step 3 (diazotization) and coupling with phenylamine to give methyl red

Explain why the temperature used in step 3 must be kept between 0 °C and 10 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The temperature must be kept between 0 °C and 10 °C because:
> 
> - Above 10 °C, the diazonium salt decomposes / reacts with water / forms a phenol / nitrogen gas is evolved **[1 mark]**
> - Below 0 °C, the reaction rate is too slow / the diazotization does not proceed at a practical rate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 0–10 °C range is a compromise between two competing requirements:
> 
> - The upper limit (below 10 °C) prevents the diazonium salt from decomposing. Above this temperature the N–N<sup>+</sup> group leaves as nitrogen gas and the diazonium ion reacts with water to form a phenol derivative, destroying the intermediate before it can be used.
> - The lower limit (above 0 °C) ensures the reaction proceeds fast enough to be practical.
>

parts.problemMd:
Methylamine reacts with propanoyl chloride to form CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub>.

i) State the name of the mechanism for this reaction.

[1]

An incomplete mechanism for this reaction is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Incomplete addition-elimination mechanism diagram showing methylamine approaching propanoyl chloride with blank spaces for curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, and the second product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-3-amides/assets/001-incomplete-addition-elimination-mechanism-diagra.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

ii) Complete the mechanism in Fig. 3.1. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles. Also show the formula of the second product formed.

[5]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - (Nucleophilic) addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed mechanism is:

![Completed addition-elimination mechanism showing methylamine reacting with propanoyl chloride, with all curly arrows, lone pairs, dipoles, formal charges on the intermediate, and HCl identified as the second product](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-3-amides/assets/002-completed-addition-elimination-mechanism-showing.png)

**[5 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for the correct dipole on the C=O bond **AND **the lone pair on the amine nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for the curly arrow from the amine nitrogen to the δ+ carbon **AND **a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the δ– oxygen
> 
> 1 mark for the correct formal charges: – on oxygen and + on nitrogen in the intermediate **AND **the lone pair on the oxygen in the intermediate
> 
> 1 mark for the curly arrow from the N–H bond to the + nitrogen **AND **a curly arrow from the C–Cl bond to the chlorine **AND **A curly arrow from the oxygen lone pair to the C–O bond
> 
> 1 mark for HCl identified as the second product

> **[exam-tip]**
> The addition-elimination mechanism proceeds in two stages:
> 
> Addition:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen of methylamine attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon.
> - The C=O π bond breaks, the oxygen becomes negatively charged (–), and the nitrogen becomes positively charged (+).
> 
> Elimination:
>

parts.problemMd:
Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk of a spider's web is at least five times as strong as steel, and twice as elastic as nylon. The silk fibre is composed of many identical protein chains, which are mainly made from the amino acids glycine, alanine and serine, shown in Fig. 1.1, with smaller amounts of four other amino acids.

![Structural formulae of glycine, alanine and serine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-4-amino-acids/assets/007-structural-formulae-of-glycine-alanine-and-serin.png)

Amino acids can exist as zwitterions. Draw the zwitterion structure for glycine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The zwitterion structure of glycine is:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino acid forms a zwitterion, the hydrogen ion from the –COOH group is transferred to the –NH<sub>2</sub> group. This produces a molecule with both a positive charge (on the nitrogen) and a negative charge (on the oxygen), but with no overall charge.
> 
> To draw the zwitterion of glycine: move the H from –COOH to –NH<sub>2</sub>, add a positive charge to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, and add a negative charge to give –COO<sup>–</sup>.
> 
> Do not show individual single bonds in the structural formula.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Much research has been carried out in recent years investigating the exact structure of silk. The silk of a spider's web is at least five times as strong as steel, and twice as elastic as nylon. Amino acids can act as acids or bases. Construct equations to show:

i) the reaction between alanine and HCl (aq),

[1]

ii) the reaction between serine and NaOH (aq).

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction between alanine and HCl (aq) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH + HCl → <sup>+</sup>H<sub>3</sub>NCH(CH<sub>3</sub>)COOH + Cl<sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between serine and NaOH (aq) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)COOH + NaOH → H<sub>2</sub>NCH(CH<sub>2</sub>OH)COONa + H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Amino acids exist as zwitterions in solution. Think of the amino acid as having two separate functional groups: an acidic –COOH group and a basic –NH<sub>2</sub> group.
> 
> When HCl is added, the H<sup>+</sup> ion protonates the –NH<sub>2</sub> group to give –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>. The –COOH group remains unchanged.
> 
> When NaOH is added, the OH<sup>–</sup> ion deprotonates the –COOH group to give –COO<sup>–</sup>, with the Na<sup>+</sup> forming the sodium salt. Water is produced.

parts.problemMd:
The *M*<sub>r</sub> of a silk protein molecule is about 600,000. Assuming it is made from equal amounts of the three amino acids in Fig. 1.1, calculate the average number of amino acid residues in the protein chain. Show your working.

[*M*<sub>r</sub> (glycine) = 75;   *M*<sub>r</sub> (alanine) = 89;     *M*<sub>r</sub> (serine) = 105]

number of residues .............................................
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the average number of amino acid residues in the protein chain:

- List the known values:

  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(glycine) = 75
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(alanine) = 89
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(serine) = 105
  - *M*<sub>r</sub>(protein chain) = 600 000
- Determine the *M*<sub>r</sub> of one repeating unit of three amino acid residues (each residue loses one water molecule when forming the chain):

(75 − 18) + (89 − 18) + (105 − 18)

= 57 + 71 + 87 = 215

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the number of three-residue sets in the protein chain:

$\frac{600000}{215}$

= 2791

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total number of amino acid residues:

2791 x 3 = **8372**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for calculating the *M*<sub>r</sub> of one repeating unit of three amino acid residues: 215
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the number of three-residue sets in the protein chain: 2791
> 
> 1 mark for calculating the total number of amino acid residues: 8372

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino acid joins a protein chain via a peptide bond, one water molecule (*M*<sub>r</sub> = 18) is lost per residue. Subtract 18 from each amino acid *M*<sub>r</sub> to find the residue *M*<sub>r</sub>.
> 
> The second step gives the number of repeating three-residue sets. Multiply by 3 to get the total number of individual amino acid residues.
> 
> If you did not subtract 18 from each *M*<sub>r</sub> value (using 75 + 89 + 105 = 269 instead of 215), you would still score 2 marks if the method for steps 2 and 3 is correct.

parts.problemMd:
A mixture of amino acids may be separated using electrophoresis. A typical practical set-up is shown in Fig. 2.1.

**Fig. 2.1**

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Some amino acids remain stationary because:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark per point):
> 
> - The amino acid is uncharged / neutral / a zwitterion **OR** charges balance / are equal
> - It is equally attracted by the anode / + and the cathode / – **OR**
> It is attracted by neither the anode nor the cathode
> - The pH of the buffer is at the isoelectric point / IEP of the amino acid
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a sample of amino acids is placed between two oppositely charged electrodes:
> 
> - The positively charged amino acids will move toward the negative electrode
> - The negatively charged amino acids will move toward the positive electrode
> - Amino acids with an overall neutral charge will remain stationary
> 
> If the pH of the buffer is at the isoelectric point of the amino acid, neither the positively nor negatively charged ions will dominate and the amino acid will exist as a neutral zwitterion

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Alanine has a high melting point because:
> 
> - Alanine exists as a zwitterion / ionic form in the solid state **[1 mark]**
> - The zwitterions form an ionic lattice / strong electrostatic forces exist between them, requiring more energy to break **[1 mark]**

ii) The structural formula of alanine in the solid state:

![Displayed structural formula of alanine as a zwitterion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-4-amino-acids/assets/014-displayed-structural-formula-of-alanine-as-a-zwi.png)

Draw and label **three** spots on the diagram in Fig. 1.1 of the electrophoresis paper to indicate the likely position of each of these species after electrophoresis. Explain your answer.

parts.solutionMd:

![Annotated electrophoresis result showing valine at origin and val-lys and lysine to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/34-nitrogen-compounds/34-4-amino-acids/assets/018-annotated-electrophoresis-result-showing-valine-.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for valine on the cross
> 
> 1 mark for Val-Lys and Lys on the right of the cross (in any order)
> 
> 1 mark for the relative order of Val-Lys and Lys (on the same side of the cross)
> 
> Explanation of movement:
> 
> - Val does not move as it is a zwitterion / neutral (at pH 6) **OR**
> Lys / Val-Lys move towards the negative pole as they are positively charged **[1 mark]**
> - Lys moves the furthest as it has the lowest *M*<sub>r</sub> (with the same positive charge) **OR**
> Val-Lys moves the least as it has the largest *M*<sub>r</sub> (with the same positive charge) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The isoelectric point is the pH at which an amino acid exists as a zwitterion, which means that the overall charge depends on the pH of the buffer solution
> 
> Val will exist as a zwitterion as the buffer pH (6.0) equals its isoelectric point
> 
> Lysine and val-lys will have a positive charge overall as the basic side chain amine group is protonated to form –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> at pH 6.0
> 
> Lysine and val-lys have the same overall charge at pH 6 as both contain two NH<sub>2</sub> groups that are protonated (one on the side chain, one on the terminal amine)
> 
> The larger the *M*<sub>r</sub>, the less the amino acid or dipeptide will trave, which explains why valine, lysine, and val-lys can be separated

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Tryptophan is a naturally occurring α-amino acid. Its structure is shown below.

Deduce the molecular formula for tryptophan and write a balanced equation for the reaction of tryptophan with dilute nitric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecular formula and equation are:
> 
> - Molecular formula: C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Equation: C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>12</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an amino group reacts with a dilute acid it is protonated:
> 
> RNH<sub>2</sub> + H<sup>+</sup> → RNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>
> 
> Tryptophan has only one basic amino group, which is the α-amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) attached to the central carbon
> 
> The nitrogen in the indole ring is part of the aromatic π system; its lone pair is delocalised into the ring and cannot be protonated by dilute acid
> 
> Adding one mole of HNO<sub>3</sub> contributes 1H, 1N, and 3O to the molecular formula of tryptophan, giving the ammonium nitrate salt C<sub>11</sub>H<sub>13</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>5</sub>

parts.problemMd: State the names of **two** classes of organic molecules that can take part in condensation polymerisation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two classes of organic molecules that can take part in condensation polymerisation include:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Dicarboxylic acids
> - Hydroxy acids / hydroxycarboxylic acids
> - Diols
> - Diamines
> - Amino acids
> - Diacyl chlorides / dioyl chlorides
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To undergo condensation polymerisation, each monomer must have two reactive functional groups, either two identical groups (one at each end) or two complementary groups that can react with each other.
> 
> The key combinations are:
> 
> - Carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) + alcohol forms a polyester
> - Carboxylic acid (or acyl chloride) + amine forms a polyamide.
> 
> In both cases a small molecule (water or HCl) is eliminated at each step.
> 
> Amino acids can self-polymerise because every amino acid already contains both –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH groups in the same molecule.

> - Polyalkenes only have (weak) van der Waals forces between chains **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than van der Waals forces
> **OR**
> Polyalkenes require much less energy to separate the chains **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrogen bonding can form between the –C=O and –N–H groups on adjacent polyamide chains. Polyalkenes have no N, O, or F atoms, so no hydrogen bonding is possible.
> 
> The first mark is for identifying the type of force in each polymer. The second mark is for naming van der Waals forces specifically in polyalkenes. The third mark is for explicitly comparing the strengths.
> 
> Van der Waals forces are weak because they require large electron clouds or high molecular mass to become significant. Polyalkene chains can slide past each other relatively easily.

parts.problemMd: Explain how the molecule NH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl can undergo condensation polymerisation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why NH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COCl can undergo condensation polymerisation:
> 
> - The molecule contains two different functional groups: an amine (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and an acyl chloride (–COCl) **[1 mark]**
> - These two groups react with each other, forming an amide linkage and eliminating HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A molecule can self-polymerise if it contains two complementary reactive groups, one at each end. Here, the –NH<sub>2</sub> at one molecule reacts with the –COCl of the next molecule, building up the polymer chain.
> 
> Each step eliminates HCl (not water), but it is still called condensation polymerisation because a small molecule is lost each time a new bond forms.

ii) One repeat unit of Lycra<sup>®</sup> is:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Lycra® in Fig. 2.2 is a polyurethane formed from the diisocyanate P and HOCH₂CH₂OH.

Polyurethanes are polymers made by the reaction of a diisocyanate with a diol, as shown in Fig. 2.1. R¹ and R² are hydrocarbon groups.

Fibres of Lycra<sup>®</sup> are strong due to the intermolecular forces between the polymer chains. Complete the table to state two types of intermolecular force responsible for this property, and the groups involved.

| **Intermolecular force** | **Group(s) involved** |
|---|---|
|   |   |
|   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Intermolecular force** | **Group(s) involved** |
|---|---|
| Hydrogen bonding | –NH |
| Van der Waals forces / induced dipole–dipole forces | –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– / benzene rings |

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for hydrogen bonding **AND** –NH group correctly identified.
> 
> 1 mark for van der Waals forces (accept induced dipole–dipole / London dispersion) **AND** –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– or benzene/aromatic rings correctly identified.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hydrogen bonding occurs between the H on the –NH group of one chain and the lone pair on the C=O of an adjacent chain. Both the force and the group must be correct for the mark.
> 
> The –C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>– section contains only C and H, so no polar bonds, making the strongest force here van der Waals. Large aromatic groups produce relatively strong van der Waals forces.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Examples of commercially important synthetic polymers:
> 
> - Synthetic polyamide: Nylon / Kevlar / Nomex **[1 mark]**
> - Synthetic polyester: Terylene / PET / polylactic acid (PLA) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 2.3 shows the repeat unit of Nylon 66.

![Repeat unit of Nylon 66 polyamide showing the amide linkage between the hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid derived segments](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/024-repeat-unit-of-nylon-66-polyamide-showing-the-am.png)

**Fig. 2.3**

Nylon 66 is heated under reflux with dilute sulfuric acid.

Draw the skeletal formulae of the **two** organic products formed.
parts.solutionMd:
The two organic products formed from the acid hydrolysis of Nylon 66 are:

![Skeletal formulae of the two hydrolysis products: the protonated hexamethylenediamine salt with two –NH~3~^+^ groups, and adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) with two –COOH groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/025-skeletal-formulae-of-the-two-hydrolysis-products.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of the diamine product with both –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> groups (protonated under acidic conditions).
> 
> 1 mark for correct skeletal formula of hexanedioic acid (adipic acid) with both –COOH groups.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Under acidic conditions (dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, heated under reflux), the amide bonds are hydrolysed. Each –CO–NH– bond breaks to give a –COOH group and a –NH<sub>2</sub> group. In acidic solution the amine is immediately protonated to –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>.
> 
> The two products are: (1) the protonated diamine (hexane-1,6-diamine with both ends as –NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) and (2) hexanedioic acid (adipic acid, HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH).
> 
> If alkaline hydrolysis (NaOH) were used instead, the products would be different: the diamine would be neutral (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and the diacid would be deprotonated (carboxylate salt, –COO<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>).

parts.problemMd: Explain how ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How ethane-1,2-diamine acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base:
> 
> - The nitrogen atoms have lone pairs of electrons
> **AND**
> Which can accept a proton (H<sup>+</sup>) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A Brønsted–Lowry base is any species that accepts a proton. Ethane-1,2-diamine has two nitrogen atoms, each with a lone pair. Either lone pair can accept H<sup>+</sup> from an acid.
> 
> Both conditions are needed for the mark: the lone pair must be identified and the proton acceptance stated.

parts.problemMd: Construct an equation to show the reaction of ethane-1,2-diamine with an excess of hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction of ethane-1,2-diamine with excess hydrochloric acid is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → ClH<sub>3</sub>NCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub>Cl
> **OR**
> C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 2HCl → C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> With excess HCl, both –NH<sub>2</sub> groups are protonated. Each nitrogen accepts one H<sup>+</sup> from HCl, forming the dihydrochloride salt. Make sure you use 2HCl to show both groups react.
> 
> The product has the formula C<sub>2</sub>N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>. The original H<sub>8</sub> gains two extra H atoms (one per NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), and two Cl<sup>-</sup> ions balance the charge.

parts.problemMd: In terms of *n*, state the number of molecules of water formed in the condensation polymerisation of *n* molecules of a dicarboxylic acid and *n* molecules of a diol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> In terms of *n*, the number of molecules of water formed is:
> 
> - 2*n* − 1 **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow 2*n* (if candidate treats the polymer as having no free end groups).

> **[exam-tip]**
> Try small values to find the pattern:
> 
> - For *n* = 1 (one acid + one diol): one ester bond forms, releasing 1 water
> - For *n* = 2: three ester bonds form, releasing 3 water molecules
> - For *n* = 3: five water molecules. The pattern is 2*n* − 1.
> 
> The 2*n* answer arises if you assume a fully cyclic or infinite-chain polymer where both ends have also reacted. Both answers can be credited.

parts.problemMd:
Lactic acid has the structural formula CH<sub>3</sub>CHOHCOOH.

i) State the names of the **two** functional groups present in lactic acid.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of lactic acid.

[1]

iii) State the type of stereoisomerism shown by lactic acid.

[1]

iv) Draw three-dimensional structures for the two stereoisomers of lactic acid.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two functional groups present in lactic acid are:
> 
> - Alcohol / hydroxyl
> **AND**
> Carboxylic acid / carboxyl **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of lactic acid is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxypropanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The type of stereoisomerism shown by lactic acid is:
>

Nomex® and Kevlar® are two examples of polyamides containing benzene rings. Nomex® is made from 1,3-diaminobenzene and benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid.

Draw **one** repeat unit of the Nomex<sup>®</sup> polymer. The newly formed linkages must be shown fully displayed.
parts.solutionMd:
One repeat unit of the Nomex<sup>®</sup> polymer is:

![One repeat unit of the Nomex polyamide polymer showing the amide linkage –CO–NH– between the 1,3-substituted benzene rings, with continuation bonds at both ends](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/006-one-repeat-unit-of-the-nomex-polyamide-polymer-s.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct amide linkage (–CO–NH–) shown fully displayed between the two monomers.
> 
> 1 mark for correct repeat unit with 1,3-substituted benzene rings and continuation bonds at both ends.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Place the two monomers side by side. The –COOH of the diacid reacts with one –NH<sub>2</sub> of the diamine, eliminating water and forming the amide bond –CO–NH–. Draw this bond with C=O and N–H both explicitly shown.
> 
> The 1,3-substitution means the chain is angled (kinked) at each benzene ring, unlike the straight chain in Kevlar. Make sure the bonds come from the 1 and 3 positions, not from 1 and 4.

parts.problemMd:
Kevlar<sup>®</sup> is made from 1,4-diaminobenzene and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.

Draw **two adjacent polymer chains** of Kevlar<sup>®</sup>, each showing **one** repeat unit. Clearly show the strongest intermolecular force between the two chains.
parts.solutionMd:
Two adjacent polymer chains of Kevlar<sup>®</sup>, each showing one repeat unit:

![Two adjacent parallel Kevlar polymer chains each showing one repeat unit, with a hydrogen bond drawn as a dashed line between the N–H group of one chain and the C=O group of the adjacent chain, with a lone pair shown on the oxygen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-1-condensation-polymerisation/assets/007-two-adjacent-parallel-kevlar-polymer-chains-each.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct structure of both repeat units (1,4-substituted benzene rings, amide linkages, continuation bonds).
> 
> 1 mark for hydrogen bond correctly drawn as a dashed line from the lone pair on the C=O oxygen of one chain to the H on the N–H of the adjacent chain.
> 
> Accept other orientations with the monomers the other way around.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The strongest intermolecular force in Kevlar is hydrogen bonding. It forms between the lone pair on the oxygen of a C=O group on one chain and the hydrogen on the N–H group of an adjacent chain.
> 
> Always start the hydrogen bond arrow / dashed line at the lone pair on oxygen. The bond points towards the H on nitrogen.
> 
> Drawing two adjacent parallel chains (rather than one long chain) is essential here. Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force and must be shown between separate chains.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Nomex® and Kevlar® are two examples of polyamides containing benzene rings. Nomex® is made from 1,3-diaminobenzene and benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid.

The 1,3-substitution means the chain is angled (kinked) at each benzene ring, unlike the straight chain in Kevlar. Make sure the bonds come from the 1 and 3 positions, not from 1 and 4.

Kevlar® is made from 1,4-diaminobenzene and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.

State whether Kevlar<sup>®</sup> or Nomex<sup>®</sup> will have the higher melting point. Explain your answer in terms of the structure of the polymer chains.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The polymer with the higher melting point is:
> 
> - Kevlar<sup>®</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The 1,4-substitution in Kevlar creates straight, linear polymer chains, so adjacent chains can pack more closely together. The 1,3-substitution in Nomex creates a kinked chain, so chains pack less closely.
> **AND**
> Closer packing makes the hydrogen bonds between chains more effective / stronger, requiring more energy to separate the chains **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key difference between Kevlar and Nomex is the substitution pattern: Kevlar uses 1,4-substitution (para), giving a straight chain; Nomex uses 1,3-substitution (meta), giving a kinked chain.
> 
> You can also give the reverse argument: Nomex has the lower melting point because its kinked chains pack less closely, giving weaker and fewer hydrogen bonds between chains.
> 
> Both marks require you to link chain shape to packing to intermolecular force strength to melting point. Simply stating "Kevlar is straighter" without explaining why that affects the melting point is not sufficient for the second mark.

Glycolic acid polymerises to form polyglycolic acid (PGA). The structure of glycolic acid is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Displayed formula of glycolic acid showing a hydroxyl group (–OH) bonded to a CH₂ group, bonded to a carboxylic acid group (–COOH)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-2-predicting-the-type-of-polymerisation/assets/005-displayed-formula-of-glycolic-acid-showing-a-hyd.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the systematic name of glycolic acid.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of glycolic acid is:
> 
> - 2-hydroxyethanoic acid
> **OR**
> hydroxyethanoic acid **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Glycolic acid (HOCH<sub>2</sub>COOH) contains two functional groups: a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) and a hydroxyl group (–OH).
> 
> The name is built from: hydroxy- (for –OH) + ethan- (two carbons) + -oic acid (for –COOH) = 2-hydroxyethanoic acid. The locant 2 is not required as the –OH can only be on C-2.

type of polymerisation: ..............................

functional group: ..............................
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

State the type of polymerisation involved in the formation of PGA and state the name of the functional group formed between the monomers.

type of polymerisation: ..............................

functional group: ..............................

The type of polymerisation and functional group formed are:

- Type of polymerisation: condensation
- Functional group: ester

State whether PGA is biodegradable. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether PGA is biodegradable and why:
> 
> - PGA is biodegradable **[1 mark]**
> - The ester linkage / ester bond can be hydrolysed / undergoes hydrolysis **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> PGA is a polyester. Ester bonds can be broken down by hydrolysis (reaction with water or enzymes), making PGA biodegradable.
> 
> This contrasts with addition polymers such as poly(ethene), which contain only C–C and C–H bonds in the backbone. These cannot be hydrolysed and are therefore non-biodegradable.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Glycine and serine are amino acids with the systematic names 2-aminoethanoic acid and 2-amino-3-hydroxypropanoic acid respectively.

Glycine and serine can react to form condensation polymers containing ester and amide linkages.

State the names of the functional groups that react to form:

i) an ester linkage

[1]

ii) an amide linkage

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The functional groups that react to form an ester linkage are:
> 
> - Hydroxyl / –OH
> **AND**
> carboxylic acid / –COOH **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The functional groups that react to form an amide linkage are:
> 
> - Amine / amino / –NH₂
> **AND**
> carboxylic acid / –COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> An ester linkage forms from a reaction between a hydroxyl group (–OH) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). Only serine has a hydroxyl group, so ester formation requires at least one serine monomer.
> 
> An amide linkage forms from a reaction between an amine group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). Both glycine and serine have these groups, so amide linkages can form between any combination of the two amino acids.

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by the term *hydrolysis*.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The meaning of the term hydrolysis is:
> 
> - The breakdown of a compound by reaction with water **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The word *hydrolysis* comes from the Greek roots *hydro* (water) and *lysis* (breaking apart). Remembering this helps you recall the definition without memorising it word for word.

parts.problemMd: State the reagents and conditions required for the acid hydrolysis of a polyamide.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for the acid hydrolysis of a polyamide are:
> 
> - Dilute acid (dilute HCl / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Acid hydrolysis of a polyamide requires H<sup>+</sup> ions as a catalyst and heat under reflux to supply enough energy to break the amide bonds. Without the acid catalyst, hydrolysis is extremely slow at any practical temperature.

**Fig. 1.1**

Draw the skeletal formulae of the organic products formed when the polyamide is treated with dilute acid and heated under reflux.
parts.solutionMd:
The skeletal formulae of the acid hydrolysis products are:

![Skeletal formulae of the acid hydrolysis products: dicarboxylic acid and protonated diamine salt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-3-degradable-polymers/assets/013-skeletal-formulae-of-the-acid-hydrolysis-product.png)

> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of the dicarboxylic acid
> 
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of the diamine salt / protonated diamine

>

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows a section of a nylon polymer.

![Section of a nylon polyamide polymer chain showing repeating amide linkages](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/07/aqa-chemistry-trial-june.png)

Explain why clothing made from nylon is easily damaged by spillages of strong acids or strong alkalis.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why nylon clothing is easily damaged by strong acids and alkalis:
> 
> - The amide linkages in nylon can be hydrolysed by strong acids and strong alkalis **[1 mark]**
> - Hydrolysis breaks the polymer chains, destroying the structural integrity of the fabric / creating holes in the fabric **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nylon is a polyamide, which means it contains amide bonds (–CO–NH–). Strong acids and alkalis catalyse the hydrolysis of these bonds, breaking the long polymer chains into shorter fragments. Once the polymer chains are broken, the fabric loses its structural integrity.
> 
> This is why polyamide fabrics and equipment should be kept away from corrosive chemicals in the laboratory.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Fig. 1.1 shows a section of a nylon polymer.

Fig. 1.2 shows the structure of Nomex, an aromatic polyamide.

![Structure of the Nomex aromatic polyamide repeat unit showing benzene rings and amide linkages](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/35-polymerisation/35-3-degradable-polymers/assets/005-structure-of-the-nomex-aromatic-polyamide-repeat.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Explain why Nomex has a higher melting point than nylon.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why Nomex has a higher melting point than nylon:
> 
> - The benzene rings make the Nomex chains more rigid and planar, allowing the chains to pack together more closely **[1 mark]**
> - This results in stronger intermolecular forces (van der Waals' forces / hydrogen bonding) between chains, requiring more energy to overcome **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Melting point depends on the strength of intermolecular forces between polymer chains. The more closely chains can pack, the stronger the forces between them.
> 
> Nylon has a flexible aliphatic backbone, while Nomex contains rigid, planar benzene rings. The planar rings allow Nomex chains to pack together more tightly than the flexible chains in nylon, creating stronger van der Waals' forces and more hydrogen bonding between chains.

Table 1.1 shows the structural formulae of three amino acids.

**Table 1.1**

| **Amino Acid** | **Structural formula** |
|---|---|

| **U** | C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |
| **V** | H<sub>2</sub>N(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CO<sub>2</sub>H |

State which of the amino acids, **T**, **U** or **V**, has the highest pH in an aqueous solution, and explain your answer.

amino acid ......................................................

explanation ......................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The amino acid with the highest pH in aqueous solution:
> 
> - Amino acid V **[1 mark]**
> - It has two amine / NH<sub>2</sub> groups (which can be protonated) **OR** it has an additional amine / NH<sub>2</sub> group on its side chain / R group (compared to T and U) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A higher pH means a more basic solution. Amino acids are amphoteric, but if the amine group count exceeds the carboxylic acid count, the amino acid produces a more basic solution.
> 
> Amino acid V has two –NH<sub>2</sub> groups and one –COOH group, giving it a greater capacity to accept protons than T or U (which each have one –NH<sub>2</sub> and one –COOH group). More proton acceptance means a higher pH.

parts.problemMd: State how many different dipeptides could be formed from a reaction mixture consisting of amino acids **T** and **U**.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of different dipeptides that could be formed from amino acids T and U:
> 
> - 4 / four **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A dipeptide contains two amino acid residues. The four possibilities when two different amino acids (T and U) are present are:
> 
> - T–T
> - U–U
> - T–U
> - U–T
> 
> Note that T–U and U–T are different dipeptides because the amino acid at the N-terminus differs. Students often forget the self-combinations (T–T and U–U) or forget that order matters.

parts.problemMd: Despite containing a high proportion of carbon and hydrogen atoms, many polypeptides are soluble in water. Explain why. In your answer, you should refer to the functional groups present in a polypeptide chain.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason why polypeptides are soluble in water despite their high C and H content:
> 
> - Hydrogen bonds form between the polar N–H and C=O groups (peptide bonds) in the polypeptide chain and water molecules **[1 mark]**
> - This allows the polypeptide to interact with and dissolve in water **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow ion-dipole attractions between the NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and CO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> end groups of the zwitterion and polar water molecules for the first marking point

> **[exam-tip]**
> Although the majority of a polypeptide chain is made up of C–C and C–H bonds (which are non-polar), the peptide bonds (–CO–NH–) contain polar C=O and N–H groups. These groups can form hydrogen bonds with water.
> 
> In addition, amino acids exist as zwitterions at physiological pH, with NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and CO<sub>2</sub><sup>–</sup> end groups. These charged groups form strong ion-dipole interactions with water molecules, further aiding solubility.

parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> - Step 1: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CH<sub>2</sub> and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / heat **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: CH<sub>3</sub>COCl and AlCl<sub>3</sub> / heat **[1 mark]**
> - Step 3: NaOH and I<sub>2</sub> / Cl<sub>2</sub> / Br<sub>2</sub>, then H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Step 4: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Steps 1 and 2 both involve Friedel-Crafts electrophilic substitution of the benzene ring.
> 
> Step 1 adds an isopropyl group (alkylation). A halogen carrier catalyst such as AlCl<sub>3</sub> is needed to generate the carbocation electrophile:
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCl → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH<sup>+</sup>
> 
> Step 2 adds an acyl group (acylation). An acyl chloride and halogen carrier are required:
> 
> AlCl<sub>3</sub> + CH<sub>3</sub>COCl → AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>
> 
> Step 3 converts the methyl ketone to a carboxylic acid via the haloform (iodoform) reaction:
> 
> R-CO-CH<sub>3</sub> + 3I<sub>2</sub> + 4OH<sup>-</sup> → CHI<sub>3</sub> + RCOO<sup>-</sup> + 3I<sup>-</sup> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> The carboxylate RCOO<sup>-</sup> is then acidified with H<sup>+</sup> to give RCOOH.
> 
> Step 4 uses LiAlH<sub>4</sub> in dry ether to reduce the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol.

Cuminyl alcohol can be synthesised from benzene by the following route shown in Fig. 2.1.

Step 2: CH3COCl and AlCl3 / heat

Step 2 adds an acyl group (acylation). An acyl chloride and halogen carrier are required:

AlCl3 + CH3COCl → AlCl4^-^ + CH3CO^+^

Draw the reaction mechanism for step 2.
parts.solutionMd:
The reaction mechanism for step 2 is:

![Curly arrow mechanism for Friedel-Crafts acylation electrophilic substitution showing arenium intermediate and loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/022-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-friedel-crafts-acylati.jpeg)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the ring system to the positively charged carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium intermediate structure with a positive charge, the horseshoe covering more than half the ring but not extending past carbons 2 and 6
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring
> 
> 1 mark for the correct benzene product AND H<sup>+</sup> shown
> 
> The origin and destination of curly arrows must be clear and unambiguous, or the marks are not awarded.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common mistakes in benzene electrophilic substitution mechanisms:
> 
> - Not drawing the hydrogen that is being substituted
> - Drawing the substituted hydrogen in the wrong position
> - Forgetting to place the positive charge in the correct position on the intermediate
> - Drawing the ring inside the intermediate structure incorrectly
> 
> The general mechanism: the electrophile attacks the pi system of benzene, forming a positively charged arenium (carbocation) intermediate. A curly arrow then shows the C–H bond electrons returning to restore aromaticity, releasing H<sup>+</sup>.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Cuminyl alcohol can be synthesised from benzene by the following route shown in Fig. 2.1.

Deduce the number of peaks that would be present in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of cuminyl alcohol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of <sup>13</sup>C NMR peaks in cuminyl alcohol is:
> 
> - 7 peaks **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Look for symmetry within the molecule to identify equivalent carbon environments, as these give only one peak between them.
> 
> Cuminyl alcohol (4-isopropylbenzyl alcohol) has 7 distinct carbon environments:
> 
> - C1: ring carbon bearing the CH<sub>2</sub>OH group
> - C2 and C6: equivalent ring carbons (ortho to CH<sub>2</sub>OH, meta to isopropyl)
> - C3 and C5: equivalent ring carbons (ortho to isopropyl)
> - C4: ring carbon bearing the isopropyl group
> - CH<sub>2</sub>: the methylene carbon of CH<sub>2</sub>OH
> - CH: the methine carbon of the isopropyl group
> - CH<sub>3</sub>: both methyl groups of the isopropyl group are equivalent

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The synthesis of ethanal from ethane:
> 
> i) Step 1: Ethane → chloroethane
> 
> - Reagent: Cl<sub>2</sub> / chlorine **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: UV light / high temperature **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction type: free radical substitution / halogenation **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Step 2: Chloroethane → ethanol
> 
> - Reagent: aqueous NaOH / NaOH(aq) / aqueous KOH / KOH(aq) **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: heat under reflux **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution / hydrolysis **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Step 3: Ethanol → ethanal
> 
> - Reagent: acidified potassium dichromate(VI) / K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
> **OR**
> Acidified potassium manganate(VII) / KMnO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: distillation **[1 mark]**
> - Reaction type: oxidation **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conversion of an alkane to a haloalkane is hard to control industrially, as it is difficult to prevent multiple products from forming. It is included here to test your ability to apply knowledge of organic reactions to synthesis problems.
> 
> The mechanism types are shown in brackets in the mark scheme but are not essential for the mark.
> 
> The dichromate ion, Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup>, is the oxidising species, so sodium dichromate(VI) is also an acceptable reagent for step 3.

parts.problemMd:
The following reaction pathway in Fig. 3.1 is used to produce compounds **A** and **B**, which when reacted together, form a branched ester molecule, compound **C**.

Suggest suitable reagents and conditions for the synthesis of compound **A** via step 1 and give the name for this type of reaction.

![Reaction pathway showing oxidation of an aldehyde to carboxylic acid (compound A) via step 1, and reduction of a ketone to secondary alcohol (compound B) via step 2, followed by esterification to form compound C](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/028-reaction-pathway-showing-oxidation-of-an-aldehyd.png)

**Fig. 3.1**
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Suitable reagents and conditions for the synthesis of compound **A** via step 1:
> 
> - K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / potassium dichromate(VI)
> **OR**
> KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / acidified / with acid **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidation **[1 mark]**
> 
> Sodium dichromate(VI) is also accepted for the first marking point.
> 
> Ions such as Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> are not accepted as a reagent must be something that can be found on a laboratory shelf.

> **[exam-tip]**
> An ester is commonly made from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
> 
> A carboxylic acid cannot be produced from a ketone, so compound **A** must come from the oxidation of an aldehyde.
> 
> The question asks for the names of reagents, not ions. Writing Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2-</sup> alone would not score the mark.
