Compound **G** is a naturally occurring aromatic compound that is present in raspberries.

The functional groups present in compound **G** are:

Complete Table 5.1 with information about the reactions of the three stated reagents with compound **G**.

**Table 5.1**

| **Reagent** | **Observation** | **Structure of organic product** | **Type of reaction** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Na (s) |   |   |   |
| Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) |   |   |   |
| I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq) |   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Reagent** | **Observation** | **Structure of organic product** | **Type of reaction** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Na (s) | **Final answer:** **Effervescence / bubbles / fizzing** | ![Structural formula of the sodium phenoxide product formed when compound G reacts with sodium metal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/003-structural-formula-of-the-sodium-phenoxide-produ.jpeg) | **Final answer:** **Redox** |
| Br<sub>2</sub> (aq) | **Final answer:** **Decolourises / white precipitate** | ![Structural formula of the dibrominated phenol product formed when compound G reacts with bromine water at positions 2 and 6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/004-structural-formula-of-the-dibrominated-phenol-pr.jpeg) | **Final answer:** **Electrophilic substitution** |
| I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq) | **Final answer:** **Yellow precipitate (CHI**<sub>**3**</sub>**)** | ![Structural formula of the organic product of the iodoform reaction showing both carboxylate (-COO-Na+) and phenoxide (-O-Na+) sodium salt groups](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/005-structural-formula-of-the-organic-product-of-the.jpeg) | **Final answer:** **Oxidation** |

**[9 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for effervescence / bubbles observed with Na (s)
> 
> 1 mark for correct product structure from Na (s) reaction
> 
> 1 mark for redox as the reaction type for Na (s)
> 
> 1 mark for bromine decolourising or white precipitate observed with Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)
> 
> 1 mark for correct dibrominated product structure from Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)
> 
> 1 mark for electrophilic substitution as the reaction type for Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)
> 
> 1 mark for yellow precipitate (CHI<sub>3</sub>) observed with I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq)
> 
> 1 mark for correct product structure from I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq) — must show both the carboxylate group (-COO<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> / -COONa) from the iodoform reaction **AND **the phenoxide group (-O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> / -ONa) from deprotonation by NaOH
> 
> 1 mark for oxidation as the reaction type for I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Na (s) reacts with the phenolic -OH group, breaking the O–H bond to form the phenoxide -O<sup>-</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> Bromine water reacts with the phenol group via electrophilic substitution. The -OH group is 2,4,6-directing; however, position 4 is occupied by the ketone side chain, so bromine substitutes at positions 2 and 6.
> 
> I<sub>2</sub> / NaOH (aq) is used in the iodoform reaction. The methyl ketone group reacts: first, all three H-atoms on the CH<sub>3</sub> group are replaced by iodine to form a -CI<sub>3</sub> group; the alkaline solution then hydrolyses this intermediate to give the carboxylate salt (-COONa) and yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate. Under alkaline conditions, the phenol is simultaneously deprotonated to give the phenoxide (-ONa). Both groups must be shown in the product structure.

**Extract:**

Compound **G** is a naturally occurring aromatic compound that is present in raspberries.

The dye H can be made from compound **G** by the route shown below in Fig. 5.1.

![Synthesis route for azo dye H from compound G via aryl amine J and diazonium salt K](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/006-synthesis-route-for-azo-dye-h-from-compound-g-vi.png)

**Fig. 5.1**

i) Draw the structures of the amine **J** and the intermediate **K** in the boxes above.

[2]

ii) Suggest reagents and conditions for

step 1 ........................................................................................................................

step 2 ........................................................................................................................

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structures are:

Compound **J**:

![Structural formula of amine J — the primary aryl amine used in diazotisation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/007-structural-formula-of-amine-j-the-primary-aryl-a.jpeg)

Compound **K**:

![Structural formula of diazonium salt K formed by diazotisation of amine J](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/008-structural-formula-of-diazonium-salt-k-formed-by.jpeg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of compound **J**
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of compound **K**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> Step 1:
> 
> - NaNO<sub>2</sub> and HCl
> **OR**
> HNO<sub>2</sub> (formed in situ) **[1 mark]**
> - Temperature below 10 °C **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 2:

> - NaOH(aq) / alkaline conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **J** is an aryl primary amine. For diazotisation (step 1), the amine is converted to a diazonium ion (-N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>) using NaNO<sub>2</sub> and HCl.
>

> For the coupling step (step 2), the diazonium salt **K** reacts with compound **G** under alkaline conditions. NaOH converts the phenol in **G** to a phenoxide ion, which is a much more reactive coupling partner, directing the azo group to the ortho or para position.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The dye H can be made from compound G by the route shown below in Fig. 5.1.

Fig. 5.1

Explain why dye **H** is very stable.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Dye **H** is very stable because:
> 
> - Delocalised electrons in the π bonding systems of the two benzene rings **[1 mark]**
> - The delocalisation is extended through the -N=N- group, which acts as a bridge between the two rings **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Azo dyes contain two arene rings connected by the -N=N- (azo) group.
> 
> The π electrons are delocalised across both benzene rings and the azo bridge, spreading the electron density over the entire conjugated system.
> 
> This extended delocalisation makes the molecule very stable, as the energy is distributed over a larger area rather than being confined to individual bonds.

parts.problemMd:
Benzocaine is an ester based compound that is used medicinally as a local anaesthetic in pain relievers and cough drops. One of the first industrial processes to manufacture benzocaine was the five-step reaction shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Five-step synthesis route for benzocaine showing conversion of benzene through methylation, nitration, oxidation, esterification, and reduction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/043-five-step-synthesis-route-for-benzocaine-showing.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the systematic name of benzocaine.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of benzocaine is:
> 
> - Ethyl 4-aminobenzoate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzocaine is an ester, so its name follows the alkyl alkanoate format.
> 
> The alcohol portion: ethanol (2 carbons) → gives the 'ethyl' part of the name.
> 
> The acid portion: 4-aminobenzoic acid (benzoic acid with an amino group at position 4) → gives '4-aminobenzoate'.
> 
> So: ethanol + 4-aminobenzoic acid → ethyl 4-aminobenzoate + water.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzocaine is an ester based compound that is used medicinally as a local anaesthetic in pain relievers and cough drops. One of the first industrial processes to manufacture benzocaine was the five-step reaction shown in Fig. 1.1.

Step 1 involves the reaction of benzene with bromomethane.

i) State a suitable catalyst for step 1.

[1]

ii) Draw a mechanism for step 1. Include all necessary curly arrows, charges and the structure of **A**.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A suitable catalyst for step 1:
> 
> - AlBr<sub>3</sub> / aluminium tribromide 
> **OR**
> FeBr<sub>3</sub> / iron tribromide **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for step 1 is:

![Curly arrow mechanism for Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene with bromomethane electrophile showing arenium intermediate and loss of H+](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/044-curly-arrow-mechanism-for-friedel-crafts-alkylat.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the ring to the positively charged carbon of <sup>+</sup>CH<sub>3</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for the correct arenium intermediate structure with a positive charge, the horseshoe covering more than half the ring but not extending past carbons 2 or 6
> 
> 1 mark for a curly arrow from the C–H bond back into the ring AND the correct structure of compound **A** (methylbenzene) shown

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of benzene with bromomethane is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction. It is most commonly performed with a chloroalkane and AlCl<sub>3</sub>, but since bromomethane is specified, an AlBr<sub>3</sub> or FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst is required. The halogen in the catalyst must match the halogen in the halogenoalkane.
> 
> The catalyst generates the electrophile:
> 
> CH<sub>3</sub>Br + AlBr<sub>3</sub> → <sup>+</sup>CH<sub>3</sub> + AlBr<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup>
> 
> The first curly arrow must start touching the ring boundary (not from inside the ring) and point to the positive carbon of the electrophile.
> 
> The horseshoe in the intermediate must be centred about carbon 1 and not extend past carbons 2 or 6.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzocaine is an ester based compound that is used medicinally as a local anaesthetic in pain relievers and cough drops. One of the first industrial processes to manufacture benzocaine was the five-step reaction shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.1

Step 1 involves the reaction of benzene with bromomethane.

The correct structure of compound A (methylbenzene)

Concentrated sulphuric acid and concentrated nitric acid are used to form the ion required for step 2.

The following equilibrium is the first step in the formation of the ion:

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> ⇋ HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>NO<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>

i) State the roles of each acid in this reaction.

[2]

ii) Use your answer to part **(i)** to suggest the relative strengths of the acids.

[1]

iii) Different isomers with the molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> can be formed during step 2.

Draw the structure of the isomer **B**. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The roles of each acid in this reaction:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid
> **AND**
> It donates a proton / H<sup>+</sup> to nitric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Nitric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base
> **AND**
> It accepts a proton / H<sup>+</sup> from sulfuric acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The relative strengths of the acids:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid is stronger than nitric acid (as it donates a proton to nitric acid)
> **OR**
> Nitric acid is weaker than sulfuric acid (as it accepts a proton from sulfuric acid) **[1 mark]**

iii) The structure of isomer **B** is:

![Skeletal structure of 4-nitromethylbenzene (compound B, p-nitrotoluene)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/045-skeletal-structure-of-4-nitromethylbenzene-compo.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of isomer **B**
> 
> Explanation
> 
> - The methyl / CH<sub>3</sub> group on methylbenzene activates positions 2, 4 and 6 on the ring
> **AND**
> The nitro / NO<sub>2</sub> group must attach to carbon-4 to form the product of step 3 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reversible arrow in the equilibrium is not directly relevant to answering part (i). So, focus on which species loses and which gains a proton.
> 
> The overall equation for nitronium ion formation is:
> 
> HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
> 
> For part (ii): since both H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and HNO<sub>3</sub> are normally proton donors, whichever donates a proton to the other must be the stronger acid. Your answer must include comparative language (e.g. 'stronger than', 'weaker than').
> 
> For part (iii): the methyl group donates electron density to the π-system, activating positions 2, 4, and 6. Since the product of step 3 must have the nitro group at carbon-4, isomer **B** is 4-nitromethylbenzene (p-nitrotoluene).

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzocaine is an ester based compound that is used medicinally as a local anaesthetic in pain relievers and cough drops. One of the first industrial processes to manufacture benzocaine was the five-step reaction shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Five-step synthesis route for benzocaine showing conversion of benzene through methylation, nitration, oxidation, esterification, and reduction](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2023/06/_uvCi8Ff_benzocaine-synthesis-adapted.png)

{align=center} **Fig. 1.1**

Suggest reagents and conditions for steps 3–5 of the synthesis.

step 3 ................................................................................

step 4 ................................................................................

step 5 ................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for steps 3 to 5 of the synthesis are:
> 
> Step 3:
> 
> - Hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII), heat under reflux, then dilute acid / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 4:
> 
> - Ethanol / warm with ethanol **[1 mark]**
> - Concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 5:
> 
> - Tin / Sn and concentrated hydrochloric acid / HCl, heat under reflux
> **OR**
> Iron / Fe and concentrated hydrochloric acid / HCl, heat under reflux
> **OR**
> Hydrogen / H<sub>2</sub> and nickel / Ni catalyst **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 3 is the complete oxidation of the alkyl arene side chain to a carboxylic acid using alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> under reflux. The product is initially a carboxylate salt, which is then acidified with dilute acid to give the carboxylic acid.
> 
> Step 4 is esterification: the carboxylic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst, warmed gently.
> 
> Step 5 is the reduction of a nitro group (-NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amine (-NH<sub>2</sub>). This can be done with Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl, or H<sub>2</sub>/Ni. Note that LiAlH<sub>4</sub> and NaBH<sub>4</sub> are not suitable for this reduction.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Benzocaine is an ester based compound that is used medicinally as a local anaesthetic in pain relievers and cough drops. One of the first industrial processes to manufacture benzocaine was the five-step reaction shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.2 shows an alternative reaction scheme for the production of benzocaine.

![Alternative reaction scheme for benzocaine production via Friedel-Crafts acylation followed by nitration, esterification, and reduction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/046-alternative-reaction-scheme-for-benzocaine-produ.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Suggest why this reaction scheme is an improvement.

[1]

ii) Suggest why this reaction scheme may not work.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) This reaction scheme is an improvement because:
> 
> - There are fewer steps in the reaction scheme **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) This reaction scheme may not work because:
> 
> - The nitration of benzoyl chloride does not preferentially form 4-nitrobenzoyl chloride / nitration does not occur at carbon-4 of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Chemists aim to minimise the number of steps in any reaction scheme as this improves efficiency and overall atom economy.
> 
> The key difference between the two schemes is in the first two steps. Fig. 1.1 uses methylation then nitration; Fig. 1.2 uses acylation then nitration.
> 
> Fig. 1.1 converts 4-nitromethylbenzene to 4-nitrobenzoic acid (an extra oxidation step). Fig. 1.2 avoids this by starting with Friedel-Crafts acylation.
> 
> However, the acyl chloride group in benzoyl chloride is an electron-withdrawing meta-director. Nitration of benzoyl chloride preferentially places the nitro group at carbon-3, not carbon-4. This gives 3-nitrobenzoyl chloride, which would produce the wrong isomer of benzocaine.

Step 1 is not completed in acidic conditions.

Suggest reagents and conditions for each of steps 1 to 3.

step 1 ................................................................................

step 2 ................................................................................

step 3 ................................................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for each step are:
> 
> Step 1:
> 
> - Ethanolic / alcoholic sodium hydroxide / NaOH
> **OR**
> Ethanolic / alcoholic potassium hydroxide / KOH **[1 mark]**
> - Heated under reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 2:
> 
> - Steam / water vapour / H<sub>2</sub>O (g) at 300 °C **[1 mark]**
> - Concentrated sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst
> **OR**
> Concentrated phosphoric acid / H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> catalyst **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 3:

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 1 is not completed in acidic conditions. Alkaline / basic conditions with an ethanolic base give the elimination reaction (forming propene). If aqueous conditions were used instead, nucleophilic substitution would give propan-2-ol directly.

> Step 2 converts propene into propan-2-ol via hydration. This requires steam, an acid catalyst, and a temperature of 300 °C (and approximately 7 MPa pressure).

parts.problemMd:
Ethene is used in the radical-free synthesis of 1-aminopropane as shown.

ethene $\overset{\mathrm{step}1}{\rightarrow}$ compound **A** $\overset{\mathrm{step}2}{\rightarrow}$ compound **B** $\overset{\mathrm{step}3}{\rightarrow}$ propylamine

Identify which step of the reaction scheme could use potassium cyanide dissolved in ethanol. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The step that could use potassium cyanide / KCN dissolved in ethanol is step 2. Marks are only awarded if step 2 is correctly identified.
> 
> - It cannot be step 1 because the cyanide ion / CN<sup>-</sup> is a nucleophile
> **AND**
> It will not react with / attack the C=C double bond of ethene **[1 mark]**
> - It cannot be step 3 because the reaction of CN<sup>-</sup> / KCN with compound **B** does not produce an amine
> **AND**
> A reduction step is required to convert the nitrile group to an amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are three steps and two marks, which combined with 'explain your answer' suggest that you should gain marks for explaining why two steps cannot use potassium cyanide.
> 
> Potassium cyanide provides CN<sup>-</sup> ions, which act as nucleophiles. Nucleophiles attack electron-deficient centres (positive or partial positive carbons), not electron-rich C=C double bonds.
> 
> Step 2 is a nucleophilic substitution: the CN<sup>-</sup> ion displaces the halide from compound **A** (a haloalkane), extending the carbon chain by one to give compound **B** (a nitrile). This is why KCN in ethanol is the correct reagent rather than not HCN, which is used for nucleophilic addition to carbonyl groups.

> Compound **A** must be able to react with the cyanide ion (CN<sup>-</sup>) via nucleophilic substitution, so it must contain a C–X bond (a haloalkane).

[3]

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the formation of the nitronium ion is:
> 
> - HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the electrophilic substitution nitration of 1,3-dimethylbenzene is:

![mechanism showing curly arrows and intermediate for electrophilic substitution of 1,3-dimethylbenzene with nitronium ion](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/035-mechanism-showing-curly-arrows-and-intermediate-.jpg)

Suggest, with the aid of suitable diagrams, why 1,3-dimethyl-2-nitrobenzene is likely to be the more abundant product.
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram showing the directing effect of the methyl groups on the benzene ring is:

![1,3-dimethylbenzene ring numbering diagram showing positions 2, 4 and 6 activated by both methyl groups at C1 and C3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/36-organic-synthesis/36-1-organic-synthesis/assets/037-1-3-dimethylbenzene-ring-numbering-diagram-showi.png)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1,3-dimethyl-2-nitrobenzene is likely to be the more abundant product:
> 
> - Methyl / CH<sub>3</sub> groups direct attacks to the 2, 4 and 6 positions (on the ring) **[1 mark]**
> 
> - Position 2 is ortho to both methyl groups (doubly activated), whereas position 5 is meta to both methyl groups **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Alkyl groups activate the 2, 4 and 6 positions on a benzene ring.
> 
> As the diagram shows, position 2 is ortho to both methyl groups (at C-1 and C-3), so it is doubly activated and is a more reactive position than position 5.
> 
> Position 5 is meta to both methyl groups and is therefore not preferentially activated, making 1,3-dimethyl-5-nitrobenzene the less abundant isomer.
> 
> Although mononitration is theoretically possible on positions 2, 4, 5 and 6, it is most likely at positions 2, 4 and 6 (those activated by both methyl groups).

A labelled diagram of the apparatus for thin-layer chromatography is:

![A labelled diagram of TLC apparatus showing a TLC plate in a beaker of solvent. The pencil baseline is near the bottom of the plate. Two spots are marked on the baseline and the beaker is covered with a lid. The solvent level is below the baseline.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/006-a-labelled-diagram-of-tlc-apparatus-showing-a-tl.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for pencil baseline labelled **AND **sealed container / lid shown
> 
> 1 mark for solvent labelled **AND **level of solvent shown below the pencil baseline
> 
> 1 mark for two spots labelled on the baseline

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always include the lid on the beaker in your diagram. This prevents evaporation of the volatile organic solvents used as the mobile phase.
> 
> The solvent level must be below the pencil baseline. If the solvent touches the spots, they will dissolve directly into the solvent rather than being carried up the plate.

parts.problemMd: State the two factors that determine the distance travelled by a compound in thin-layer chromatography.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two factors that determine the distance travelled by a compound in thin-layer chromatography are:
> 
> - The solubility of the compound in the mobile phase **[1 mark]**
> - The adsorption of the compound by the stationary phase **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A compound that is very soluble in the mobile phase is carried further up the plate. A compound that adsorbs strongly to the stationary phase is held back and travels a shorter distance.
> 
> For TLC using a solid stationary phase such as silica, the correct term for the interaction with the stationary phase is adsorption.

parts.problemMd: State the equation used to calculate the retention factor, *R*<sub>f</sub>, of a compound.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation used to calculate the retention factor, *R*<sub>f</sub>, of a compound is:
> 
> - *R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{\text{distance travelled by compound}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent front}}$ **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This equation is not often specifically asked for in a question. You are more likely to be asked to apply it to calculate an *R*<sub>f</sub> value from a chromatogram.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The equation used to calculate the retention factor, *R*~f~, of a compound is:

*R*~f~ = \$\$\frac{\text{distance travelled by compound}}{\text{distance travelled by solvent front}}\$\$

Calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of the compound shown in the chromatogram below. Show your working.

![A developed TLC plate showing a baseline at 2 cm, a compound spot at 16 cm, and a solvent front at 20 cm from the bottom of the plate.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/007-a-developed-tlc-plate-showing-a-baseline-at-2-cm.png)
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of the compound:

- Determine the distances from the baseline:

Distance travelled by solvent front = 20 − 2 = 18 cm

Distance travelled by compound = 16 − 2 = 14 cm

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value:

*R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{spot}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent} \mathrm{front}}$

*R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{14}{18}$

*R*<sub>f</sub> = **0.78**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both distances correctly measured from the baseline: solvent front = 18 cm **AND **compound = 14 cm
> 
> 1 mark for correct *R*<sub>f</sub> value: 0.78 (Allow 0.777–0.778)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Distances are measured from the pencil baseline, not from the bottom of the plate. In this chromatogram, the baseline is at 2 cm, so subtract 2 cm from each measurement before dividing.
> 
> The *R*<sub>f</sub> value has no units because it is a ratio.

parts.problemMd:
A student sets up a thin-layer chromatography experiment.

Explain why:

i) the baseline is drawn in pencil rather than ink.

[1]

ii) a lid is placed on the container during the experiment.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The baseline is drawn in pencil rather than ink because:
> 
> - Pencil does not dissolve in / is not carried up the plate by the solvent **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A lid is placed on the container because:
> 
> - To prevent evaporation of the solvent / to maintain a saturated atmosphere **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both are standard precautions in TLC. Ink would dissolve in the solvent and be carried up the plate, interfering with the chromatogram. A lid prevents solvent evaporation, which would cause the solvent front to stop moving.

parts.problemMd:
A student runs a thin-layer chromatography experiment and plans to determine the compounds from their *R*<sub>f</sub> values.

Describe the steps that the student needs to perform to determine the identity of the compounds.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The steps to determine the identity of the compounds are:
> 
> - Measure the distance travelled by the solvent
> **OR**
> Measure the distance to the solvent front **[1 mark]**
> - Measure the distance travelled by each compound / component / spot **[1 mark]**
> - Calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value using the equation *R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{compound}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$ **[1 mark]**
> - Compare the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of each spot with data table / reference values to identify the compound **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks how to go from a chromatogram to an identification. State the two distances measured (compound and solvent front), write the *R*<sub>f</sub> equation, and explain that the calculated *R*<sub>f</sub> values are compared against known reference data.

parts.problemMd:
The compounds in the mixture are colourless.

Suggest how the student could locate the spots on the TLC plate.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Expose the TLC plate to UV light
> **OR**
> Place the TLC plate in an iodine vapour chamber **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Colourless compounds are not visible under normal light. Two common methods to reveal spots are UV light (if the silica contains a UV-active indicator) and iodine vapour, which temporarily stains organic compounds brown.

parts.problemMd:
The student runs another TLC practical on a mixture of benzaldehyde and benzyl alcohol using 7:3 pentane / diethyl ether as a solvent.

The student's chromatogram is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![TLC chromatogram showing spots for benzaldehyde and benzyl alcohol with distances marked for Rf calculation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/002-tlc-chromatogram-showing-spots-for-benzaldehyde-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> values for both compounds in the chromatogram. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> values for benzaldehyde and benzyl alcohol:

- Apply the *R*<sub>f</sub> equation:

*R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{compound}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$

- Calculate *R*<sub>f</sub> for benzaldehyde:

*R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{3.2}{5.0}$

*R*<sub>f</sub> (benzaldehyde) = **0.64** **[1 mark]**

- Calculate *R*<sub>f</sub> for benzyl alcohol:

*R*<sub>f</sub> = $\frac{1.5}{5.0}$

*R*<sub>f</sub> (benzyl alcohol) = **0.30** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A compound that is very soluble in the mobile phase has a high *R*<sub>f</sub> (close to 1); a compound that adsorbs strongly to the stationary phase has a low *R*<sub>f</sub> (close to 0).

parts.problemMd: Explain why the maximum *R*<sub>f</sub> value of a compound cannot exceed 1.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The maximum *R*<sub>f</sub> value cannot exceed 1 because:
> 
> - *R*<sub>f</sub> is a ratio of the distance a compound has travelled to the distance travelled by the solvent **[1 mark]**
> - An *R*<sub>f</sub> value of 1 means the compound is fully soluble in the mobile phase and does not interact with the stationary phase **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Think about what *R*<sub>f</sub> physically represents: the distance the compound travels as a fraction of the solvent front distance. Since the compound cannot travel further than the solvent, the maximum ratio is 1. An *R*<sub>f</sub> of exactly 1 would mean the compound has no interaction with the stationary phase at all.

parts.problemMd:
Thin layer chromatography was used to analyse the contents of a bottle containing butan-2-ol and butanone.

The contents of the bottle were dissolved in hexane and spotted onto the silica plate.

Explain why butanone has a higher *R*<sub>f</sub> value than butan-2-ol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Butanone has a higher *R*<sub>f</sub> value than butan-2-ol because:
> 
> - Butan-2-ol is more polar than butanone
> **OR**
> Butan-2-ol contains hydrogen bonding **[1 mark]**
> - Butan-2-ol adsorbs more strongly to the silica gel / stationary phase
> **OR**
> Butanone is more soluble in the mobile phase / solvent **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore, butanone travels further on the TLC plate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Butan-2-ol contains an -OH group which enables hydrogen bonding, making it more polar than butanone. More polar compounds adsorb more strongly to the polar silica gel stationary phase and travel less far up the plate, giving a lower *R*<sub>f</sub> value.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Thin layer chromatography was used to analyse the contents of a bottle containing butan-2-ol and butanone. 

The contents of the bottle were dissolved in hexane and spotted onto the silica plate.

State the names of the stationary and mobile phases in this chromatography experiment.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The stationary and mobile phases in this chromatography experiment are:
> 
> - Stationary phase = silica gel **[1 mark]**
> - Mobile phase = hexane **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In thin-layer chromatography, the stationary phase is a layer of silica gel (SiO<sub>2</sub>) or alumina (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) coated onto a plate. The mobile phase is the liquid solvent that moves up the plate by capillary action.

parts.problemMd:
The student repeats the experiment using a more polar solvent instead of 7:3 pentane / diethyl ether.

Suggest and explain the effect on the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of benzyl alcohol.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect on the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of benzyl alcohol is:
> 
> - The *R*<sub>f</sub> value would increase **[1 mark]**
> - Benzyl alcohol is more soluble in a polar solvent / has a greater affinity for the polar mobile phase, so it travels further up the plate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzyl alcohol contains an -OH group and is relatively polar. A polar solvent increases the solubility of polar compounds in the mobile phase, reducing their interaction with the stationary phase and causing them to travel further, increasing their *R*<sub>f</sub> value.

parts.problemMd:
Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is used to analyse samples of organic compounds.

Fig. 3.1 shows the structure of ibuprofen.

![Skeletal formula of ibuprofen](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/001-skeletal-formula-of-ibuprofen.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Calculate the *M*<sub>r</sub> of ibuprofen to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
The *M*<sub>r</sub> of ibuprofen (C<sub>13</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is:

*M*<sub>r</sub> = (12.0 x 13) + (1.0 x 18) + (16.0 x 2)

*M*<sub>r</sub> = **206.0** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular formula of ibuprofen is C<sub>13</sub>H<sub>18</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. When counting atoms in a skeletal formula, remember that hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are not shown.

parts.problemMd: State **two** advantages of using TLC for the analysis of organic samples.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Advantages of using TLC to analyse organic samples include:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Quick analysis time
> - Many samples can be processed simultaneously
> - High degree of accuracy / repeatability / reproducibility
> - (Very) small sample sizes are needed
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> TLC is widely used in organic chemistry because it requires only small amounts of material, gives results quickly, and can test many samples side by side. The *R*<sub>f</sub> value of each spot can then be compared against reference data.

parts.problemMd:
Thin-layer chromatography was performed on a sample of ibuprofen.

Only one spot was expected on the TLC plate but two were observed.

Suggest why the ibuprofen sample produced two spots on the TLC plate rather than one.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ibuprofen sample produced two spots because:
> 
> - The sample contains an impurity / is not pure **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In chromatography, each compound in a sample produces one spot. If only one compound is expected but two spots appear, the sample must contain an impurity. A pure sample gives a single spot; a mixture gives multiple spots.

parts.problemMd:
Dinitrobenzene has the molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.

i) Draw the skeletal formulae of the three structural isomers of dinitrobenzene.

[3]

ii) State the type of structural isomerism shown.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The three structural isomers of dinitrobenzene are:

![Skeletal formulae of 1,2-dinitrobenzene, 1,3-dinitrobenzene and 1,4-dinitrobenzene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/003-skeletal-formulae-of-1-2-dinitrobenzene-1-3-dini.png)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for each correct skeletal formula:
> 
> - 1,2-dinitrobenzene
> - 1,3-dinitrobenzene
> - 1,4-dinitrobenzene
> 
> ii) The type of structural isomerism shown is:
> 
> - Positional / position isomerism **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When drawing di-substituted isomers of benzene, place one functional group at carbon-1 and keep it fixed. Then move the second functional group around the ring one carbon at a time, starting from carbon-2 and ending at carbon-4.

parts.problemMd: State the factors that determine the distance travelled by a spot in thin-layer chromatography.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The factors that determine the distance travelled by a spot in thin-layer chromatography are:
> 
> - Solubility in the mobile phase / solvent **[1 mark]**
> - Adsorption by / strength of adsorption onto the stationary phase / silica gel **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The distance a compound travels depends on two opposing interactions:
> 
> 1. How soluble it is in the mobile phase (which carries it up the plate)
> 2. How strongly it adsorbs onto the stationary phase (which holds it back).

parts.problemMd:
Samples of 1,2-dinitrobenzene and 1,4-dinitrobenzene are spotted on a thin-layer chromatography plate coated with silica gel.

The solvent used to run the thin-layer chromatography experiment is hexane.

Suggest why each sample is applied to the thin-layer chromatography plate using a fine capillary tube rather than a dropping pipette.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - A fine capillary tube produces a smaller / more concentrated spot
> **OR**
> A smaller spot produces a better / more accurate chromatogram
> **OR**
> To avoid smudging / smearing the spot **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question tests understanding of practical technique. A smaller, more concentrated spot gives a cleaner chromatogram and makes accurate *R*<sub>f</sub> calculation easier. A large or smeared spot makes measurements unreliable.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Samples of 1,2-dinitrobenzene and 1,4-dinitrobenzene are spotted on a thin-layer chromatography plate coated with silica gel.

The solvent used to run the thin-layer chromatography experiment is hexane.

The factors that determine the distance travelled by a spot in thin-layer chromatography are:
- Solubility in the mobile phase / solvent
- Adsorption by / strength of adsorption onto the stationary phase / silica gel

Fig. 1.1 shows the chromatogram with the spot for 1,4-dinitrobenzene.

![TLC plate showing a spot for 1,4-dinitrobenzene with the solvent front marked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/004-tlc-plate-showing-a-spot-for-1-4-dinitrobenzene-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Draw the expected position of the spot for 1,2-dinitrobenzene. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The expected position of the spot for 1,2-dinitrobenzene is:

![TLC plate showing spots for 1,4-dinitrobenzene and 1,2-dinitrobenzene, with the 1,2-dinitrobenzene spot lower on the plate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-1-thin-layer-chromatography/assets/005-tlc-plate-showing-spots-for-1-4-dinitrobenzene-a.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the spot correctly placed below the existing spot on the chromatogram
> 
> - The silica gel / stationary phase is polar
> **OR**
> The hexane / mobile phase is non-polar **[1 mark]**
> - 1,2-dinitrobenzene is more polar
> **AND**
> 1,2-dinitrobenzene adsorbs more strongly to the stationary phase / is less soluble in the mobile phase
> **AND**
> Therefore, 1,2-dinitrobenzene does not travel as far **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both compounds are dinitrobenzene isomers, so the difference in their positions on the chromatogram must be due to their structural differences. 1,2-dinitrobenzene has both nitro groups on adjacent carbons and is therefore more polar. A more polar compound adsorbs more strongly to the polar silica gel and travels less far up the plate.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Samples of 1,2-dinitrobenzene and 1,4-dinitrobenzene are spotted on a thin-layer chromatography plate coated with silica gel.

The solvent used to run the thin-layer chromatography experiment is hexane.

1,2-dinitrobenzene is more polar and adsorbs more strongly to the stationary phase / is less soluble in the mobile phase, therefore 1,2-dinitrobenzene does not travel as far.

Explain what the student could do to reverse the relative positions of the 1,2-dinitrobenzene and 1,4-dinitrobenzene spots.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> To reverse the relative positions of the spots, the student could:
> 
> - Replace the hexane with a polar solvent / use a polar solvent **[1 mark]**
> - 1,2-dinitrobenzene is more soluble in a polar solvent
> **AND**
> Therefore, 1,2-dinitrobenzene travels further / the positions are reversed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Polar compounds are more soluble in polar solvents. Switching to a polar solvent increases the solubility of 1,2-dinitrobenzene in the mobile phase, so it moves further up the plate relative to 1,4-dinitrobenzene, reversing their positions.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about gas chromatography.

Name the **three** types of chemical that gas chromatography is used for.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The three types of chemical that gas chromatography is used for are:
> 
> - Gases **[1 mark]**
> - Volatile liquids **[1 mark]**
> - Solids in their vapour form **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Gas chromatography (also called gas-liquid chromatography) is used for identifying and separating chemicals that are volatile, meaning they can exist as, or be converted to, a gas under the column conditions.
> 
> All three accepted answers share the key property of volatility: they can all be vaporised and carried through the column by the gas mobile phase.

parts.problemMd: State the physical nature of the stationary phase used in gas-liquid chromatography.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The stationary phase used in gas-liquid chromatography is:
> 
> - A non-volatile / high boiling point liquid **[1 mark]**
> - (Coated) on an inert solid support **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stationary phase must be a liquid so that components can dissolve into (partition into) it from the gas mobile phase.
> 
> It must be non-volatile (have a high boiling point) so it does not evaporate during the analysis and contaminate the carrier gas.

parts.problemMd: State the type of chemical used as the mobile phase in gas chromatography. Give one specific example of a suitable carrier gas.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mobile phase in gas chromatography is:
> 
> - An inert (carrier) gas **[1 mark]**
> 
> One suitable example:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Helium / He
> - Nitrogen / N<sub>2</sub>
> - Argon / Ar
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mobile phase must be an inert gas so that it does not react with any of the components being separated or with the stationary phase.
> 
> The alternative name for gas chromatography is gas-liquid chromatography. This tells you directly that the mobile phase is a gas and the stationary phase is a liquid.

parts.problemMd:
Results in gas chromatography are based on retention time.

i) Define the term retention time.

[1]

ii) State **three **factors that retention time depends upon.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Answers to the questions on retention time in gas chromatography:
> 
> i) The definition of retention time is:
> 
> - The time taken for a component to travel through the column
> **OR**
> The time taken from injection to detection / emergence of the sample **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Three factors that retention time depends upon are:
> 
> Any **three** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - The attraction between the sample and the stationary phase
> - The attraction between the sample / component and the mobile phase
> - The polarity of the sample / component
> - The volatility of the sample / component
> - The chemical structure of the sample / component
> 
> **[3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): the key word in retention time is retained. The retention time is the time a component spends in the column, measured from injection to detection.
> 
> For part (ii): all the listed factors influence how strongly the component partitions into the stationary phase relative to the gas mobile phase. A component with a greater affinity for the stationary phase (due to its polarity, chemical structure, or low volatility) travels more slowly through the column and has a longer retention time.

parts.problemMd: State what information the relative size or area under the peak on a gas chromatogram provides.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative size or area under a peak on a gas chromatogram tells you:
> 
> - The relative concentration / amount / abundance of that component in the mixture **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The area under the peak (not just the peak height) is proportional to the abundance of that component. A tall, narrow peak and a shorter, broader peak could represent the same amount of a compound. Always refer to peak area, not peak height, when describing abundance.

parts.problemMd:
Gas chromatography is carried out using a polar stationary phase and argon as the carrier gas.

Use the chromatogram in Fig. 1.1 to answer the following questions.

![Gas chromatogram showing three peaks for compounds A, B and C plotted as detector response against retention time. Compound A has the shortest retention time, compound B has the tallest peak, and compound C has the longest retention time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-2-gasliquid-chromatography/assets/002-gas-chromatogram-showing-three-peaks-for-compoun.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State which compound has the lowest retention time.

[1]

ii) State which compound is the least polar.

[1]

iii) State which compound has the greatest interaction with the stationary phase.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Using Fig. 1.1 to answer each part:
> 
> i) The compound with the lowest retention time is:
> 
> - **A** **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The least polar compound is:
> 
> - **A** **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The compound with the greatest interaction with the stationary phase is:
> 
> - **C** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): read the retention time directly from the x-axis. Compound A elutes first and therefore has the lowest retention time.
> 
> For part (ii): the stationary phase is polar, so it attracts polar compounds more strongly, slowing their movement through the column. Compound A has the shortest retention time, meaning it interacts least with the polar stationary phase. It is therefore the least polar compound.
> 
> Parts (i) and (ii) are linked: when a polar stationary phase is used, the compound with the shortest retention time is always the least polar.
> 
> For part (iii): compound C has the longest retention time. It spends the most time in the column, meaning it has the greatest solubility in / interaction with the stationary phase.

parts.problemMd: State the difference between the mobile phases used in column chromatography and gas-liquid chromatography.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference between the mobile phases is:
> 
> - The mobile phase in column chromatography is a liquid
> **AND**
> The mobile phase in gas-liquid chromatography is a gas **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Mobile phase" is another term for the eluent, the substance that carries the components through the system.
> 
> In column chromatography (which uses the same principles as TLC), the mobile phase is a liquid solvent. In gas-liquid chromatography, the mobile phase is replaced by an inert carrier gas such as helium, argon, or nitrogen.

parts.problemMd:
Three compounds, **A**, **B** and **C**, of similar volatility, are mixed together. The mixture is then analysed in a gas chromatograph.

The gas chromatogram produced is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Gas chromatogram showing three peaks for compounds A, B and C plotted as detector response against retention time. **Fig. 1.1**

State which compound, **A**, **B** or **C**, has the greatest affinity for the stationary phase. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:

> - Compound **C**
> **AND**
> It has the greatest retention time **[1 mark]**
> - A longer retention time indicates the compound spends more time dissolved in / partitioned into the stationary phase, so it has a greater affinity for it **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In GLC, a longer retention time means the component is slowed down by the stationary phase. This occurs because it has a greater affinity for (is more soluble in) the stationary phase relative to the gas mobile phase.

parts.problemMd: Suggest how gas chromatography could be used to confirm that oil pollution found on a beach originated from a specific oil tanker.
parts.solutionMd:

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
A mixture of volatile esters can be analysed using gas chromatography, coupled with mass spectrometry.

Describe how each method contributes to the analysis.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> How each method contributes to the analysis:
> 
> - Gas chromatography separates the ester mixture into its component compounds **[1 mark]**
> - Mass spectrometry ionises each separated compound and produces a mass spectrum / fragmentation pattern **[1 mark]**
> - The fragmentation pattern is compared to a database of known compounds for identification **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question is worth 3 marks but only mentions 2 methods, which means that each method needs a little extra detail to earn all 3 marks.
> 
> GC-MS is used to separate and identify volatile compounds. The GC stage separates the mixture; the MS stage identifies each component. The key final step is database matching, which completes the identification.

parts.problemMd: Define the term retention time.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Retention time is:
> 
> - The time between injection and detection / emergence of a component
> **OR**
> the time that each component remains in the column **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Defining retention time is not a common exam question, but it is possible. Two equivalent definitions are accepted:
> 
> - The time between injection and detection of a component
> - The time that each component remains in the column
> 
> The retention time depends on the compound’s relative affinity for the mobile gas phase versus the stationary phase.

parts.problemMd:
A mixture of two volatile esters, methyl propanoate and propyl methanoate, is analysed by gas chromatography followed by mass spectrometry.

Explain why the mixture of esters can be separated by gas chromatography.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The mixture of esters can be separated by gas chromatography because:
> 
> - The esters have different retention times
> **OR**
> The esters appear at different times in the chromatogram **[1 mark]**
> - The esters have different affinities for the mobile and stationary phases
> **OR**
> The esters have different solubilities in the stationary phase **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The different structures of methyl propanoate and propyl methanoate mean they interact differently with the stationary phase. One ester partitions more into the stationary phase (spending more time there, moving more slowly); the other moves more readily with the mobile gas phase.
> 
> Although these esters are structural isomers with similar properties, the subtle differences in their structures give them slightly different retention times, allowing separation.

parts.problemMd:

> **[exam-tip]**

> 
> Gas chromatograms are often misinterpreted, so make sure you are reading retention time (x-axis) and not peak height.

parts.problemMd:
Two of the compounds in the organic mixture are hydrocarbons with similar retention times.

The mass spectra of the two compounds revealed that they have the same molecular formula but with subtle differences indicating structural isomerism is present.

The mass spectrum of one of the isomers is shown in Fig. 1.2.

Both isomers are tested with bromine water, which remains orange.

![Mass spectrum showing molecular ion peak at m/e = 86 with major fragment peaks at m/e = 57, 43, and 29, consistent with a straight-chain hexane isomer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-2-gasliquid-chromatography/assets/005-mass-spectrum-showing-molecular-ion-peak-at-m-e-.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Deduce the molar mass and hence the molecular formula of the isomers.

molar mass ................................................................................

molecular formula ................................................................................

[2]

ii) Deduce the identity of the fragments responsible for the following signals.

*m / e* = 29 ................................................................................

*m / e* = 43 ................................................................................

*m / e* = 57 ................................................................................

[3]

iii) Deduce the skeletal formula of the isomer responsible for this spectrum.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) Molar mass and molecular formula:
> 
> - Molar mass = 86 (g mol<sup>-1</sup>) **[1 mark]**
> - Molecular formula = C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Fragments responsible for the signals:
> 
> - *m/e* = 29 = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - *m/e* = 43 = C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - *m/e* = 57 = C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**

iii) Skeletal formula:

![Skeletal formula of hexane showing a chain of 6 carbon atoms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-2-gasliquid-chromatography/assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-hexane-showing-a-straight-ch.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the skeletal formula of hexane showing a straight chain of 6 carbon atoms

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular ion peak (*m/e* = 86) equals the molar mass, assuming singly charged ions only.
> 
> The question tells you that the molecules are hydrocarbons and that bromine water does not decolourise — so the molecules are saturated (only single bonds). Using these clues with *m/e* = 86:
> 
> - 6 carbons (72) + 14 hydrogens (14) = 86 g mol<sup>-1</sup>, consistent with the bromine water test (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>)
> - 7 carbons would require only 2 hydrogens (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>2</sub>), which is unrealistic
> 
> All fragments carry a single positive charge and contain only carbon and hydrogen.
> 
> The peak at *m/e* = 57 corresponds to C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub><sup>+</sup>, which is a four-carbon fragment. This is only possible for straight-chain hexane; a branched isomer such as 2,3-dimethylbutane could not readily form this fragment.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two of the compounds in the organic mixture are hydrocarbons with similar retention times.

The mass spectra of the two compounds revealed that they have the same molecular formula but with subtle differences indicating structural isomerism is present.

The mass spectrum of one of the isomers is shown in Fig. 1.2.

i) Deduce the molar mass and hence the molecular formula of the isomers.

molar mass ................................................................................

molecular formula ................................................................................

Molar mass = 86 (g mol^-1^)
Molecular formula = C~6~H~14~

There is a small peak at *m / e* = 87 in the mass spectrum. This is known as the [M+1] peak.

i) State the identity of the isotope responsible for the [M+1] peak.

[1]

ii) Suggest the type of molecules for which this [M+1] peak would become more pronounced. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The isotope responsible for the [M+1] peak:
> 
> - Carbon-13 / <sup>13</sup>C **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Types of molecules for which the [M+1] peak becomes more pronounced:
> 
> - Molecules with longer carbon chains / more carbon atoms **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - As the number of carbon atoms in the molecule increases
> **AND**
> The probability that one of them is <sup>13</sup>C increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular ion peak assumes all carbon atoms are <sup>12</sup>C (the most abundant isotope). The [M+1] peak arises because <sup>13</sup>C has a natural abundance of approximately 1.1%.
> 
> As the number of carbon atoms in a molecule increases, the probability that at least one is <sup>13</sup>C increases. So, the [M+1] peak becomes relatively larger for compounds with more carbons.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Two of the compounds in the organic mixture are hydrocarbons with similar retention times.

The mass spectra of the two compounds revealed that they have the same molecular formula but with subtle differences indicating structural isomerism is present.

The mass spectrum of one of the isomers is shown in Fig. 1.2.

Both isomers are tested with bromine water, which remains orange.

i) Deduce the molar mass and hence the molecular formula of the isomers.

ii) Deduce the identity of the fragments responsible for the following signals.

*m / e* = 29
*m / e* = 43
*m / e* = 57

iii) Deduce the skeletal formula of the isomer responsible for this spectrum.

Mark scheme:
Molar mass = 86 (g mol^-1^)
Molecular formula = C6H14
*m/e* = 29 = C2H5+
*m/e* = 43 = C3H7+
*m/e* = 57 = C4H9+
Skeletal formula of hexane showing a straight chain of 6 carbon atoms

One other isomer present in the original mixture was 2,3-dimethylbutane.

i) Suggest **one** way in which the mass spectrum of 2,3-dimethylbutane will differ from Fig. 1.2 in part **(b)**.

[1]

ii) Suggest an alternative spectroscopic technique for distinguishing between 2,3-dimethylbutane and your answer to **(b)(iii)**.

[1]

iii) Predict which of the two isomers would have the longest retention time. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) One way in which the mass spectrum of 2,3-dimethylbutane differs:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - No peak / minimal peak at *m/e* = 57 (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub><sup>+</sup> fragment cannot readily form from 2,3-dimethylbutane)
> - More intense peak at *m/e* = 71 (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub><sup>+</sup> from loss of CH<sub>3</sub>)
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) An alternative spectroscopic technique:
> 
> - <sup>13</sup>C NMR
> **OR**
> <sup>1</sup>H NMR **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The isomer with the longest retention time:
> 
> - Hexane (the straight-chain isomer from part b) **[1 mark]**
> - Hexane is straight-chain with a greater surface area than 2,3-dimethylbutane
> **AND**
> Hexane has stronger London dispersion forces, a higher boiling point (69 °C vs 58 °C), is less volatile, and spends more time partitioned into the stationary phase **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i:
> 
> The branching in 2,3-dimethylbutane prevents the formation of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub><sup>+</sup> (m/e = 57). Loss of a methyl group (CH<sub>3</sub>) is easy due to the four equivalent methyl groups, giving a more intense peak at m/e = 71 (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>11</sub><sup>+</sup>).
> 
> For part iii:
> 
> In GLC, separation is by partitioning, where compounds dissolve into and out of the liquid stationary phase. Do not confuse this with adsorption chromatography. Hexane (straight-chain) has a greater surface area, stronger London dispersion forces, and a higher boiling point (69 °C) than 2,3-dimethylbutane (58 °C). Hexane is therefore less volatile and spends more time dissolved in the stationary phase, giving it the longer retention time.

parts.problemMd:
Benzene is analysed using carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy.

Explain why the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of benzene contains only one peak.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explaining why the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of benzene contains only one peak:
> 
> - All six carbon atoms are in the same chemical environment **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The key to this question is symmetry. Benzene has a perfect hexagonal structure, so every carbon atom has exactly the same bonding environment. In <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectroscopy, carbon atoms in the same chemical environment absorb at the same frequency and produce a single combined peak.
> 
> Any molecule where all carbons are symmetrically equivalent will show only one <sup>13</sup>C peak. Benzene is the classic example, but watch for other symmetric molecules such as cyclohexane.

parts.problemMd:
Fig. 1.1 shows the skeletal formula of methylbenzene.

![Structure of methylbenzene showing the benzene ring with a methyl group attached](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-3-carbon-13-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/010-structure-of-methylbenzene-showing-the-benzene-r.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the number of peaks that would appear in the low-resolution <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of methylbenzene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of peaks in the low-resolution <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of methylbenzene is:
> 
> - 4 / four **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To count the number of peaks in a low-resolution <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, identify how many groups of protons are in different chemical environments. Two protons are in the same environment if they occupy identical positions within the molecule by symmetry.
> 
> For methylbenzene, there are four distinct proton environments:
> 
> - The CH<sub>3</sub> group: 3 protons
> - The two ring C–H groups adjacent to the methyl-bearing carbon: 2 protons
> - The two ring C–H groups one further position around the ring: 2 protons
> - The ring C–H group directly opposite the methyl group: 1 proton
> 
> The two pairs of ring protons are each equivalent by symmetry, so each pair counts as one environment. The key to any benzene derivative NMR question is spotting the symmetry elements of the molecule.

parts.problemMd:
There are three isomers of dimethylbenzene shown in Fig. 1.2:

- 1,2-dimethylbenzene
- 1,3-dimethylbenzene
- 1,4-dimethylbenzene

![Skeletal formulae of the three dimethylbenzene isomers: 1,2-dimethylbenzene, 1,3-dimethylbenzene, and 1,4-dimethylbenzene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-3-carbon-13-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/011-skeletal-formulae-of-the-three-dimethylbenzene-i.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

Complete Table 1.1 to show the number of expected peaks in the low-resolution <sup>1</sup>H NMR and <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra of the three dimethylbenzene isomers.

**Table 1.1**

| **Isomer** | **Number of peaks in **<sup>**1**</sup>**H NMR spectrum** | **Number of peaks in **<sup>**13**</sup>**C NMR spectrum** |
|---|---|---|
| 1,2-dimethylbenzene |   |   |
| 1,3-dimethylbenzene |   |   |
| 1,4-dimethylbenzene |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The completed table is:

| **Isomer** | **Number of peaks in **<sup>**1**</sup>**H NMR spectrum** | **Number of peaks in **<sup>**13**</sup>**C NMR spectrum** |
|---|---|---|
| 1,2-dimethylbenzene | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **4** |
| 1,3-dimethylbenzene | **Final answer:** **4** | **Final answer:** **5** |
| 1,4-dimethylbenzene | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **3** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for 1,2-dimethylbenzene: <sup>1</sup>H = 3 **AND** <sup>13</sup>C = 4
> 
> 1 mark for 1,3-dimethylbenzene: <sup>1</sup>H = 4 **AND** <sup>13</sup>C = 5
> 
> 1 mark for 1,4-dimethylbenzene: <sup>1</sup>H = 2 **AND** <sup>13</sup>C = 3

> **[exam-tip]**
> To count NMR environments in substituted benzenes, draw each structure and identify all lines of symmetry. Carbons or hydrogens that are mirror images of each other through a line of symmetry are equivalent and produce one combined peak.
> 
> For the three dimethylbenzene isomers:
> 
> - 1,2-dimethylbenzene has one plane of symmetry bisecting the bond between the two methyl-bearing carbons. This gives 4 <sup>13</sup>C environments (the two equivalent methyl carbons plus three distinct ring environments) and 3 <sup>1</sup>H environments.
> - 1,3-dimethylbenzene has one plane of symmetry through the carbon positioned between the two methyl groups. This gives 5 <sup>13</sup>C environments and 4 <sup>1</sup>H environments.
> - 1,4-dimethylbenzene is the most symmetric, with two planes of symmetry. All four ring C–H groups are equivalent, and the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent. This gives 3 <sup>13</sup>C environments and 2 <sup>1</sup>H environments.
> 
> As a general rule, the more symmetric the molecule, the fewer NMR peaks it produces.

parts.problemMd:
Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is added as a standard reference chemical when obtaining an NMR spectrum.

i) State the structural formula of TMS.

[1]

ii) State two reasons why TMS is suitable for use as a standard reference chemical in NMR spectroscopy.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The structural formula of TMS is:
> 
> - Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two reasons why TMS is suitable as a standard reference chemical:
> 
> Any **two** from (1 mark for each point):
> 
> - Volatile / has a low boiling point
> - Non-toxic
> - Inert / chemically unreactive
> - Produces a single peak (all 12 hydrogen atoms / all four carbon atoms are in the same environment)
> - Its peak appears far to the right (upfield) / far from most other peaks so it does not overlap with the sample
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), TMS is a silicon atom bonded to four methyl groups. Its structural formula is Si(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>. You can also write it as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>Si.
> 
> For part (ii), you need any two distinct reasons. The most commonly tested are:
> 
> - TMS produces a single, sharp peak because all 12 protons (and all four carbons) are equivalent by symmetry.
> - Its peak appears at 0 ppm, well to the right of almost all organic compound peaks, so there is no overlap with the sample.
> - TMS is volatile, so it can be easily removed from the sample after analysis.
> - TMS is inert and does not react with the sample.
> 
> Note that TMS gives a signal of zero on both the <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C NMR scales. All other peaks are measured as shifts relative to TMS.

parts.problemMd: State the number of peaks in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of 1,3-dichlorobenzene.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of peaks in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of 1,3-dichlorobenzene is:
> 
> - 4 / four **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To determine the number of <sup>13</sup>C environments in 1,3-dichlorobenzene, draw the structure and look for a vertical plane of symmetry. The plane passes through the two chlorine-bearing carbons (C1 and C3) and the carbon directly opposite (C5 or C2, depending on numbering).
> 
> With this symmetry:
> 
> - C1 and C3 are equivalent (both carry Cl)
> - C2 (between the two Cl groups) is unique
> - C4 and C6 are equivalent
> - C5 (directly opposite C2) is unique
> 
> This gives four distinct <sup>13</sup>C environments, so four peaks.
> 
> A common mistake is to count all six carbons separately and give 6 peaks. Always look for the symmetry axis before counting.

parts.problemMd:
i) Deduce the number of peaks that would be present in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of ethylbenzene, shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Skeletal formula of ethylbenzene with one aromatic ring carbon labelled with an asterisk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-3-carbon-13-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/014-skeletal-formula-of-ethylbenzene-with-one-aromat.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

[1]

ii) Use the Data Booklet to state the <sup>13</sup>C chemical shift range, δ / ppm, for the carbon atom labelled with an asterisk (*) in Fig. 1.1.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The number of peaks in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of ethylbenzene is:
> 
> - 6 / six **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The <sup>13</sup>C chemical shift range for the asterisked carbon is:
> 
> - 110–160 ppm **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i), ethylbenzene has an ethyl group (–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) attached to a benzene ring. To count the six environments:
> 
> - The CH<sub>3</sub> carbon: 1 environment
> - The CH<sub>2</sub> carbon next to the ring: 1 environment
> - The ring carbon bonded to the ethyl group (C1): 1 environment
> - The two ring C–H groups adjacent to C1 (C2 and C6, equivalent by symmetry): 1 environment
> - The two ring C–H groups at C3 and C5 (equivalent by symmetry): 1 environment
> - The ring C–H at C4 (directly opposite the ethyl group): 1 environment
> 
> Total: 6 environments, giving 6 peaks.
> 
> For part (ii), the asterisk is on one of the ring carbons. The Data Booklet gives a shift of 110–160 ppm for sp<sup>2</sup> alkene or arene carbons. This is the range to quote.

parts.problemMd:
Compound **A** is an isomer of dinitrobenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.

Part of the mass spectrum of **A** is shown in Fig. 2.2.

![Mass spectrum of compound A showing a fragment ion peak at m/e = 76](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-a-level-chemistry-25/37-analytical-techniques/37-3-carbon-13-nmr-spectroscopy/assets/012-mass-spectrum-of-compound-a-showing-a-fragment-i.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

State the formula of the fragment ion responsible for the peak at *m/e* = 76 in Fig. 2.2.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The formula of the fragment ion responsible for the peak at *m/e* = 76 is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The positive charge must be shown. C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub> without a charge is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A fragment ion is produced when a molecule loses one or more atoms or groups after ionisation. The *m/e* value tells you the mass-to-charge ratio of the fragment.
> 
> Dinitrobenzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) has *M*<sub>r</sub> = (6 x 12) + (4 x 1) + (2 x 14) + (4 x 16) = 168. The peak at *m/e* = 76 is well below the molecular ion, so it is a fragment, not the intact molecule.
> 
> Benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) has *M*<sub>r</sub> = 78. Losing two hydrogen atoms gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub> with mass 76. The fragment ion is therefore C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.
> 
> Always include the positive charge on any ion in a mass spectrum. Missing this is one of the most common ways to lose a mark on this type of question.

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

Compound **A** is an isomer of dinitrobenzene, C~6~H~4~N~2~O~4~.

The three structural isomers of dinitrobenzene are: 1,2-dinitrobenzene, 1,3-dinitrobenzene, and 1,4-dinitrobenzene.

The <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of compound **A** contains exactly four peaks.

Deduce which of the three isomers drawn in **(b)** is compound **A**. Explain your reasoning by stating the number of peaks expected in the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectra of the other two isomers.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Deducing the identity of compound A from the <sup>13</sup>C NMR data:
> 
> - Compound **A** is 1,3-dinitrobenzene **[1 mark]**
> - 1,2-dinitrobenzene would produce exactly 3 peaks in its <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum **[1 mark]**
> - 1,4-dinitrobenzene would produce exactly 2 peaks in its <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To identify which isomer has four <sup>13</sup>C peaks, count the carbon environments in each structure by looking for lines of symmetry:
> 
> - 1,2-dinitrobenzene has one plane of symmetry between the two NO<sub>2</sub>-bearing carbons. This gives 3 unique <sup>13</sup>C environments.
> - 1,3-dinitrobenzene has one plane of symmetry through the carbon between the two NO<sub>2</sub> groups. This gives 4 unique environments, matching compound A.
> - 1,4-dinitrobenzene has two planes of symmetry. This gives only 2 unique environments.
> 
> For the first mark, just state which isomer compound A is. The next two marks require you to justify by accounting for the other two isomers. Showing your reasoning is essential here.

parts.problemMd:
An unknown alcohol was analysed and found to contain 64.9% carbon, 13.5% hydrogen and the rest oxygen.

The molar mass of the alcohol is 74.12 g mol<sup>-1</sup>.

Calculate the empirical formula and the molecular formula of the unknown alcohol. Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the molecular formula of the unknown alcohol:

- Calculate the percentage of oxygen:

% O = 100 − 64.9 − 13.5 = 21.6%

- Calculate the moles of each element per 100 g:

moles of C = $\frac{64.9}{12.0}$ = 5.41

moles of H = $\frac{13.5}{1.0}$ = 13.5

moles of O = $\frac{21.6}{16.0}$ = 1.35

**[1 mark]**

- Divide by the smallest value (1.35) to find the atom ratio C : H : O = 4 : 10 : 1

- The empirical formula is:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the empirical formula mass:

empirical formula mass = (4 × 12.0) + (10 × 1.0) + 16.0

empirical formula mass = 74.0 g mol<sup>-1</sup>

- This matches the given molar mass, so the molecular formula is:

**Final answer:** **C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**10**</sub>**O**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correctly calculating the moles of C, H, and O
> 
> 1 mark for correct empirical formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O
> 
> 1 mark for correct molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O
> 
> Allow molar mass of 74.12 g mol<sup>-1</sup> as given; accept *M*<sub>r</sub> = 74

> **[exam-tip]**
> The percentage of oxygen is not given directly, so you must calculate it first:
> 
> 100 − 64.9 − 13.5 = 21.6%.
> 
> Divide all mole values by the smallest (1.35) to get the whole number ratio C : H : O = 4 : 10 : 1.
> 
> Since the empirical formula mass (74.0) matches the given molar mass (74.12 g mol<sup>-1</sup>), the empirical formula and molecular formula are the same: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O.
